caption: External slitlamp photograph of the right eye with magnified iris lesion (blue arrowheads) (A) and fundus photograph of the right eye (B).
scenario: A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

options.A: Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
options.B: Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
options.C: Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
options.D: Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED

answer: Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED
distractors: Ask about low back pain and order HLA-B27 testing
Ask about oral ulcers and perform fluorescein angiography
Ask about tattoos and order chest computed tomography to evaluate for lymphadenopathy
explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

caption: A, The anterior segment of the right eye revealed a clear cornea, iris with an ectropion uvea, prominent vascularization, and an irregularly shaped pupil, (arrowheads). The lens exhibited a posterior subcapsular cataract. B, Examination of the posterior pole demonstrated a triangular-shaped fold in the macula, accompanied by diffuse, shallow subretinal fluid (arrowheads).
scenario: An 11-day-old boy was referred for evaluation of right eye leukocoria. Pregnancy and delivery were unremarkable. Examination of the right eye showed fix and follow visual acuity. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the pupil was irregular, with a posterior subcapsular cataract. Following dilation, elongated ciliary processes were visible. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Fundus evaluation of the right eye was limited by lens opacity; however, a yellow, vascularized membrane was seen over the macula extending toward the optic nerve. Ultrasound confirmed findings (axial lengths: OD, 16.6 mm; OS, 18.6 mm). A diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) was made (Figure 1). To clear the visual axis, a lensectomy and vitrectomy via a limbal approach were performed at age 13 days. During hyaloid removal, peripheral traction with subretinal fluid was noted. Perfluoro-n-octane (PFO) was used to stabilize the retina, followed by endolaser photocoagulation. Air-fluid exchange was performed, PFO was removed, and 16% sulfur hexafluoride was used as tamponade. On follow-up, small PFO bubbles were seen in the vitreous and subretinal space outside the macula. The retina remained attached.

options.A: Return to the operating room immediately for retained PFO removal
options.B: Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities
options.C: Return later for secondary lens placement with concurrent PFO removal
options.D: Initiate corticosteroid drops to aid PFO absorption

answer: Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities
distractors: Return to the operating room immediately for retained PFO removal
Return later for secondary lens placement with concurrent PFO removal
Initiate corticosteroid drops to aid PFO absorption
explanation: Retained PFO in the vitreous and subretinal space after retinal surgery B. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

caption: A, External photograph at first presentation demonstrating an inferonasal granular white opacity without overlying epithelial defect, deep vessels in the corneal stroma, and associated corneal thickening. B, Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) showing hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening.
scenario: A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected interstitial keratitis of the right eye. He noted progressive blurry vision but denied eye pain or antecedent trauma. Visual acuity on presentation was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed a 5-mm inferonasal granular white opacity in the anterior corneal stroma without overlying epithelial defect. There were deep vessels visible in the anterior corneal stroma and Descemet membrane folds (Figure 1A). The remainder of the anterior segment was unremarkable. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography demonstrated a hyperreflective infiltrate in the area of the corneal opacity with associated corneal thickening (Figure 1B). Dilated fundus examination did not reveal any vitritis or retinal findings. Examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Given the positive HSV1 and HSV2 IgG and unremarkable preliminary autoimmune and infectious workup, the patient was given topical corticosteroids and oral valaciclovir for presumed herpetic interstitial keratitis.1,2His corneal opacity persisted despite this treatment.

options.B: Refer to rheumatology for additional autoimmune workup
options.C: Perform a corneal biopsy

answer: Perform a corneal biopsy
distractors: Refer to rheumatology for additional autoimmune workup
explanation: C. Perform a corneal biopsy Corneal scraping and culture were not performed, given the intact corneal epithelium and lack of antecedent trauma or pain (option D). Given positive HSV antibodies and negative ANCA, ANA, and anti-CCP, there was low suspicion for an autoimmune etiology, and referral to rheumatology was deferred (option B). A diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis was not performed, given the lack of anterior chamber inflammation (option A). A corneal biopsy was performed (option C), which showed a few keratinocytes as well as corneal edema and inflammation without deposits, granulomatous inflammation, or infectious organisms. The patient continued topical corticosteroids. Despite treatment, the patient re-presented with necrotizing scleritis and anterior segment neovascularization (Figure 2). Broad additional workups were performed in conjunction with rheumatology, including 2 additional corneal and scleral biopsies (without evidence of amyloid, infection, or neoplasia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate/C-reactive protein, fluorescein angiogram, carotid ultrasound (to evaluate for ocular ischemic syndrome), corneal scraping and culture, and hepatitis and HIV serologies, all of which were unrevealing, and the sclerokeratitis was attributed to an undifferentiated autoimmune process. Over the course of the next few months, the patient was stabilized receiving high-dose oral prednisone and rituximab. Eight months after initial presentation, visual acuity acutely worsened to light perception, and the patient developed a new afferent pupillary defect in the right eye with ptosis and limitations in upgaze and adduction. Magnetic resonance imaging at that time demonstrated asymmetric enhancement of the tendinous portion of the right inferior rectus. B-scan ultrasound was remarkable for choroidal effusions with overlying retinal detachment. He underwent biopsy of the sclera and orbit, which, along with genetic sequencing, revealed conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma (Figure 2, inset). After diagnosis, the original sclerocorneal biopsy underwent additional sectioning, and a single distal section with a few atypical cells was detected. These stained positive for p40, which was also expressed in the tumor. This case represents a rare presentation of conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, masquerading as interstitial keratitis. Previously termed mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the ocular surface, conjunctival adenosquamous carcinoma, this tumor falls under the headingocular surface squamous cell neoplasia(OSSN).3This tumor is relatively rare, and to our knowledge, this was the first case of the tumor masquerading as interstitial keratitis.4There have been a few reports of OSSN masquerading as sclerokeratitis.5Interestingly, the majority of these cases, including the one case of OSSN presenting as interstitial keratitis, were definitively diagnosed as squamous cell carcinoma on the first biopsy.5-9 The patient’s immunosuppression was stopped, and the case was presented to tumor board. Orbital exenteration was recommended given the orbital extension of the malignancy, followed by intensity-modulated radiation therapy and adjuvant immunotherapy. The patient continues to have close follow-up for the first 2 years to monitor for recurrence, and recently, a metastasis to the abdominal muscles was discovered.10This case demonstrates the importance of revisiting a broad differential diagnosis if the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy and the importance of communication with pathology, including requesting additional sectioning in atypical cases.

caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
scenario: A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

options.C: Recommend for strabismus surgery
options.D: Reevaluate with MRI of the brain and orbit in 6 months

answer: Treat with carbamazepine
distractors: Reevaluate with MRI of the brain and orbit in 6 months
explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

caption: Red-free fundus photographs demonstrating large serous detachments and deep subretinal lesions (arrowheads) with optical coherence tomography B-scan confirming the detachment. A, Right eye. B, Left eye.
scenario: A 19-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilateral retinal detachments. His visual acuity with correction on a Snellen chart was 20/400 and 20/500 in the right and left eyes, respectively. Anterior examination revealed no anterior chamber cells and well-dilated iris with clear lens in both eyes. Posterior examination showed no vitreous cells, hyperemic and elevated discs, macular edema, and large inferior serous detachments with deep, creamy lesions throughout the posterior pole in both eyes (Figure). No retinal breaks were observed in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal and intraretinal fluid in the macula of both eyes, with a subfoveal bacillary detachment, ie, a splitting at the level of the inner segments of the photoreceptors. B-scan ultrasound confirmed retinal detachments in both eyes with no choroidal masses or detachment. Medical history included attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder, for which he took dextroamphetamine (Adderall) since childhood. The patient noted that vision was progressively worsening starting 1 week prior to presentation, during which time he was recovering from an upper respiratory tract illness and diarrhea that self-resolved. Review of systems was otherwise negative for any headache, altered mental status, chest pain, tinnitus, urinary issues, or trauma prior to presentation.

options.B: Send for infectious and inflammatory laboratory workup and start oral prednisone
options.C: Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel
options.D: Perform bilateral pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle for retinal detachment repair

answer: Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel
distractors: Send for infectious and inflammatory laboratory workup and start oral prednisone
Perform bilateral pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle for retinal detachment repair
explanation: C. Check blood pressure and obtain complete blood cell count and metabolic panel Following the patient’s initial presentation, he was found to have a blood pressure of 178/104. Basic laboratory work collected along with laboratory tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme with chest radiography were all negative except for a creatine level of 19.12 mg/dL. Given the patient’s fundus examination results and concern for elevated blood pressure, the patient was sent to the emergency department and admitted for hypertensive emergency and kidney failure (answer C). As the patient’s underlying etiology of kidney failure was investigated, his blood pressure was controlled, resulting in resolution of the serous detachments and subretinal fluid within the macula. Extensive workup including plasma and urinary metanephrines, kidney biopsy, and abdominal imaging have yet to yield an etiology. This patient’s age, relative acute onset, and lack of medical history make this an atypical presentation. Hypertensive chorioretinopathy may often be seen in younger patients as opposed to hypertensive retinopathy alone.1Along with the features of hypertensive retinopathy, such as nerve fiber layer infarcts, exudates, and arterial-venous nicking due to arterial thickening and subsequent venous compression, Elschnig spots (focal pale areas of choroidal nonperfusion) are often only seen in hypertensive chorioretinopathy secondary to retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal ischemia.2Bilateral serous retinal detachments are rare but reported in cases of malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, and hemolysis with elevated liver enzymes and low platelet syndrome.3Bacillary detachments can be seen in inflammatory disease and hypertensive chorioretinopathy.4,5The subretinal fluid is thought to be secondary to chronic choroidal ischemia leading to capillary dysregulation and decreased Na–K-ATPase activity.6 In the context of bilateral exudative detachments and prodromal episode, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) was considered (answer B).7However, the lack of inflammation and the absence of choroidal and retinal pigment epithelium undulations on OCT made this diagnosis less likely.8It is important to note that intraocular inflammation is not required for diagnosis of VKH in the presence of ocular findings such as disc hyperemia and exudative retinal detachments.9Careful attention to OCT imaging was important to rule out VKH and avoid high-dose corticosteroids in this patient, which may have worsened his blood pressure. Given the patient’s underlying etiology, immediate observation (answer A) or surgery (answer D) would not have been indicated. During his hospitalization, the patient’s blood pressure improved to systolic less than 140 with medication. Kidney biopsy revealed severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and thrombotic microangiopathy without any underlying etiology, and he started hemodialysis. Twelve weeks following presentation, his vision had improved to best-corrected visual acuity of 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye with resolution of his serous detachments. This case highlights the importance of systemic hypertension as a cause of bilateral serous retinal detachments, even in patients who are younger, previously healthy, and without more superficial signs of hypertensive retinopathy. Prompt workup and treatment are important to reduce the chance of short-term and long-term morbidity and mortality from uncontrolled hypertension.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of 2.5 × 3.0-mm nodule with telangiectasia 5 to 6 mm from the limbus, with a black arrowhead pointing to the nodule.
scenario: A 69-year-old female with a history of ulcerative colitis developed a bulbar conjunctival nodule in her left eye that was noted incidentally during an oculoplastic evaluation for dermatochalasis and eyelid herniation. She reported accompanying symptoms of bilateral eye fatigue, burning, and irritation. The patient did not report any other ocular symptoms. Visual acuity was 20/40 in the left eye and hand motion in the right eye due to a prior retinal detachment. A slitlamp examination revealed a 2.5 × 3.0-mm nodule with telangiectasia 5 to 6 mm from the limbus at the 10:00 position (Figure 1). No foreign body was found. The patient did not report fever, night sweats, or recent weight loss. Medical history was significant for ulcerative colitis, type 2 diabetes, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hypertension, and glaucoma in her right eye. At the time of presentation, her glaucoma was stable with intraocular pressure of 12 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. Current medications included latanoprost nightly in her left eye and ophthalmic prednisone 2 to 3 times per day in her right eye. Family history was negative for cancer. Social history was notable for being from Durango, Mexico, and negative for smoking or alcohol.

options.C: Perform an excisional biopsy
options.D: Observe and follow up in 3 months

answer: Perform an excisional biopsy
distractors: Observe and follow up in 3 months
explanation: C. Perform an excisional biopsy Excisional biopsy (C) is the optimal choice for this patient, as it allows for definitive histopathological examination of the nodule, particularly considering the patient’s history of ulcerative colitis and the presence of telangiectasia. Initiating topical mitomycin C (A) may be less appropriate, as it typically is used for confirmed ocular surface neoplasia, and using it without a definitive diagnosis could lead to inappropriate treatment and delay proper management. Starting systemic corticosteroids (B) usually is not ideal without clear evidence of systemic inflammation or an acute flare of ulcerative colitis and could mask the underlying condition. Finally, observing and following up in 3 months, while not an unreasonable option given the patient’s lack of symptoms, risks delaying the diagnosis of a potentially serious condition, such as a malignant neoplasm. Given the ease of an excisional biopsy and its ability to provide an immediate and accurate diagnosis, option C is likely the most appropriate approach. The biopsy revealed a monoclonal CD5+ small B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, favoring small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry showed CD20+ cells with co-expression of CD5, CD43, and BCL2, and negative results for CD3, CD10, BCL1, and SOX11. CD23 expression was noted in rare cells. Ophthalmic adnexal lymphoma (OAL) is the most common malignant neoplasm involving the ocular adnexa and representing 11% to 24% of all ocular tumors. Primary OALs are rare, accounting for 8% of extranodal lymphomas, and as many as 20% primary conjunctival lymphomas may develop into systemic disease over time, although this may be months or even years later.1-3The most common subtypes include extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) (35%-80%), followed by follicular lymphoma (approximately 20%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (approximately 8%).4Ocular adnexal SLL are rarer, with few reported cases.5,6 While less is known about ocular SLL specifically, predisposing factors for OAL, specifically MALT and DLBCL, include autoimmune conditions (eg, Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus erythematosus), immune deficiency or dysfunction, infectious etiologies (Chlamydiaspp andHelicobacter pylori), and prior radiation exposure.7-9This patient had a history of ulcerative colitis, which may bolster the link between autoimmune disease and conjunctival lymphoma. Treatment of OAL primarily depends on the extent of periocular or systemic involvement. For localized disease, complete surgical resection or external localized beam radiation therapy is often used. However, ocular SLL has an increased risk of extranodal metastases on presentation.5,6In these cases, therapy is not standardized; however, rituximab is commonly used, particularly if the tumor is large, infiltrative, and nonresectable. In our case, a complete excisional biopsy was performed with no evidence of recurrence. Nonetheless, long-term follow up is crucial, as patients with OAL and prior CLL or SLL demonstrated an increased incidence in both hematologic and solid secondary primary malignant neoplasms.10 Following a complete excisional biopsy, follow-up visits revealed no recurrence of ocular disease and good visual acuity (20/32) in the left eye. The patient was referred to hematology, and subsequent positron emission tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging orbits on last follow-up 8 months after excisional biopsy revealed no signs of systemic malignant neoplasm.

caption: A, Right eye fluorescein angiogram (FA) with insets of the computed tomography (CT) imaging of intracranial calcifications. B, Left eye fundus photograph with FA shown (lower left inset) and optical coherence tomography infrared image and B scan of chorioretinal lesions nasal to the optic nerve (lower right inset).
scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

options.A: Sulfamethoxazole, 800 mg, and trimethoprim, 160 mg, by mouth twice daily for 14 days
options.B: Serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites
options.C: Corticosteroids, 60 mg prednisone equivalent, by mouth daily

answer: Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies
distractors: Sulfamethoxazole, 800 mg, and trimethoprim, 160 mg, by mouth twice daily for 14 days
Serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites
Corticosteroids, 60 mg prednisone equivalent, by mouth daily
explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

caption: Fundus appearance at initial presentation with ultrasonography B scan (insert) and optical coherence tomography (OCT).
scenario: A 13-year-old male individual was referred to the ocular oncology service for evaluation of an optic nerve mass in the left eye. He reported decreased central vision in the left eye over the previous 2 to 3 weeks associated with mild conjunctival hyperemia and occasional eye pain. Peripheral vision was subjectively intact. He had no relevant medical history, no recent changes in health, no recent history of travel outside the country, and no family history of childhood cancer. Examination revealed an uncorrected visual acuity of 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers at 2 ft in the left eye without improvement on pinhole, normal intraocular pressures, and unremarkable anterior segment findings in both eyes. In the left eye, there was an afferent pupillary defect, a few vitreous cells that did not limit the view of the retina or optic nerve, and a fluffy-appearing, white, elevated optic nerve lesion associated with a small peripapillary hemorrhage, peripapillary subretinal fluid extending into the macula and inferiorly, and scattered white lesions in the inferior retinal periphery (Figure 1). Examination of the right eye was unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion involving the left optic disc 1.9 mm in height associated with subretinal fluid and symmetric retrobulbar optic nerve size bilaterally. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits showed a 3-mm enhancing nodule of the left optic disc but was otherwise unremarkable.

options.A: Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies
options.B: Obtain a vitreous sample for diagnostic studies
options.C: Pediatric oncology consultation

answer: Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies
distractors: Obtain a vitreous sample for diagnostic studies
explanation: A. Obtain infectious and inflammatory serologic studies The initial differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory etiologies of an optic nerve mass with signs of optic neuropathy. Neoplastic causes could include optic nerve infiltration by leukemia or lymphoma, anterior extension of a retrobulbar optic nerve tumor, metastasis, vascular tumors, astrocytic hamartoma, uveal melanoma, and retinoblastoma.1Toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and fungal infections may also present as posterior white masses. Given the relatively acute onset of decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, vitritis, and serous macular detachment (Figure 1), an infectious or inflammatory etiology was suspected. Results of serologic tests for syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, andToxocara caniswere normal, butB henselaeimmunoglobulin G titers were markedly elevated (>1:1024). Given the initial diagnostic uncertainty, oncology consultation (choice C) and admission for steroids (choice D) would have been premature. Had initial noninvasive testing been unrevealing, a vitreous biopsy (choice B) may have been considered; however, this would not have led to the diagnosis ofB henselaeneuroretinitis, which is diagnosed clinically with supportive serologic testing. Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

caption: A, Fundus photographs of the left eye and the right eye (inset) showed optic disc pallor with blurred disc margins. The left eye had discontiguous blood flow in the superior retinal vessels (arrowheads). B, Fundus fluorescein angiography of the left eye showed microaneurysms at both the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina.
scenario: A 14-year old girl presented with sudden painless vision decline in the left eye for 5 days, without vision decline in the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU 6 months earlier. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

options.A: Perform diagnostic anterior chamber and/or vitreous tap
options.C: Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging

answer: Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging
distractors: Perform diagnostic anterior chamber and/or vitreous tap
explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
scenario: A Hispanic woman in her 40s was referred for an asymptomatic epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Ocular history included amblyopia of the left eye. Medical history included chronic neuropathy, ataxia, and myelopathy of unknown etiology for which she was followed up by a neurologist. Family history was positive for consanguinity, but there were no known inherited conditions. Genetic testing showed a homozygous variant of undetermined significance in theSACSgene and a variant of undetermined significance in theSLC5A7gene, but it was inconclusive whether these variants were related to her systemic conditions. Review of systems was otherwise negative. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Fundus examination revealed prominent peripapillary retinal nerve fibers with papillomacular bundle fine striae and slightly blunted foveal light reflex. There was also an irregular sheen of the nasal macula in both eyes, greater in the left eye (Figure 1). Axial length was 22.93 mm in the right eye and 22.10 mm in the left eye, with anterior chamber depth of 3.44 mm and 3.37 mm in the right and left eye, respectively.

options.B: Obtain optical coherence tomography of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer
options.C: Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling

answer: Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)
distractors: Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling
explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

caption: External photograph of right upper eyelid lesions. Examination of the patient’s right upper eyelid on presentation demonstrated a central lesion with thickening of the margin and an ulcerated and erythematous nodule near the medial canthus.
scenario: A 75-year-old woman presented with a history of enlarging, erythematous right upper eyelid lesions. She reported approximately 3 months of symptoms, with initial development of a single erythematous lesion along the eyelid margin. The lesion had previously been evaluated by another practitioner who diagnosed a hordeolum and prescribed erythromycin ointment and warm compresses. However, the lesion became progressively larger with development of a second medial lesion over the ensuing 2 months, prompting referral. She denied pain, trauma, and prior skin cancer. Her medical history was notable for essential thrombocythemia (ET) with calreticulin (CALR) gene variation. Her ocular history was notable for an upper eyelid blepharoplasty 20 years prior but was otherwise unremarkable. Examination of the right upper eyelid demonstrated a central lesion with a thickened eyelid margin, madarosis, and inspissated glands, and a medial nodular and erythematous lesion with overlying ulceration (Figure 1). There was minimal tenderness to palpation. There was no proptosis, and her extraocular muscle movements were full. There was mild conjunctival injection of the right eye without any conjunctival lesions. The remainder of her ocular examination was unremarkable.

options.C: Oral antibiotics

answer: Biopsy of eyelid lesions
explanation: ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma B. Biopsy of eyelid lesions Despite initial treatment for suspected hordeolum, the patient’s eyelid lesions progressively enlarged with new madarosis and ulceration. This raised concern for malignancy including sebaceous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, and squamous cell carcinoma, prompting biopsy (option B) as the next step. Intralesional corticosteroid injection for acute chalazion (option A), oral antibiotics for preseptal cellulitis (option C), and oral corticosteroids for inflammatory disease (option D) were not indicated given the clinical presentation and concern for malignancy. Histopathology demonstrated medium cells with horseshoe nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and mitotic figures that were CD30+, Ki67+, and ALK−, consistent with ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) (Figure 2). Initial systemic imaging showed no systemic involvement, leading to a diagnosis of primary cutaneous ALCL. Primary cutaneous ALCL is a CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder that may present as rapidly growing localized lesions in the face, trunk, or extremities.1It may be classified as ALK+ and ALK− based on presence of ALK-fusion proteins, with ALK− ALCL typically having worse prognosis due to delayed diagnosis or poor response to treatment.2,3Treatment options include CHOP chemotherapy (ie, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone), radiotherapy, or surgical resection.1 Eyelid lymphoma is overall rare, composing 5% of ocular adnexal lymphomas, and tends to be of B-cell origin.4,5ALCL involving the eyelid is very uncommon, with fewer than 25 reported cases.5,6Its infrequent presentation often leads to misdiagnosis as other periorbital pathology, such as chalazion or squamous cell carcinoma, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment.6Concerning features of progression despite treatment, development of new lesions, madarosis, or ulceration warrant biopsy. The patient’s history of ET, a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm, may have increased the risk of ALCL. ET is associated with increased risk of secondary hematological malignancies and solid tumors.7ALK− ALCL associated with ET is rare, with only 1 prior report of central nervous system ALK− ALCL occurring in a patient with ET without skin or eyelid involvement.8ET may potentially increase the risk of developing ALCL due to abnormalities of the JAK-STAT pathway.9This patient had a variant in theCALRgene, which is involved in this pathway and may deregulate hematopoietic stem cell clonal expansion while disrupting natural immunosurveillance.9Physicians should consider malignancy in persistent or enlarging eyelid lesions, especially in patients with hematological conditions such as ET. Prompt biopsy may lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment, potentially improving prognosis in patients with ALK− ALCL. In subsequent oncology visits, the patient developed new skin lesions along her face and body, with repeat biopsy confirming the same ALK− ALCL. She received orbital radiation for her eyelid lesions and started weekly methotrexate, with resolution of her eyelid lesions and marginal improvement of her other lesions. However, further testing revealed central nervous system involvement, suggesting systemic ALCL for which she began systemic and intrathecal chemotherapy. Her eyelid lesions represented the first manifestation of systemic disease, highlighting the importance of vigilance and a high index of suspicion as well as prompt biopsy to facilitate timely diagnosis and treatment.

caption: A, Fundus photograph of the right eye showing an infratemporal exudative retinal detachment. Inset, Choroidal folds in the macula. B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. C, T1 axial orbital magnetic resonance image (MRI) with gadolinium showing the right eye retinal detachment and revealing an enhancing right optic nerve mass.
scenario: A 63-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presented with gradually progressive vision loss in the right eye for the past year. Her visual acuity on presentation was 20/80 OD and 20/25 OS. Anterior examination findings of both eyes were normal with clear posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundus examination of the right eye showed choroidal folds and a macula-involving retinal detachment with no identifiable retinal break and shifting subretinal fluid (Figure 1A). Fundus examination findings in the left eye were normal. Fluorescein angiography did not identify areas of leakage. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve (Figure 1B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a contrast-enhancing area of soft-tissue thickening encircling the right optic nerve (Figure 1C). Serologies for syphilis, Lyme disease, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis were negative. Chest radiographic findings were unremarkable.

options.C: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair
options.D: Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion

answer: Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion
distractors: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair
explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

caption: Red-free scanning laser ophthalmoscopy images revealing extensive retinal vascular sheathing (inset: macular edema seen on optical coherence tomography; fluorescein angiogram revealed late dye leakage).
scenario: A previously healthy 20-year-old Asian woman was hospitalized in the neurology department after experiencing fever, malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, and neck stiffness for 2 weeks. Computed tomography scan results revealed meningoencephalitis. Her systemic inflammatory markers were elevated, including a left-shifted leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 19 610 μL (normal values, 3500-9500 μL), a monocyte count of 900 × 103μL (normal values, 100-600 × 103μL), and normal C-reactive protein level. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were suggestive of viral meningoencephalitis, including elevated protein levels (0.074 g/dL; normal values, 0.015-0.045 g/dL) and increased leucocyte (93 × 106/L; normal values, 0-8 × 106/L). Cytological examination showed an increase in lymphocytes. Intracranial pressure was elevated (>320 mm H2O), and the glucose level was 2.08 mmol/L (normal values, 2.5-4.5 mmol/L). On day 2 of hospitalization, the patient experienced blurred vision in both eyes. Her visual acuity was 20/500 in both eyes. Both eyes had normal pupillary responses, color vision, and intraocular pressures. The results of an anterior chamber examination were unremarkable. The results of scanning laser ophthalmoscopy of both eyes revealed substantial inflammation, including marked disc edema, retinal vein dilation and tortuosity, extensive retinal vascular sheathing (Figure 1). Optical coherence tomography showed vitritis and cystoid macular edema in both eyes. Fluorescein angiogram revealed tortuous dilatation of retinal venous vessels with fluorescence leakage, while the optic disc exhibited hyperfluorescence.

options.C: Initiate immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin
options.D: Intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor

answer: Evaluate for systemic infectious disease
distractors: Initiate immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin
Intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor
explanation: B. Evaluate for systemic infectious disease Administering systemic corticosteroids (choice A) would not be the preferred answer because corticosteroids could suppress the immune response, potentially worsening an undiagnosed infectious process. Initiating immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin (choice C) was not recommended as the next step because intravenous immunoglobulin is typically used for autoimmune or inflammatory conditions rather than primary infectious diseases. Performing an intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (choice D) would not be the next recommended step because there was not proof that the cystoid macular edema was vascular endothelial growth factor driven vs inflammation driven. This patient was diagnosed with bilateral frosted branch angiitis (FBA). FBA may be idiopathic or associated with infections, inflammation, or tumors.1Prior to initiating intraocular or systemic corticosteroid treatment, it is important to exclude infectious diseases. Bacterial cultures of the patient’s cerebrospinal fluid were negative. However, next-generation sequencing of the cerebrospinal fluid indicated Epstein-Barr virus infection. Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with FBA combined with viral meningoencephalitis and treated with ganciclovir and corticosteroids. The termfrosted branch angiitiswas first reported by Ito et al2in 1976 and named after its distinctive retinal appearance. FBA is a rare retinal vasculitis characterized by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of the perivascular space.1,2The co-occurrence of viral meningoencephalitis and FBA is uncommon. FBA predominantly affects young, healthy individuals, with a higher prevalence in female individuals (61%) compared with male individuals (39%). The age at onset has a bimodal distribution, peaking in childhood and between ages 25 and 30 years. Favorable prognoses have been observed in patients undergoing systemic corticosteroid therapy.3Common conditions associated with FBA include cytomegalovirus retinitis, HIV retinitis, and toxoplasma chorioretinitis.4,5However, several systemic diseases may be associated with FBA, including graft vs host disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, Crohn disease, large cell lymphoma, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.6-8The prognosis of FBA is variable,9and may be complicated by macular scarring, retinal neovascularization, or epiretinal membranes. Clinicians, including infectious disease specialists and ophthalmologists, should be aware of the vision-threatening potential of FBA and try to provide timely diagnosis and treatment, potentially reducing the risk of poor ocular outcomes. Patients with FBA may experience a sudden decrease in visual acuity. Severe cases may result in light perception, although some patients maintain 20/20 visual acuity in both eyes.1Fluorescein angiogram may be important to diagnosis FBA, as it can reveal extensive perivascular fluorescein leakage. High-dose corticosteroids have been associated with resolution of retinal abnormalities and improvement of visual acuity in idiopathic FBA. Cases associated with systemic disease typically will need treatment of the primary disease along with corticosteroids for the retina. Some patients may experience relapse if the primary disease recurs.4The extensive vasculitis and sensitivity to short-term corticosteroid treatment suggest that FBA might be a specific vascular reaction triggered by various stimuli, potentially mediated by immune complexes.10 The patient received high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy and ganciclovir. Four weeks later, the FBA and macular edema had disappeared (Figure 2). Seven weeks later, the patient’s visual acuity improved to 20/40 in both eyes. Continued vision loss is likely due to delayed functional recovery compared with structural recovery.
