Importantly, bilateral optic disc edema from ALL does not necessarily imply papilledema (ie, opening pressure on lumbar puncture may be normal) as direct infiltration of the optic nerve(s) can occur by leukemic cells, which prompts the need for radiation.7Unilateral disc edema can also occur and signify ALL relapse. Other diseases can cause a similar presentation. In one report,8a 16-year-old patient with pancytopenia, bilateral disc edema, and an elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture was found to have aplastic anemia secondary to a myeloproliferative leukemia virus oncogene variation (hypocellular marrow without blast cells on bone marrow biopsy). The mechanism for elevated intracranial pressure secondary to ALL is unknown. We postulate that leukemic infiltration of the central nervous system (CNS) reduces cerebrospinal fluid egress causing increased intracranial pressure. This patient’s cytospin level from her lumbar puncture was unremarkable. However, in a comparison of flow cytometry immunophenotyping with cytospin conventional cytomorphology, cytospin sensitivity was only 29%.9Children with ALL are routinely treated with intrathecal chemotherapy regardless of the presence of blast cells in the CSF, owing to high rates of CNS relapse even if no CNS disease is detected at the time of diagnosis (which implies a high likelihood of undetected blast cells).10 The patient started treatment with low-dose (250 mg twice daily) oral acetazolamide to decrease CSF production. She underwent bone marrow biopsy and was diagnosed with B-cell ALL. At her follow-up visit, she retained perfect visual acuity (20/20 OU), and her papilledema had resolved. Soon after, treatment with inotuzumab was initiated for the patient in a clinical trial.

caption: Preoperative appearance of a subconjunctival mass of the left eye after inferior temporal Ahmed valve surgery.
scenario: A 20-year-old woman presented with complaints of blurred vision in her left eye over several weeks and a growing, bulging left-eye mass. Her history was notable for bilateral colobomas involving the iris, optic nerve, and retina; congenital cataracts after lensectomy of the left eye; retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy of the left eye requiring a scleral buckle and silicone oil; and intractable glaucoma in the left eye requiring a superior trabeculectomy, an inferotemporal Ahmed tube implant, and multiple diode cyclophotocoagulation treatments. Because of the high risk of retinal redetachment, the silicone oil was retained throughout the glaucoma procedures. The patient presented 9 months after the last cyclophotocoagulation procedure. At presentation, she was taking dorzolamide-timolol, brimonidine, netarsudil, and latanoprost for her left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and light perception OS. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 11 mm Hg OD and 20 mm Hg OS. Examination of the left eye revealed a large, firm, pink subconjunctival mass inferotemporally near the Ahmed valve (Figure 1). There was a left hypertropia of more than 45° by Hirschberg test. The anterior chamber was deep with fine silicone oil bubbles superiorly. The aphakic left eye revealed a well-positioned tube. Cup-disc ratios were 0.7 OD and 0.8 OS. The retina was centrally attached under silicone oil with a stable peripheral tractional retinal detachment.

options.A: Bleb revision with excision of the mass
options.C: Silicone oil removal from the vitreous cavity
options.D: Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation and removal of the mass and Ahmed valve

answer: Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation and removal of the mass and Ahmed valve
distractors: Bleb revision with excision of the mass
Silicone oil removal from the vitreous cavity
explanation: D. Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation and removal of the mass and Ahmed valve Although neoplasia is in the differential diagnosis of a slow-growing subconjunctival mass (choice B), it is less likely in this case because of the atypical appearance (Figure 1), as well as the temporal relationship of the appearance of the mass after tube-shunt surgery. Silicone oil removal (choice C) was not performed owing to the risk of retinal redetachment. Therefore, choice D was the best option for maximizing both cosmesis and comfort measures because mass excision alone (choice A) would not have minimized further egress of the intraocular emulsified oil through the tube and into the growing subconjunctival mass. Plus, concomitant supplemental diode laser would best preempt future pain owing to uncontrolled high IOPs (choice D). To our knowledge, this is one of the largest subconjunctival silicone oil granulomas described in the literature, and it is a reminder to surgeons that silicone oil can migrate with scleral melt, with globe rupture, through both sutured and unsutured sclerostomies, and with or without a glaucoma implant.1-9Silicone oil migration is more likely when there is no lens, can occur even with inferiorly placed glaucoma implants, and has been reported for both valved and nonvalved implants.2-5Silicone oil migration can present as chemosis, eyelid swelling, an eyelid mass, ptosis, an orbital mass, a nasopharyngeal silicone oil polyp, and/or, as in this case, a subconjunctival mass and strabismus.1-9Silicone oil can also migrate intracranially, with or without an optic nerve pit.8Silicone oil granuloma formation after retina surgery, with or without a history of tube-shunt surgery, should be considered among postoperative complications. In this case, risk factors for oil migration were being aphakic and having a tube. Also, the oil had been in the eye for more than 2 years, and over time, silicone oil tends to emulsify, which facilitates its ability to migrate. Intraoperatively, the subconjunctival mass appeared to be an encapsulated area of scar tissue encased around silicone oil bubbles. The resected episclera and capsule was a 2.5 × 2.1 × 0.5-cm aggregate of multiple fragments of tan-pink soft tissue with histopathologic findings (Figure 2A) showing an exuberant giant cell reaction to nonpolarizable foreign material and round empty vacuoles of varying sizes, similar to other reports.2,3,6-9Postoperatively, silicone oil remained in the posterior segment with an approximate 30% fill. Photographs taken 1 month after surgery (Figure 2B) showed resolving eyelid edema and a well-healing inferior temporal conjunctival peritomy with a desirable cosmetic outcome. The large subconjunctival mass of the left eye is noticeably absent. At the last follow-up 2 months after surgery, the patient’s visual acuity was hand motion OS with an IOP of 15 mm Hg while receiving the same preoperative glaucoma medications. In this case, the potential risks to minimize granuloma formation (eg, earlier oil removal, earlier tube removal, longer tube length) would have not justified the small benefit of preventing a rare event, with only more than a dozen similar cases reported in the literature.

caption: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome–like presentation of multilobulated pockets of subretinal fluid and choroidal thickening and undulations. A, Serous retinal detachment (asterisk). B, Substantial choroidal thickening (asterisk) and undulations and multilobulated subretinal fluid (arrowheads).
scenario: A white man in his early 80s with history of autoimmune pancreatitis, recurrent colon polyps, and benign prostatic hyperplasia developed rapid, painless vision loss of both eyes over a 2-week period 6 months after cataract surgery. Vision was 20/250 OD and 20/60 OS. The anterior segment was unremarkable in either eye, while the posterior segment examination noted 1+ vitreous cell, asteroid hyalosis, and a multilobulated, serous retinal detachment (RD) in the right eye and trace vitreous cell and a multilobulated, serous RD in the left eye. Imaging included B-scan, optical coherence tomography, and fundus autofluorescence, which revealed diffuse choroidal and ciliary body thickening, multifocal pockets of subretinal fluid, and speckled hyperautofluorescence and hypoautofluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1). No poliosis or skin changes were noted. A review of systems was unremarkable, most notably a lack of any pulmonary symptoms. A focused laboratory evaluation identified a significantly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level and antinuclear antibody titer, but serum lysozyme, syphilis, and tuberculosis testing had negative results. To better differentiate between Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome, a lymphoproliferative disorder, or sarcoidosis as the underlying cause of the vitreous inflammation and multilobulated, serous RD in both eyes, a computed tomographic scan was performed. It showed marked lymphadenopathy throughout the mediastinum and diffuse scleral thickening in both eyes. The institute’s radiologists believed these computed tomography findings were nonspecific and could be indicative of either sarcoidosis or intraocular lymphoma.

options.A: Perform a diagnostic vitrectomy in the right eye
options.B: Inject intravitreal antibiotics for endophthalmitis in both eyes
options.C: Perform ciliary body–choroidal biopsy in the right eye
options.D: Treat the patient with systemic steroids for presumed VKH syndrome

answer: Perform ciliary body–choroidal biopsy in the right eye
distractors: Perform a diagnostic vitrectomy in the right eye
Inject intravitreal antibiotics for endophthalmitis in both eyes
Treat the patient with systemic steroids for presumed VKH syndrome
explanation: Biopsy-proven, Harada-like ocular sarcoidosis in both eyes C. Perform ciliary body–choroidal biopsy in the right eye With the patient’s advanced age and inconclusive clinical picture, the diagnosis of a lymphoproliferative disorder vs sarcoidosis was unclear, and a biopsy was considered necessary for definitive diagnosis. With primarily choroidal and ciliary body involvement in both eyes, the sensitivity of a diagnostic vitrectomy for intraocular lymphoma was believed to be insufficient because of the relatively mild vitritis (choice A). Although some advocate a combined pars plana vitrectomy with choroidal biopsy in cases such as this one to increase diagnostic yields, we wanted to avoid, if possible, complications related to operating on an eye with active uveitis (eg, hypotony, inducing rhegmatogenous RD).1The protracted course, unremarkable review of systems, and lack of pain or hypopyon made an underlying infectious etiology unlikely (choice B). Because of the diagnostic dilemma, conflicting treatment algorithms, and risk of future central nervous system involvement with intraocular lymphoma, an incisional flap-based ciliary body–choroidal biopsy was performed in the right eye (choice C). An initial approach with ocular biopsy was favored because of the difficult location of many of the enlarged lymph nodes within the patient’s chest. Systemic corticosteroids were not given until the biopsy could be performed because of the concern that their use may limit diagnostic yield (choice D).2 Pathological changes within the choroid were consistent with sarcoidosis with multiple, multinucleated giant cells and noncaseating granulomas (Figure 2). Because of the enlarged lymph nodes and concern about an additional process, our colleagues performed a biopsy of the lymph nodes; those results were also consistent with sarcoidosis. The patient was given systemic corticosteroids (1 mg/kg with slow taper) and 20 mg of oral methotrexate per week because of ocular and pulmonary involvement.3 This case highlights the importance of a tissue diagnosis in uveitis, especially when the treatment algorithms and prognosis could vary (eg, local and systemic chemotherapeutics for lymphoma vs corticosteroids and immunomodulatory therapy for sarcoidosis).4Furthermore, this patient’s presentation was unusual: an isolated, sarcoid-associated, posterior uveitis is uncommon, reported in only 12% of all cases of ocular sarcoidosis, and only 6% of serous RDs in patients with uveitis can be attributed to sarcoidosis.5,6However, an isolated posterior uveitis associated with sarcoidosis represents the largest portion of patients with severe vision loss attributed to the disease and is a documented risk factor for poor visual outcomes.5,7To complicate matters, VKH syndrome and sarcoidosis may have a similar underlying genetic risk factor, and patients can develop both sequentially.8,9Although multilobulated, serous RDs with intraocular inflammation are most commonly associated with VKH syndrome, intraocular lymphoma and sarcoidosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis. The patient’s systemic corticosteroids were tapered and oral methotrexate continued. Three years later, the serous RDs and choroidal thickening have completely resolved, and his visual acuity has returned to 20/20 OU with good long-term prognosis. He is currently being monitored every 6 months.

caption: Subretinal fluid and choroidal effusions following a laser peripheral iridotomy. A, Fundus photography showed substantial choroidal effusions with overlying serous retinal detachments (asterisk). B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging identified choroidal congestion, thickening, and undulations as well as shallow subretinal fluid.
scenario: A White woman in her 40s was referred to an outside ophthalmologist after developing nausea and a headache following a dilated eye examination. She was found to have narrow angles in both eyes and a laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) was performed in her left eye. Two weeks later she developed flickering photopsias and a temporal scotoma progressing to a “brown tint” of her vision in her left eye. Her vision had decreased in her left eye and macular and optic nerve edema were noted and she was subsequently referred to us. In our clinic, her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/50 OS, and she had normal intraocular pressure, a shallow anterior chamber but open angle in both eyes, a patent LPI in the left eye, and clear crystalline lenses in both eyes. The rest of her anterior segment was unremarkable. The posterior examination was notable for shifting subretinal fluid with choroidal detachments without retinal breaks, inflammation, or optic nerve edema and leopard spotting, while her right eye was unremarkable (Figure, A). Fluorescein angiography was unrevealing, while optical coherence tomography showed shallow subretinal fluid and an irregular and thickened choroid (Figure, B). Ultrasonography showed an axial length of 20.0 mm, thickened sclera, anteriorly rotated ciliary body, and 360° of ciliochoroidal detachments in both eyes but worse in the left eye. Results of a systemic laboratory evaluation for infectious and noninfectious disorders were unremarkable. Systemic corticosteroids failed to resolve the subretinal fluid and her vision declined.

options.A: Repeat LPI in the left eye
options.B: Perform an LPI in the right eye
options.C: Sclerectomy in the left eye
options.D: Perform a clear lens exchange in the left eye

answer: Sclerectomy in the left eye
distractors: Repeat LPI in the left eye
Perform an LPI in the right eye
Perform a clear lens exchange in the left eye
explanation: C. Sclerectomy in the left eye Despite high-dose corticosteroids, vision continued to decline and the choroidal effusions and retinal detachment enlarged in the left eye making a subtle, underlying inflammatory-driven disorder unlikely. With small effusions and shallow anterior chamber in the right eye as well, her presentation was unlikely related to the LPI alone. Prolonged hypotony, malignant hypertension, underlying causes of elevated uveal venous pressure (eg, pulmonary hypertension, arteriovenous fistulas, and Sturge-Weber syndrome), uveal effusion syndrome, and several neoplastic conditions are other underlying etiologies of choroidal effusions. However, this patient’s blood pressure had been within normal limits at multiple measurements, she had no known underlying systemic diseases with an unremarkable echocardiogram and pulmonary function test results, and a thorough review of systems did not raise concern for cancer. Thus, this patient’s presentation was most consistent with idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome. On follow-up, the patient’s intraocular pressure had remained within normal ranges making a repeated LPI in the left eye incorrect as she had not developed angle closure (choice A). Furthermore, her current condition had likely been exacerbated by the original LPI. The response in the left eye also would make choice B potentially dangerous because of concern of instigating a similar set of events in the right eye and not solve the worsening issues within the left eye. While a clear lens exchange (choice D) is an effective solution to narrow angles and a shallow anterior chamber, surgical complications are common in eyes with abnormal sclera.1,2Further, choice D would only address a by-product of the underlying process, narrow angles, and not the disease itself but incur substantial surgical risk making it incorrect.3While a recent randomized trial showed that cataract surgery with concurrent sclerostomy reduced perioperative complications in nanophthalmic eyes including the development of choroidal effusions, the surgeries were performed in eyes that did not already have choroidal effusions.3There are 3 subtypes of uveal effusion syndrome.4Nanophthalmic eyes with hyperopia (type I) and eyes with histologically abnormal sclera but otherwise normal (type II) respond to sclerectomies; however, otherwise normal eyes (type III) do not respond to sclerectomy.4,5This patient with type II idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome needed the underlying pathophysiology addressed, her abnormal and thick sclera, with a 4-quadrant nearly full-thickness sclerectomy (choice C).6The choroidal effusions and serous detachment improved following the procedure but did not fully resolve. Thus, a second 4-quadrant sclerectomy with 2 full-thickness sclerostomies were performed resulting in complete resolution of the choroidal effusions and continued improvement in the serous retinal detachment. This case shows idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome that appears to have been exacerbated by an LPI. Several groups have reported choroidal effusions developing after an LPI and other ocular laser procedures; however, in none of these cases did the patient develop concurrent serous detachments.7,8In a large case series on uveal effusion syndrome and sclerectomies, a single procedure resulted in 83% of eyes with an anatomical success and increased to 96% after a second procedure.5This resulted in visual improvement by 2 or more lines in 56% of eyes, stabilization in 35%, and worsening in only 9%.5Prophylactic sclerectomies should be considered in nanophthalmic eyes or eyes with abnormally thick sclera when ocular surgery is being planned to reduce the risk of developing uveal effusions and serous detachments and the associated vision loss.9 After two 4-quadrant nearly full-thickness sclerectomies, the patient’s choroidal effusions resolved and her serous retinal detachment nearly resolved. Her visual acuity was 20/40 OS at postoperative month 1. In the future, prophylactic sclerectomies in the right eye will be performed once the left eye has stabilized because of continued shallowing of her anterior chamber.

caption: Fundus photograph of both eyes.
scenario: A 49-year-old African American woman with no significant medical history came to the clinic because of abnormal retinal findings and mildly decreased visual acuity. She was told about these same findings 10 years ago but did not have a repeated eye examination until recently by another retina specialist. She reported no family history of retinal diseases. She initially received anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) treatment, but was later referred because of a concern about either the idiopathic or paraneoplastic variant of acute exudative polymorphous vitelliform maculopathy (AEPVM). Initial workup by her primary care physician was unremarkable for malignancy. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/60 OD and 20/50 OS. An anterior segment examination was normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed multiple vitelliform lesions involving the macula and superior macula bilaterally (Figure 1). Fluorescein angiography revealed staining of these lesions with a pseudohypopyon appearance of the central vitelliform lesion in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed hyperreflectance corresponding to the yellow pigment in the vitelliform lesions in the subretinal space. No evidence of a choroidal neovascular membrane was present on examination or imaging.

options.A: Computed tomographic scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
options.C: Genetic testing

answer: Genetic testing
distractors: Computed tomographic scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
explanation: This patient had multifocal Best disease, a variant of Best disease. Best disease is typically an autosomal dominant maculopathy caused by mutations in theBEST1(VMD2) gene, resulting in abnormal lipofuscin accumulation in the macula. These patients typically show symptoms in the first 2 decades of life with a classic “egg yolk” lesion in the central macula. Further retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) thinning and pigment changes arise as this lesion breaks down in the “pseudohypopyon stage,” with corresponding hyperautofluorescence of this pseudohypopyon demonstrated on fundus autofluorescence1,2(Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography demonstrates hyperreflectance corresponding to the lipofuscin in the subretinal space. Eventually all of the yellow pigment may be taken up, leaving behind corresponding atrophic retinal pigment epithelium. Patients typically maintain good BCVA, often 20/30 to 20/40, unless a choroidal neovascular membrane develops. Electroretinography is typically normal, but the electro-oculogram is abnormal with a low ratio of light peak to dark trough (Arden ratio). A less commonly described variation of the disease is known as autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy, related to an autosomal recessive mutation of theBEST1gene on chromosome 11. Examination often reveals diffuse retinal pigment epithelium changes with multifocal whitish or yellowish punctate deposits seen in the macula and mid periphery.3In this patient, the vitelliform lesions were multifocal within the macula, though larger than the lesions seen in autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy. Genetic testing revealed that she was heterozygous for aBEST1gene mutation, suggesting an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Differentiating Best disease from idiopathic and paraneoplastic AEPVM is challenging because of significant overlap on examination and imaging. Idiopathic AEPVM presents bilaterally as serous retinal detachments with vitelliform deposits or bleblike lesions along the arcades; these lesions can regress in the span of months. Patients with paraneoplastic AEPVM may have a history of cancer, especially melanoma orBRAF/MEKinhibitor usage, and may present unilaterally.4,5To date, no patient with AEPVM has shown mutations inBEST1orperipherin/RDS, making genetic testing a highly useful diagnostic tool given the clinical similarities.6 Lesions do not respond to anti-VEGF therapy if no choroidal neovascular membrane is present (choice B). Given the patient’s 10-year history of these ocular lesions without systemic issues, as well as her initial negative workup, whole-body imaging (choice A) and antiretinal antibody testing (choice D) may not need to be the next immediate steps in workup. However, in the absence of an established diagnosis and negative genetic results, whole-body imaging should be pursued to rule out malignancy. Recently, genetic testing via saliva testing has become a reliable and accessible resource that may be more cost-effective and convenient than electrophysiologic testing.7As more gene therapies become available for patients, genetic testing will have a greater influence on management and prognosis.8In this case, genetic testing provided a definitive diagnosis that helped rule out a potentially life-threatening diagnosis. The patient was reassured that her condition was not paraneoplastic nor immediately blinding. Whole-body imaging was performed at a later time for unrelated medical issues, and no occult malignancy was found. She is being evaluated semiannually with ancillary OCT and fundus autofluorescence.

scenario: A man aged 57 years presented to the emergency department after 3 weeks of bilateral periorbital pain and swelling with associated headaches. He reported diplopia and pain with extraocular movement. There were no constitutional, dermatologic, or neurologic symptoms. The patient endorsed a history of Crohn disease, and his medication had been changed from infliximab to ustekinumab 6 weeks prior owing to persistent intestinal inflammation. Clinical examination revealed bilateral periorbital edema, diplopia with decreased abduction in the right eye and decreased adduction in the left eye, chemosis, proptosis, and conjunctival hyperemia (Figure 1A). Visual acuity and neurologic and fundus examination findings were otherwise normal with no sign of optic neuropathy. Laboratory investigation showed a mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate but was otherwise unremarkable. Levels of antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, IgG4 levels, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, thyrotropin, and thyroglobulin receptor antibody were all normal. Orbital computed tomography showed moderate bilateral lateral rectus muscle enlargement and mild enlargement of the left medial rectus muscle (Figure 1B) with mild, homogenous enhancement. Prednisone was started at a dose of 60 mg daily, and the patient’s symptoms resolved; however, eye pain immediately recurred when weaning the prednisone. An orbitotomy with lateral rectus biopsy was performed, which showed a prominent chronic inflammatory process with infiltrates composed of a mixture of epithelioid histiocytes and small-sized lymphocytes associated with severe muscle atrophy. Prednisone was restarted.

options.C: Perform further imaging to exclude a solid-organ primary malignancy
options.D: Perform further thyroid function tests and thyroid imaging

answer: Change therapies for Crohn disease
distractors: Perform further imaging to exclude a solid-organ primary malignancy
Perform further thyroid function tests and thyroid imaging
explanation: Medication-induced orbital myositis secondary to ustekinumab B. Change therapies for Crohn disease The patient had features of a corticosteroid-responsive bilateral orbital myositis (OM). OM was first described in 1903.1It can occur at any age and more commonly affects women.2It commonly presents as painful diplopia or orbital inflammation with chemosis, proptosis, or conjunctival hyperemia. The horizontal recti muscles are most frequently affected, although the superior or inferior recti can also be involved.3The inflammatory process (Figure 2) appears to be mediated by helper T-cell type 1, with significant elevations in interleukin 12, tumor necrosis factor α, and interferon γ.4Diagnosis of OM is based on physical examination and radiologic features excluding other etiologies and may require tissue biopsy when features are atypical or response to corticosteroids is inadequate. Acute idiopathic OM is the most common form of OM and typically affects a single muscle and is corticosteroid responsive. Recurrent OM occurs in 15% of patients and is more common in men. OM is more likely to be recurrent if multiple extraocular muscles are involved on presentation or if there is a lack of response to initial corticosteroid treatment.2,5In such cases, adverse effects from long-term corticosteroids often necessitate the use of alternative maintenance therapy, such as infliximab, rather than continuing corticosteroids indefinitely (option A).6 Autoimmune and infectious causes of OM should be considered in atypical cases and include IgG4-related disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, spondyloarthropathies, vasculitis, Lyme disease, herpes zoster, and cysticercosis. Ocular manifestations occur in 3% of patients with IBD,7although IBD-associated OM is a rare extraintestinal manifestation, which is more commonly bilateral and recurrent.8 Medication-induced OM has been reported, particularly with bisphosphonates and monoclonal antibody therapies, and usually occurs early after commencing treatment. Medication-induced OM improves rapidly with removal of the causative agent9; it usually involves more than 1 extraocular muscle and may have atypical features. Although IBD-associated OM was a possible cause of this patient’s symptoms, the early symptom onset after commencing ustekinumab raised the possibility of medication-induced OM, in which case stopping the potential causative agent is required (option B). To our knowledge, there have been 2 previous cases of OM related to ustekinumab that have been reported on the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Events Reporting System, including in 1 patient with Crohn disease.10 Rarely, OM can be a paraneoplastic phenomenon. In this setting, OM is usually bilateral and affects most or all the extraocular muscles; therefore, paraneoplastic disease would be considered less likely in the presented scenario (option C).8Treatment of the primary lesion typically leads to resolution. OM can be difficult to distinguish from Grave ophthalmopathy; however, the lack of upper eyelid retraction and normal thyroid antibodies would favor OM in this case (option D). Early treatment of OM may prevent extraocular muscle fibrosis and strabismus; therefore, it is important to reach a diagnosis, start corticosteroid treatment, and identify and treat any underlying cause. The patient’s treatment was changed from ustekinumab to vedolizumab for treatment of Crohn disease. In the subsequent 3 months, he was able to successfully wean prednisone without recurrence of eye symptoms.

caption: A, Episcleral and scleral thickening (yellow brackets) adjacent to normal tissue (white brackets) on ultrasound biomicroscopy. B, Retrolenticular plaque (yellow arrowhead) and vitreous debris (white arrowhead) on inferotemporal longitudinal B-scan.
scenario: A 55-year-old man with advanced primary open-angle glaucoma presented with 1 day of decreased vision and eye pain. He had undergone trabeculectomy and 5-fluorouracil injection 1 month prior. On initial examination, his visual acuity was 20/25. He had diffuse conjunctival hyperemia without bleb purulence or leakage and more than 50 cells per high-power field of a 1 × 1-mm area of light on slitlamp biomicroscopy. He was treated for blebitis with topical fortified antibiotics but subsequently developed vitritis. He underwent vitreous tap and injection of vancomycin and amikacin followed by pars plana vitrectomy with bleb revision. Separate vitreous samples from each procedure were sent for Gram stain and bacterial and fungal culture on chocolate and Sabouraud agar with no growth. His eye pain worsened significantly, and ultrasound biomicroscopy showed scleral thickening (Figure 1A). Lab workup for autoimmune scleritis including tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies was negative. He was admitted to the hospital and started intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam treatment. His vision continued to decline to counting fingers because of the development of a dense cataract with retrolenticular plaque (Figure 1B).

options.C: Repeat aqueous or vitreous sampling

answer: Repeat aqueous or vitreous sampling
explanation: Aspergillus fumigatus endophthalmitis and scleritis C. Repeat aqueous or vitreous sampling Patients with postoperative intraocular inflammation require thorough evaluation for infectious causes. Until absence of infection has been established, steroids (choice A) should be used cautiously. Lack of improvement while receiving sufficiently broad antibiotic therapy suggests alternative etiologies rather than inadequate coverage (choice B). When the diagnosis is unclear and vision loss progresses, intraocular fluid testing for atypical organisms, including mycobacteria and fungi, and masquerade syndromes such as lymphoma should be considered (choice C) over continued observation (choice D). An aqueous sample was sent for broad-range bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal polymerase chain reaction, which returned positive forAspergillus fumigatus. The patient started oral voriconazole and high-dose indomethacin treatment and received intravitreal and subconjunctival voriconazole injections. He underwent pars plana vitrectomy with lensectomy and additional intravitreal voriconazole (Figure 2). A dense retrolenticular plaque and multiple vitreous fungal “snowballs” were found intraoperatively; there was no vasculitis or chorioretinitis. Glaucoma filtering surgery creates a permanent pathway between the intraocular and subconjunctival spaces, thereby conferring a lifelong risk of endophthalmitis. Antifibrotic agents including mitomycin C and 5-fluorouracil further increase the endophthalmitis risk.1Fungal involvement is important to consider especially in cases of postsurgical inflammation with poor response to antibiotic therapy. While endogenousAspergillusendophthalmitis presents with chorioretinitis, retinal necrosis, and vascular invasion,2the presentation of exogenousAspergillusendophthalmitis varies depending on primary infection site and can spare the retina.3Fibrinous anterior chamber reaction with hypopyon may occur early and progress to fungal condensation with pupillary or posterior capsular membranes.4 Substantial pain in the setting of fungal endophthalmitis may suggest concurrent scleritis. Aspergillus scleritis occurs most commonly after ocular surgery such as pterygium excision,5but can also occur after glaucoma filtering surgery. Scleral involvement manifests as recurrent abscesses, sectoral or diffuse thickening, or necrosis.5,6 Diagnosis of fungal endophthalmitis requires intraocular fluid sampling with fungal culture. Aqueous aspirates are positive with negative vitreous cultures in about 15% of cases; therefore, both anterior chamber and vitreous samples should be obtained.7If cultures are unrevealing, broad-range polymerase chain reaction  is an emerging diagnostic tool that simultaneously detects viral, bacterial, and fungal material in small-volume samples.7 Intraocular amphotericin B has historically been the first-line therapy for fungal endophthalmitis, but poses the risk of retinal necrosis and often requires repeated injections for adequate effect.3Newer agents such as voriconazole have demonstrated high intraocular penetration and oral bioavailability without vision-threatening adverse effects.8Surgical removal of areas of fungal condensation, closure of filtration sites, and removal of implants are required. Patients with glaucoma may need additional shunt devices after infection resolution for intraocular pressure control. Optimal therapy forAspergillusscleritis has not been established but requires long-term systemic antifungal therapy. Although scleral debridement is occasionally pursued, subconjunctival administration of antifungal agents may be a tissue-sparing approach to treatment. High-dose nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents provide analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects when systemic steroids are contraindicated because of active fungal infection. After 6 weeks of oral voriconazole, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/80 with a +10-diopter lens because of persistent macular edema.

caption: Widefield color image of the left eye of a 49-year-old man with acute loss of vision. There is marked hemorrhagic disc edema with flame hemorrhages emanating from and surrounding the optic nerve.
scenario: A 49-year-old man with a history of diabetes, hypertension, intravenous drug abuse, and multiple sexual partners presented to the emergency department with painless vision loss in both eyes for 10 days, left eye worse than right eye, and photophobia in both eyes. His visual acuity was count fingers OD and 20/70 OS. Intraocular pressure was 20 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS. There were 1+ (10-12 cells/high-power field) anterior chamber cells in both eyes with very hazy posterior pole details in the right eye and minimal vitreous haze in the left eye. There was a hazy view to the posterior pole in the right eye with disc edema and multiple flame hemorrhages surrounding the nerve. Examination of the posterior pole in the left eye revealed partial obstruction of all vessels and a complete halo on the disc with numerous flame hemorrhages emanating from and surrounding the optic nerve, along with a few dot blot hemorrhages within the macula (Figure). His blood pressure was 173/137 mm Hg, but the rest of his vital signs were normal.

options.A: Obtain HIV and syphilis serology results
options.C: Inject intravitreal foscarnet
options.D: Obtain computed tomographic scan of the brain

answer: Obtain HIV and syphilis serology results
distractors: Obtain computed tomographic scan of the brain
explanation: Syphilitic panuveitis and optic neuritis A. Obtain HIV and syphilis serology results In this patient with hemorrhagic optic neuritis and evidence of panuveitis, infection must first be ruled out before initiating any systemic corticosteroids (choice A). A patient with a history of drug use and many sexual partners further supports ruling out an infection, particularly syphilis and HIV. Idiopathic demyelinating optic neuritis is a common cause of optic nerve edema with abnormal visual function in patients younger than 50 years, although it typically does not present with panuveitis.1Therefore, beginning methylprednisolone would not be appropriate without proper systemic workup (choice B). Cytomegalovirus optic neuritis should be on the differential diagnosis for any patient with substantial risk factors for HIV/AIDS, although there were no signs suggestive of cytomegalovirus retinitis on examination and therefore treatment with foscarnet is not appropriate (choice C). Intracranial imaging may be warranted in the evaluation of papilledema, but magnetic resonance imaging of the brain would be more appropriate than computed tomography of the head, as it better detects optic neuritis and cerebrospinal fluid outflow obstructions (choice D).1Additionally, his subsequent blood pressure measurements lowered and his initial reading was felt to be transient in the setting of an emergency visit, and thus, hypertension was not felt to be the causative etiology. Syphilis, tuberculosis, HIV, Lyme disease, andBartonellaare common culprits of infectious optic neuropathies, so a detailed history on sexual practices, drug use, travel history, and exposure to cats should be taken.1Primary syphilis includes a painless chancre; secondary syphilis includes a macular papular rash involving the palms and soles, condylomata lata, and lymphadenopathy; and tertiary syphilis includes gummas, aortitis, and tabes dorsalis. Ocular syphilis can occur at any stage of the syphilitic infection, and its varying, wide range of clinical presentations makes it known as the “great masquerader.”2,3SinceTreponema pallidumcannot be cultured in vitro, the diagnosis of syphilis relies on treponemal and nontreponemal serologic testing. Nontreponemal testing is generally used as an initial screening test, monitoring therapeutic response to treatment, and includes the rapid plasma reagin and Veneral Disease Research Laboratory (VRDL) tests.4However, they may be associated with false-positive results in patients with autoimmune diseases, tuberculosis, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, pregnancy, rickettsia infections, and other spirochetal infections.2Treponemal testing consists of the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption andTreponemamicrohemagglutin assay; since they are highly sensitive and specific for syphilis, they are traditionally used as confirmatory tests after nontreponemal testing, although they cannot be used to assess treatment response.5,6Alternatively, the reverse syphilis testing algorithm begins with a treponemal test followed by a confirmatory nontreponemal test. This algorithm has a higher sensitivity in diagnosing primary and secondary syphilis at 98.3% compared with 72.9% via the traditional pathway.7,8 HIV testing should be pursued in cases of suspected syphilis because of the high incidence of coinfection (20%-70%).6Syphilis and HIV are mandatory reportable diseases in all 50 states. On positive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test results and signs of ocular syphilis (especially with retinal or optic nerve involvement), an infectious disease specialist should be consulted and lumbar puncture should be performed with cerebral spinal fluid VRDL testing with repeated lumbar puncture to monitor for successful treatment.5,9,10The treatment of neurosyphilis is with intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days; in the case of a penicillin allergy, desensitization (recommended), ceftriaxone, doxycycline, or tetracycline are alternatives.3,4The visual outcome after treatment is variable, with syphilis uveitis having the most improvement and optic neuritis having poor visual prognosis.3,5,9 Fundus autofluorescence did not reveal a classic placoid lesion, but his rapid plasma reagin test and syphilis antibody test results were both positive. HIV testing was negative. This patient was treated with intravenous penicillin (after desensitization) and lumbar puncture, which returned a positive VDRL result. The patient returned 1 year later with improvement of visual acuity to 20/40 OU with resolution of his disc edema in both eyes.

caption: Color fundus photograph (A) and optical coherence tomography of the macula (B) illustrating intraretinal and subretinal fluid at the nasal macula. The white line indicates the position of the optical coherence tomography scan.
scenario: A patient with a history of normal-tension glaucoma presented with a blurred spot in the central vision of the right eye. Examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/50 OD, 20/30 OS, and intraocular pressure of 13 mm Hg OU. In the right eye, dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula revealed subretinal fluid and cystoid spaces within the outer nuclear layer and inner nuclear layer in the nasal macula (Figure 1). Results of the left eye fundus examination and macular OCT were normal. In both eyes, the optic cup appeared very deep with a large cup-disc ratio. Five years prior to presentation, the patient started treatment with latanoprost nightly in both eyes for an enlarged cup-disc ratio presumed due to normal-tension glaucoma. At that time, intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS and central corneal thickness was normal. Visual field and OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer were without reproducible defects over 5 years of follow-up. The patient denied a family history of eye disease.

options.C: OCT of the optic nerve head

answer: OCT of the optic nerve head
explanation: C. OCT of the optic nerve head The differential diagnosis of macular fluid includes choroidal neovascularization, central serous chorioretinopathy, myopic foveoschisis, optic pit maculopathy, and cystoid macular edema. In this case, the subretinal and intraretinal fluid in multiple retinal layers contiguous with the optic nerve point to the optic nerve, rather than vascular leakage, as the source of the fluid. Therefore, fluorescein angiography (choice B) and OCT-angiography of the macula (choice D), tests that detect vascular sources of fluid, are not indicated, and anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (choice A), a treatment for vascular leakage, is not appropriate. Although optic pit maculopathy without inner retinal schisis cavity has been reported, the pattern and distribution of fluid is most consistent with optic pit maculopathy.1,2However, clinical examination and OCT of the optic nerve revealed a very deep cup (1388 μm from the Bruch membrane opening) without a focal depression seen in optic pit (Figure 2). Glaucoma can lead to increased cup depth, although this patient's cup depth is far outside the range seen in glaucoma.3Excessively deep optic cups have been reported in optic pit but are common in cavitary optic disc anomaly (CODA).4Rarely, macular schisis occurs secondary to glaucoma,5but the normal intraocular pressure, normal retinal nerve fiber layer on OCT, very deep optic cup, and normal visual fields (data not shown) make CODA, rather than glaucoma, the likely diagnosis in this patient. Congenital excavated optic nerve abnormalities (optic nerve coloboma, optic pit, morning glory anomaly, and CODA) have a risk of vision loss around age 20 to 40 years due to macular fluid.4These abnormalities are usually unilateral and sporadic, but are rarely autosomal dominant because of a triplication upstream of theMMP19gene,6,7which encodes an extracellular matrix protease in the optic nerve.6In CODA, optic nerve abnormalities are highly penetrant with variable phenotype (optic pit, morning glory, atypical coloboma, glaucomatous cupping, and excessively deep optic cups).4The central retinal artery is often not visible and retinal vessels appear to emanate directly from the cup edge. The optic cup may gradually enlarge, and excavation may develop from a previously normal optic nerve.7These features of CODA mimic glaucoma, but should not be confused to avoid unnecessary treatments. In excavated optic nerve abnormalities, histologic studies and swept-source OCT imaging reveal that dysplastic retina herniates through the lamina cribrosa or juxtapapillary sclera and protrudes into the subarachnoid space.8Fluid is thought to follow a pressure gradient through the defect into the retinal stroma and subretinal space. The source of the fluid may be liquified vitreous and/or cerebrospinal fluid.8,9 A period of observation is recommended since the macular fluid may spontaneously resolve, but persistent macular fluid may lead to permanently decreased vision to the 20/200 level or worse. The optimal treatment is debated, but vitrectomy alone may be sufficient in some.10 A visit 2 months later showed improved visual acuity to 20/20 and spontaneous regression of intraretinal and subretinal fluid. Latanoprost was stopped. Over the next 4 years, the patient remained stable without recurrent fluid or visual field changes.

scenario: A 12-year-old girl presented for assessment of abnormal gait. A year prior, she was found to have bilateral panuveitis with occlusive retinal periphlebitis involving all quadrants of the central and peripheral retina with capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Her subsequent workup revealed elevated inflammatory markers and subcentimeter chest and abdominal lymph nodes. Given a positive interferon-γ release assay, therapy was initiated with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE) and corticosteroids for presumed tuberculosis. At the time of presentation, she had completed RIPE therapy and was taking mycophenolate mofetil with resolution of her ocular manifestations. She complained of new bilateral lower extremity weakness with associated lower back pain. Clinical examination results revealed a wide-based Trendelenburg gait with right foot drop and diminished strength of lower extremity flexors. Laboratory testing results showed a normal white blood cell count, vitamin B12, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, C-reactive protein, and antinuclear antibody levels. She had negative test results for Lyme disease, syphilis, and HIV. Computed tomography showed small supraclavicular and mediastinal lymph nodes and an enlarged spleen. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated mild lacrimal gland prominence and low thoracic/high lumbar spine and cauda equina nerve roots hyperintensity and abnormal enhancement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a lymphocytic pleocytosis with an elevated protein level, negative syphilis antibody results, and an absence of organisms on acid-fast bacilli smear, Gram stain, and culture.

options.C: Reinitiate RIPE therapy

answer: Perform a lacrimal gland biopsy
explanation: B. Perform a lacrimal gland biopsy A right orbitotomy with lacrimal gland biopsy was performed (choice B) allowing for histopathologic confirmation of sarcoidosis (Figure 2). Sarcoidosis is a protean multisystem inflammatory disorder classically defined histologically by well-formed, non-necrotizing, “naked” epithelioid granulomas. Focal histologic necrosis can be seen, particularly in the lacrimal gland.1Neurosarcoidosis can manifest anywhere in the nervous system including as intramedullary spinal cord lesions.2Neurologic manifestations occur in approximately 5% of adults with sarcoidosis and is even rarer in children.3Fifty-five pediatric cases have been reported of which 10 presented as isolated neurosarcoidosis.4The average age of presentation of pediatric neurosarcoidosis is 12 years and the most common manifestations are seizure, cranial neuropathies, hypothalamic dysfunction, and optic nerve swelling.4Spinal cord involvement is unusual in children, and to our knowledge, this is the third case reported in the literature.4Symptoms present subacutely, with varying combinations of pain, limb paraparesis, paresthesias, and bowel or bladder dysfunction.2Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies typically show a lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein level.5 Obtaining tissue diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis can be challenging. There are reports of injurious spinal cord biopsies6; therefore, it is crucial to perform a systematic search for extraneural areas wherein a biopsy would confer less morbidity. The lacrimal gland is the most commonly involved ocular site in sarcoidosis and morbidity associated with lacrimal gland biopsy is limited to temporary ptosis and dry eye.7Therefore, it is considered safer than a thoracic lymph node biopsy (choice D). Serum and CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme and lysozyme levels are diagnostically unreliable with low sensitivity and specificity, respectively; however, if elevated, they may help with suspecting a diagnosis.8 In retrospect, the patient’s initial ocular manifestations were likely secondary to sarcoidosis. The differential diagnosis for granulomatous uveitis with a retinal occlusive periphlebitis (Figure 1A) primarily includes syphilis, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis; an isolated periphlebitis or venulitis can also be due to Eales disease. Because of the initial inability to exclude tuberculosis and demonstrate systemic sarcoid findings, she did not meet the criteria published in the international consensus guideline for probable ocular sarcoidosis.9On her second presentation, she had more compatible findings including lacrimal gland and lymph node enlargement and splenomegaly. Recurrence of tuberculosis following RIPE therapy is extremely rare.10Given the patient’s paucity of infectious symptoms, sterile CSF studies, negative histochemical stains, and improvement with immunosuppression, tuberculosis recrudescence was excluded (choice C). Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause an ascending paralysis with muscular weakness and reflex abnormalities but is associated with a prodromal flulike illness and CSF studies without lymphocytosis. Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause ophthalmoplegia with diplopia but generally does not cause ocular inflammation (choice A). The patient was treated with systemic corticosteroids and infliximab with subsequent gait normalization. This case highlights the need for high clinical suspicion for a neurosarcoidosis diagnosis, the importance of searching for extraneural involvement for potential biopsy sites, and the relatively low morbidity associated with lacrimal gland biopsy.
