B, Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrating disc leakage (blue arrowhead) and blockage in the region of the macular lesion (pink arrowhead).
scenario: A 58-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a retinal detachment in his left eye. His visual acuity on presentation was 20/20 in the right eye and hand motion only in the left eye. Examination of the right eye was normal. Anterior segment examination of the left eye revealed around 30 cells per high-power field of a 1 mm × 1 mm light beam and diffuse stellate-appearing keratic precipitates. Posterior examination results showed a vitreous cell that precluded a clear view of the posterior pole and inferior snow banking. Most notable was a large, white, preretinal lesion in the inferior macula and a near-total retinal detachment with no identifiable retinal break and shifting subretinal fluid (Figure). His medical history included psoriatic arthritis, for which he had been taking adalimumab. Four months prior to presentation, he had traveled to Costa Rica on vacation and fallen ill with fevers, night sweats, and myalgias. He started a 6-week course of oral ciprofloxacin and his adalimumab was discontinued. After returning to the United States, he developed dyspnea with exertion. He was found to have an ejection fraction (EF) of 20% to 25% with 4-chamber dilation and was diagnosed with cardiomyopathy. Results of limited infectious workup, including blood and stool cultures and tests for leptospirosis and dengue fever, were negative.

options.B: Obtain aqueous sample for cultures and polymerase chain reaction
options.C: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair

answer: Obtain aqueous sample for cultures and polymerase chain reaction
distractors: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair
explanation: Ocular and disseminated toxoplasmosis with toxoplasmic myocarditis B. Obtain aqueous sample for cultures and polymerase chain reaction On presentation, an aqueous sample was obtained and sent for cultures and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (answer B). The focal, white, macular lesion with moderate overlying vitritis resembled the “headlight-in-the-fog” appearance of toxoplasma retinitis rather than a bacterial endophthalmitis (answer A). Surgical repair was deferred because of  concern for active infectious retinitis (answer C). Given suspected infectious cardiomyopathy, serum toxoplasma IgG and IgM antibodies were drawn, infectious disease was consulted, and the patient started empirical treatement with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Systemic steroids (answer D) were deferred to avoid exacerbation of suspected disseminated toxoplasmosis. PCR from the aqueous fluid was positive forToxoplasma gondii. Systemic bloodwork revealed an elevated toxoplasma IgM (>160.0 mg/dL, reference range <8.0 mg/dL; to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 0.01) and IgG (>400.0 mg/dL, reference range <7.20 mg/dL; to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 0.01), suggesting recent infection. The patient’s case was discussed with both infectious disease and cardiology specialists. The patient’s trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment was maintained for suspected toxoplasmosis with both ocular and cardiac involvement. Ocular toxoplasmosis is most commonly encountered as necrotizing retinitis or retinochoroiditis. Clinical presentations may vary depending on a patient’s immunocompetency status. This patient was taking adalimumab, a tumor necrosis factor α antagonist that can cause relative immunocompromise and may actually increase the risk of infection in the first 90 days after discontinuation.1In immunocompetent patients, ocular toxoplasmosis frequently presents as isolated retinitis.2In immunocompromised patients, atypical presentations, including uveitis, optic disc granulomas, or serous retinal detachments, are more common.3Diagnosis of toxoplasma retinochoroiditis is typically made clinically, given its classic “headlight-in-the-fog” appearance. In atypical presentations, PCR from ocular fluids may be performed.4 Historically, pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine have been the mainstay of treatment of toxoplasma retinochoroiditis.5More recently, alternative treatment options have emerged including oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and intravitreal clindamycin. Corticosteroids may be added for patients mounting severe inflammatory responses.6 Retinal detachments occur in only 6% of patients with toxoplasma retinochoroiditis and portend a poor visual prognosis. The majority of these patients have less than 20/200 visual acuity despite treatment.7 Toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis can occur in conjunction with acute systemic toxoplasmosis. One study found that 11% of patients with ocular toxoplasmosis had serologic evidence of acute systemic infection, as this patient did, and these patients were more likely to have severe intraocular inflammation.8Even rarer is toxoplasma myocarditis, a complication most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals. Postmortem analysis of HIV-infected patients showed cardiac toxoplasmosis in 12% of patients.9Systemic antiprotozoal treatment has shown to be beneficial in acute toxoplasmic myocarditis.10Though diagnostic cardiac biopsy was not performed on this patient, remarkable improvement in EF after initiation of treatment led to a presumptive diagnosis of toxoplasma myocarditis. Shortly after initiating trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment, the patient experienced remarkable systemic improvement. A repeated echocardiogram performed at 6 weeks after presentation showed improvement in EF to 40%, and after 3 months, normalization to 55%. Although his exudative retinal detachment improved, he later developed a retinal break. Despite surgical repair, he ultimately regained only count fingers visual acuity.

caption: External photographs show bilateral upper eyelid ecchymosis and edema, temporal subconjunctival hemorrhage of the right eye, and a right temple mass (asterisk).
scenario: A 13-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history and no ocular history was brought to the emergency department by his parents for bilateral eyelid ecchymosis and edema for 1 month, as well as a mass on the right temporal area that was persistent for the past month and a half. He had hit the right side of his head on a table 1 month before symptoms developed, but had no other recent trauma. The mass had not changed in size, was not tender, and had no other associated symptoms. His parents had not noticed any change in vision. At bedside, the patient was playful and in no acute distress. On examination, he fixed and followed in each eye. His pupils were equal and reactive to light without afferent pupillary defect. Both eyes were soft to palpation and his extraocular movements were full. Externally, his examination was notable for bilateral upper eyelid ecchymosis and edema, as well as a soft, well-circumscribed mass on the right temporal region (Figure 1). There was no obvious proptosis. He was also noted to have subconjunctival hemorrhage temporally on the right eye. Otherwise, findings of his anterior examination and dilated fundoscopic examination were normal.

options.B: Reassurance and treatment with cool compresses and artificial tears
options.C: Contact Child Protective Services

answer: Brain/orbital imaging
distractors: Reassurance and treatment with cool compresses and artificial tears
explanation: Bilateral orbital ecchymosis without trauma in a young child warranted suspicion for neuroblastoma. This, in addition to the temporal mass, prompted urgent imaging and full ophthalmologic examination. Differential diagnoses include neuroblastoma, hematoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, hemangioma, cyst, or bleeding diathesis. While bleeding diathesis could cause ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage (D), the temporal mass indicates that the hemorrhages may represent a more ominous finding. Reassurance (B) or contacting Child Protective Services (C) is inappropriate before further workup. Findings that should prompt Child Protective Services referral include multilayer retinal hemorrhages. Neuroblastoma, a malignancy of neural crest origin, is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children. The incidence is 1 per 10 000 live births in the US.1It commonly occurs in the adrenal medulla. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but may have generalized symptoms or anemia from spontaneous tumor hemorrhage. Symptoms generally occur due to tumor growth or metastases. Sites of metastasis include bone, bone marrow, liver, orbit and spinal cord, which cause bone pain, periorbital ecchymosis and proptosis, and progressive paraplegia.1,2 Only 8% of neuroblastoma cases present with orbital signs. In the largest review of cases with orbital involvement, there were 10 patients and periorbital ecchymosis (racoon eyes) was the most common finding, followed by proptosis.3Other findings included periorbital edema, subconjunctival hemorrhage, vision loss, and decreased ocular motility.3Neuroblastoma can also cause a paraneoplastic syndrome leading to cerebellar dysfunction and opsomyoclonus.1 Diagnostic workup includes computed tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid tests, iodine-131-meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan for bone involvement, and bone marrow or primary tissue biopsy. Tissue is analyzed for cytogenetic aberrations or molecular markers.1Loss of 1p, 3p, and 11q, unbalanced gain of 17q, or amplification of MYCN protooncogene indicate poor prognosis.4Treatment is based on age and extent of spread; this includes surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.1 Prognosis depends on age, stage, and risk stratification; stratification is complex and based on chromosomal aberrations, histopathology, and extent of spread (complete risk stratification is available in the cited reference).5Neuroblastoma accounts for 15% of cancer-associated deaths in children, and patients older than 2 years have a worse prognosis. High-risk neuroblastoma is relegated to a 30% to 40% survival.2,5Orbital metastasis are associated with poor prognosis and can be misdiagnosed as orbital fractures, child abuse, benign hemorrhages, or other tumors.3Ophthalmologists can play a role in diagnosing neuroblastoma and should promptly refer to a pediatrician or oncologist when neuroblastoma is suspected. CT head and orbits showed multiple osseous lesions with intracranial and intraorbital extension (Figure 2). CT abdomen and pelvis revealed a right adrenal mass with liver and bone metastasis. Urine catecholamines were elevated. I-MIBG showed diffuse metastatic disease–stage M per International Neuroblastoma Risk Group classification. Biopsy of the adrenal mass showed poorly differentiated neuroblastoma with MYCN amplification. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed the diagnosis. Surgical intervention was deferred given diffuse metastasis and multiple orbital lesions. The patient started chemotherapy with topotecan and cyclophosphamide.

caption: A, A fundus photograph revealed a solitary, raised choroidal lesion with a creamy yellow appearance in the macular region extending nasally to the optic disc (area encircled by a dotted line). B, B-scan ultrasonography confirmed a dome-shaped choroidal mass with echodensity measuring 14 mm in diameter and 4 mm in thickness.
scenario: A 59-year-old Asian man with no history of any systemic illness presented with a 1-month history of blurred vision in his right eye. His visual acuity was 20/400 OD and 20/20 OS. The anterior segments were quiet and vitreous was clear in both eyes. Fundus examination in the right eye revealed a solitary, elevated choroidal lesion with a creamy yellow appearance in the macular region involving the optic disc (Figure 1A). Ultrasonography confirmed a dome-shaped choroidal mass with intermediate echodensity measuring 14 mm in diameter and 4 mm in thickness (Figure 1B). Fluorescein angiography demonstrated scattered pinpoint hyperfluorescence of the mass and late leakage of the disc. Indocyanine green angiography revealed hypofluorescence in both early and late phases. Optical coherence tomography disclosed a choroidal mass with undulating surface and shallow subretinal fluid. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit revealed an intraocular mass with hyperintensity on T1-weighted and hypointensity on T2-weighted scans with contrast enhancement extending into the adjacent retrobulbar fat, suspicious for scleral invasion. Blood test results including a complete blood cell count, tuberculosis, syphilis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme were all negative. The patient then developed gingivitis with a white blood cell count up to 12 350/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001) in the next 2 weeks that failed to respond to intravenous antibiotics. There were more pigments overlying the intraocular mass with prominent intraretinal hemorrhage along the optic disc compared with clinical findings at first presentation.

options.C: Treat with enucleation

answer: Perform a comprehensive systemic workup
explanation: D. Perform a comprehensive systemic workup An amelanotic choroidal mass in a middle-aged man led to concern for choroidal metastasis, amelanotic choroidal melanoma, choroidal lymphoma, and inflammatory diseases such as choroidal tubercles, sarcoidosis, or posterior scleritis. In this case, vital features, including absence of vascularity on angiography, lack of acoustic hollowness on ultrasonography (characteristic of melanoma), absence of ocular inflammation, and negative blood test results for inflammation, made initial treatment with plaque radiotherapy for choroidal melanoma (choice A) or oral corticosteroids for intraocular inflammation (choice B) less preferred options. In order to rule out choroidal metastasis or any systemic diseases that may affect the eye, a comprehensive systemic workup is necessary (choice D). More invasive procedures, such as fine-needle aspiration biopsy and enucleation (choice C), were held in reserve if other options were to fail. Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare disease caused by a clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells often with multisystem involvement.1It is predominantly a disease of childhood but is occasionally seen in adults.2Ophthalmic manifestations are mostly seen in children and normally manifest as orbital involvement.3-5In a retrospective medical record review of 76 children with LCH, 18 (23.7%) had orbital involvement and no instance of intraocular involvement was detected.3The International Registry of the Histiocyte Society reported 274 adults with biopsy-proven LCH, and no ocular involvement was detected.6We report a case of a solitary choroidal LCH that occurred in an adult with no evidence of systemic lesions. In our review of the literature, we identified 2 case reports of solitary choroidal LCH in adults.7,8One developed after a previously excised solitary cerebral parenchymal lesion and was treated with external beam radiotherapy with response.7The other one had a unifocal choroidal lesion with no systemic involvement and underwent enucleation for suspicion of a choroidal melanoma.8Review of their clinical manifestations demonstrated some common features such as an amelanotic, mildly elevated choroidal lesion in the posterior area, with echodensity on ultrasonography and hypofluorescence on ICG angiography. The standard therapeutic approach to choroidal LCH has not yet been established because of its rarity. Reported therapies for localized orbital LCH included surgical excision, corticosteroids injection, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy.9We believe patients with LCH typically are referred to an oncologist who can do a comprehensive systematic evaluation and ongoing follow-up to monitor for recurrence or progression. An ocular presentation of adult LCH is unusual. We report a rare case of a solitary choroidal LCH with rapid progression in an adult mimicking choroidal melanoma. Although rare, LCH likely should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any choroidal mass. A careful multidisciplinary evaluation is necessary. In cases in which noninvasive diagnostic modalities have failed to establish the diagnosis, a biopsy may be judged to be warranted to establish and confirm the diagnosis.10 The patient’s positron emission tomography–computed tomography findings turned out to be unremarkable. We offered the option of fine-needle aspiration biopsy in order to obtain histologic diagnosis, but patient declined this option and insisted on enucleation. With the concern of its location of wrapping around the optic disc, rapid progression, and suspicious extrascleral extension, we enucleated his right eyeball. The enucleated eyeball was clear and there was no extraocular invasion. Histopathologic analysis revealed a polymorphous cellular infiltrate composed of histiocytic cells and eosinophils (Figure 2). The histiocytes displayed irregular, cleaved nuclei and demonstrated strong immunoreactivity for langerin, S100, and CD1α. A diagnosis of solitary choroid LCH was made.

scenario: A 17-year-old previously healthy girl presented with 3 months of decreased vision in the right eye associated with throbbing pain with eye movement. The patient had no history of weakness, incontinence, or severe headaches. Initial presentation was notable for hand motion visual acuity with a 2+ relative afferent pupillary defect on the right; fundus examination revealed grade IV disc edema with obscuration of all major vessels on the disc (Figure, A). A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast was degraded by motion and orthodontic artifact but was suggestive of optic nerve enhancement consistent with optic neuritis. Results of serology tests and cerebral spinal fluid analysis were negative for infectious and inflammatory etiologies, including syphilis, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, viral etiologies, multiple sclerosis, and lupus. The patient started treatment with intravenous methylprednisone and plasmapheresis for a presumptive diagnosis of optic neuritis; however, after 3 days there was minimal improvement and a second MRI of the brain and orbits was performed (Figure, B). The second MRI revealed a fusiform expansion of the right optic nerve and enhancement of the orbital, canalicular, and prechiasmatic segments of the right optic nerve, suggestive of an optic nerve glioma. Two weeks after initial presentation, the visual acuity in the right eye progressed to no light perception. Repeated MRI showed progression of the lesion with masslike expansion at the chiasm measuring 1.3 cm (anterior-posterior) × 1.5 cm (craniocaudal) × 1.1 cm (transverse). The left visual field remained full.

options.A: Transorbital biopsy of the right optic nerve for grading and immunohistochemistry
options.B: Transcranial resection of the orbital, canalicular, and prechiasmal optic nerve
options.C: Chemotherapy and/or radiation for presumptive optic nerve glioma
options.D: Observation given progression to no light perception vision

answer: Transorbital biopsy of the right optic nerve for grading and immunohistochemistry
distractors: Transcranial resection of the orbital, canalicular, and prechiasmal optic nerve
Chemotherapy and/or radiation for presumptive optic nerve glioma
Observation given progression to no light perception vision
explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma with anaplastic transformation A. Transorbital biopsy of the right optic nerve for grading and immunohistochemistry The patient’s progression was more rapid than would be expected with a typical optic pathway glioma, as optic nerve gliomas do not tend to grow as rapidly. Given the rate of aggressive progression and risk of vision loss to the left eye, the best decision is to proceed with biopsy of the right optic nerve. Complete surgical excision was not possible because of the involvement of the tumor at the chiasm; the biopsy was to evaluate the grade and immunohistochemistry of the tumor prior to starting radiation. Performing the biopsy via a transorbital (choice A) rather than transcranial route would allow radiation to start more expeditiously. Transcranial biopsy (choice B) is not preferred because of longer recovery and potential delay of radiotherapy. Chemotherapy and/or radiation prior to knowing the grade of the tumor (choice C) would not be preferred. Observation of a tumor with chiasmal involvement places the patient at significant risk for visual loss on the left side (choice D). Tumor at the chiasm, described as “masslike expansion,” would potentially threaten the entering fibers from the left optic nerve. A biopsy was performed of the right optic nerve for immunohistochemical analysis and to assess if biologic therapies could be offered. The patient was evaluated with Genetics and Oncology; no additional personal features or family history of neurofibromatosis, type 1, were observed. The pathology revealed tumor cells with round to ovoid nuclei and a K967 proliferation of 20% to 30%, consistent with pilocytic astrocytoma with anaplastic transformation. Pilocytic astrocytomas affect approximately 4.8 persons per 1 million in adults and account for approximately 3% to 5% of all childhood central nervous system tumors; approximately 2% of pilocytic astrocytomas have anaplastic features.1-3Anaplastic features are diagnosed primarily with morphological appearance, including multiple mitoses in a single high-powered field, vascular endothelial proliferation, high Ki67 proliferation index (up to 35% in some tumors), and palisading necrosis.1,4 While pilocytic astrocytoma carries a World Health Organization (WHO) grade I diagnosis, anaplastic pilocytic astrocytoma is WHO grade III.5WHO grade I pilocytic astrocytomas are slow growing, well circumscribed without invasion to surrounding tissue, and rarely require surgical intervention; in contrast, WHO grade IV pilocytic astrocytomas have more aggressive features with poorer outcomes.1,5Previous tumor sequencing of anaplastic pilocytic astrocytomas has shown associations withBRAFmutation, p16 loss, and absence of p53 mutation.6,7Radiotherapy is an option in this older patient; in children, adverse effects to the central nervous system may be prohibitive.7 Tissue obtained during biopsy was used for a tumor DNA/RNA panel, which revealed high tumor mutation burden with multiple variants in cancer genes including NF1, NOTCH1, and P53, confirming the anaplastic nature of the tumor. The patient underwent focal radiation therapy. Repeated MRI 3 months later showed interval decrease in the cisternal portion of the tumor and the right side of the optic chiasm. The patient was followed up weekly with Oncology and monthly with Neuro-Ophthalmology. A temporal field defect was noted in the left eye 3 months after biopsy. This was subjectively improving after focal radiation therapy and oral corticosteroid.

caption: Close-up external photograph demonstrating a 3-mm subcutaneous, noncompressible lesion (arrowhead) at the lateral canthus of the right eye.
scenario: A 44-year-old woman presented to the oculoplastic surgery clinic with a mass on the lateral canthus of her right eye. The mass had gradually grown over 2 months and was tender to palpation. She denied any vision changes, facial trauma, redness, or discharge from the lesion. She had an unremarkable ocular and medical history. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/20 OS. Ocular motility was full and pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. Her examination was notable for a 3-mm subcutaneous, firm, mobile, noncompressible lesion near the lateral canthus of the right eye without overlying erythema, warmth, telangiectasia, or ulceration (Figure 1). The rest of the ophthalmic and orbital examination was normal.

options.A: Trial of conservative management with warm compresses and eyelid massage
options.B: Perform excisional biopsy of the lesion to rule out malignancy
options.C: Perform incision and drainage of the lesion

answer: Perform excisional biopsy of the lesion to rule out malignancy
distractors: Trial of conservative management with warm compresses and eyelid massage
Perform incision and drainage of the lesion
explanation: B. Perform excisional biopsy of the lesion to rule out malignancy The differential diagnosis of a periorbital subcutaneous mass includes infectious or inflammatory conditions including abscess or foreign body, vascular lesions such as arteriovenous malformations, malignant neoplasms such as rhabdomyosarcoma or lymphoma, and benign neoplasms such as dermoid cysts and lipomas. A persistently growing unilateral subcutaneous periorbital lesion in an adult should raise concern for neoplasm and be promptly biopsied for histopathologic evaluation (choice B). Conservative management with warm compresses and eyelid massage (choice A) is appropriate for benign lesions arising from clogged meibomian or sebaceous glands, such as a chalazion or hordeolum, which typically present along the eyelid margins. Incision and drainage (choice C) is appropriate for an abscess, which often presents with fluctuance, local erythema, and systemic signs. Observation is only appropriate for benign conditions (choice D), which cannot be definitively diagnosed from physical examination alone. In this patient, histopathology showed a large, well-circumscribed focus of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm (Figure 2) staining positive for S100, CD68, and Sox10. These findings were consistent with a granular cell tumor (GCT), a rare, often benign, tumor of Schwann cell origin occurring mainly in the head and neck, with orbital or periorbital involvement in approximately 3% of cases.1Tumors develop during the fourth and sixth decades of life, with female predilection.2 Histologically, GCTs are composed of nests of polygonal cells with small, round nuclei and abundant cytoplasm.3Cytoplasms contain eosinophilic granules that are periodic acid–Schiff positive.4The vast majority of GCT lesions stain positive for S100, neuron‐specific enolase, Sox10, and CD68, but negative for epithelial, muscle, and melanin markers.2Approximately 1% to 3% of all GCTs are malignant, characterized by rapid growth and high rates of recurrence or morbidities.2Differentiation between malignant and benign GCTs is made by the presence of mitotic activity, necrosis, increase in nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, vesicular nuclei, spindling of cells, and pleomorphism,5none of which were present in the histopathology from this patient. Clinically, GCTs present as a slow-growing, well-demarcated, unilateral lesion.6Common manifestations include pain surrounding the lesion as seen in this patient, diplopia from extraocular motility restriction, and proptosis for deeper lesions.2Lesions with intraorbital location or extension should be assessed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging to aid in diagnosis and surgical planning.7 The treatment for GCT is complete surgical excision, irrespective of whether the lesion is benign or malignant.6If malignant, tumors can metastasize or become locally destructive; adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy are used, although their roles are unclear at this time.8The local recurrence rate of GCT after complete excision is less than 7%.2,9 As a general principle, a progressively enlarging subcutaneous periorbital mass in an adult is typically caused by infection, inflammation, or a neoplasm. After ruling out infection and inflammation, all masses should be excised and biopsied promptly to rule out malignancies, which can have devastating ocular and systemic sequelae. The patient was informed of her diagnosis and reassured. She was advised to follow up with recurrence of the lesion or new ocular concerns.

scenario: A 46-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of a persistent blurred area in his right lower visual field of both eyes. He noticed colors surrounding the dark area that lasted 2 to 3 minutes at a time and occurred multiple times per day. His medical history was significant for dyslipidemia for which he took rosuvastatin. He also reported feeling lethargic, with polydipsia and a dull mild holocephalic headache during this period. Ophthalmological examination revealed a visual acuity of 20/20 OU, pupils were equal and reactive to light with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and color vision was normal. Dilated fundus examination was normal. Humphrey 24-2 Swedish interactive threshold algorithm fast visual field testing revealed a right homonymous hemianopia denser inferiorly (Figure, A). An urgent noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head was obtained and was normal (Figure, B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was initially reported as normal but revealed subtle abnormal T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensity involving the left occipital cortex after further review (Figure, B).

options.A: Measure C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: Perform lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid contents
options.D: Perform magnetic resonance angiography of the head

answer: Measure blood glucose levels
distractors: Measure C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Perform lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid contents
Perform magnetic resonance angiography of the head
explanation: Homonymous hemianopia secondary to nonketotic hyperglycemia B. Measure blood glucose levels Homonymous visual field defects occur from processes affecting the contralateral retrochiasmal visual pathways. Neuroimaging is indicated to identify a potential culprit lesion of which the etiology is broad and includes neoplastic, vascular, trauma, and postsurgical causes.1It is a diagnostic dilemma when a patient presents with a homonymous visual field defect without an obvious abnormality on neuroimaging. In this case, measuring blood glucose levels to investigate hyperglycemia would be the next best step considering the patient’s reported lethargy and polydipsia (choice B). Measure C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (choice A) would not be the preferred option since a vasculitis and secondary infarct was not supported by the history or neuroimaging findings.2A lumbar puncture (choice C) was not recommended as the next step since the presentation was not consistent with a meningeal process based on the history, examination, and MRI findings. Given his CT and MRI already ruled out vascular and neoplastic causes, magnetic resonance angiography (choice D) was unlikely to add any additional information and would not be the next recommended step. Nonketotic hyperglycemia (NKH) is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and intracellular dehydration with little or no ketoacidosis. Patients with NKH may have neurologic manifestations depending on the location of brain involvement and include seizure, homonymous hemianopia, and hyperkinetic movement disorders.3Various positive visual phenomena including colored objects, photopsias, and complex visual hallucinations have been reported as part of homonymous visual field defects associated with hyperglycemia.1,3-6While patients with a known history of type 2 diabetes may have homonymous hemianopia as a sign of NKH indicating poor glycemic control, it is much less common for an isolated homonymous hemianopia to be the presenting sign of type 2 diabetes like in this case.1,3,4,6-8The pathophysiology of cerebral injury from hyperglycemia is unclear; proposed mechanisms include an increase in reactive oxygen species, altered neurotransmitter function, and intracellular dehydration.9 Neuroimaging usually reveals cortical hyperintensity on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences and subcortical T2 hypointensity.10In contrast, CT scans are usually unremarkable in neurological complications of NKH.5The reversibility of MRI changes and lack of significant restricted diffusion (excluding an ischemic etiology) suggests an epileptic etiology for the hemianopic visual field defect.3,5,6Seizures are common in patients with NKH, the majority of which are partial motor seizures. However, occipital lobe seizures have also been demonstrated on electroencephalogram (EEG), MRI, and visual evoked potentials.3-5Stayman et al6reported 3 patients with hyperglycemia with recurrent ictal discharges originating from the contralateral posterior quadrant on video EEG and occipital lobe hypermetabolism on18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography. Recognition of hyperglycemia as the underlying metabolic disorder causing the homonymous hemianopia is crucial for initiation of appropriate management with insulin therapy and adequate hydration. As this is a provoked seizure, maintenance antiepileptic therapy is not necessary since management primarily depends on correction of the hyperglycemia. This case highlights a rare cause of homonymous visual field defects. Consideration of an ictal etiology in the patient with hyperglycemia presenting with intermittent homonymous visual field defects is important for prompt initiation of treatment and to avoid unnecessary investigations. The patient’s bloodwork results revealed a random glucose level of 473.87 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555) and a hemoglobin A1clevel of 11.8% (normal <6%; to convert to proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01). His homonymous hemianopia was thought to reflect seizure activity in the context of hyperglycemia. He was admitted to the hospital for optimization of his blood glucose levels and a routine EEG was obtained and was normal, although a clinical event was not captured during the recording. However, he noticed immediate cessation of colored images around the visual field defect on receiving intravenous lorazepam. His blood glucose levels normalized with subcutaneous insulin, metformin, and gliclazide and his visual field defect resolved after 4 days. Repeated visual field testing 3 months later remained normal.

caption: Anterior segment photograph of the left eye demonstrating sudden enlargement of a cystic iris stromal lesion from the 2- to 7-o’clock position (arrowheads).
scenario: A 63-year-old woman was referred by optometry after waking up with cloudy vision in the left eye and an ache around the left brow. Visual acuity was 20/20 OD and light perception OS. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 15 mm Hg OD and 54 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment examination of the left eye was remarkable for a large cystic iris stromal lesion from the 2- to 7-o’clock position with iris-cornea touch. The anterior chamber was shallow in the area of the enlarged cystic lesion with a large amount of pigmented cells. The pupil was irregular with blood at the pupillary margin. Her intraocular lens was not visible because of occlusion by a cystic lesion behind the iris (Figure 1). Her ocular history was notable for indiscriminate trauma to her left eye, primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes treated with dorzolamide hydrochloride and brimonidine tartrate, and pseudophakia in both eyes. Four years prior, an inferior cystic iris stromal lesion was discovered in the left eye that measured approximately 5 × 2 mm in basal dimensions at the slitlamp. Fine-needle aspiration was negative for malignancy, and the lesion was managed by close follow-up.

options.A: YAG laser to perforate the cystic wall
options.C: Biopsy

answer: YAG laser to perforate the cystic wall
explanation: Secondary angle-closure glaucoma due to sudden enlargement of a cystic iris stromal lesion A. YAG laser to perforate the cystic wall The differential diagnosis for a cystic iris mass includes primary iris stromal and iris pigmented epithelial cysts, as well as secondary cysts related to neoplasia, trauma, inflammation, or medication.1-4Ultrasound B-scan and biomicroscopy allow for identification of internal echogenicity and involvement of surrounding structures, which aid in ruling out solid mass lesions.4,5Primary iris cysts tend to have thin walls and smooth borders, whereas secondary cysts tend to have irregular borders and rough surfaces.6This surgical history and prior ocular trauma suggest a secondary etiology in this patient. Some primary and secondary iris cystic lesions can cause decreased visual acuity, secondary glaucoma, corneal edema, and other complications.3,4As in this patient, acute angle-closure glaucoma may occur due to forward bulging of a cyst to shallow the anterior chamber.4,7Treatment options include observation (option B), which is appropriate in many cases, intralesional alcohol injection, and surgical resection.4While glaucoma tube surgery (option D) might be considered in complex cases, this would not address the underlying cause of the elevated IOP. YAG laser (option A) is another option, as illustrated in this patient with angle-closure glaucoma secondary to cystic iris lesions.4,8Since there are few reports on this treatment option, this case points out a need for future studies to further investigate YAG laser therapy. Perforation of the cystic wall initially flattened the lesion and dropped the IOP to 35 mm Hg. On postoperative day 1, however, the IOP increased to 51 mm Hg, and there was new-onset microcystic corneal edema with iris-cornea touch from the 2- to 7-o’clock position (Figure 2). Consequently, we proceeded with surgical excision of the lesion using a vitrector and ablation of the residual cyst walls and base with endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation. On postoperative day 1, visual acuity improved to count fingers OS and IOP was 14 mm Hg. Anterior segment examination was remarkable for moderate Descemet membrane folds and an iris defect from the 2- to 7-o’clock position. Ten months later, there was no recurrence of the lesion on examination and visual acuity was 20/40 OS.

caption: Slitlamp photograph showing conjunctival hyperemia and hypopyon (arrowhead) of the left eye.
scenario: A 72-year-old woman presented with new-onset decreased vision in the right eye. Her ocular history included pseudoexfoliation syndrome and glaucomatous optic neuropathy in the right eye. Past ocular surgery included uncomplicated trabeculectomy in the right eye treated with mitomycin C (3 months prior) and no ocular surgery history in the left eye. Her medical history included pulmonaryMycobacterium aviuminfection secondary to hypogammaglobulinemia. Computed tomography scan 2 months prior exhibited reactivation and she started treatment with clarithromycin (1000 mg/d), ethambutol (15 mg/kg/d), and rifabutin (300 mg/d). Best-corrected visual acuity was hand motions OD and 20/20 OS. Intraocular pressures were 4 mm Hg ODand 13 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment examination of the right eye showed substantial conjunctival hyperemia and substantial cellular response in the anterior chamber (2 to 3+) along with a 1-mm hypopyon. There was no leak at the trabeculectomy bleb (negative Seidel test). B-scan ultrasonography showed no retinal detachment or mass. Presumed diagnosis of bleb-related infectious endophthalmitis was made and she was referred for treatment. Pars plana vitrectomy was performed, including vitreous sampling, and showed very light growth ofStaphylococcus aureusin 1 colony on 1 plate, which was highly suspicious for contaminant. Intravitreal amikacin and vancomycin were administered after vitreous sampling was performed. Postoperatively, the patient initiated treatment with topical antibiotics and corticosteroids. Her visual acuity returned to 20/30. Two months later, she presented again with a similar acute vision loss in the left eye (counting fingers). Anterior segment examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, cellular reaction, and a small hypopyon (Figure).

options.A: Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics
options.B: Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics
options.C: Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids
options.D: Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids

answer: Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids
distractors: Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics
Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics
Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids
explanation: C. Review and adjust systemic medications and treat with topical corticosteroids Pars plana vitrectomy with hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics would not be the preferred answer because with the lack of surgery history, an infections etiology would be lower on the differential diagnosis (choice A). Treatment with topical and oral antibiotics would not be the preferred answer because of the insufficient intraocular penetration (choice B). Treat with systemic and topical corticosteroids would not be the preferred answer because of the importance of investigating underlying etiology prior to treatment (choice D). Rifabutin is used for the treatment and prophylaxis of theM aviumcomplex (MAC) infection.1It is a semisynthetic derivative of rifamycin SV and has broad antimicrobial activity, including against MAC. It has been shown to have a dose-associated toxicity including polyarthralgia/arthritis, aphthous stomatitis, skin pigmentation, and uveitis.2Signs and symptoms of anterior uveitis with or without hypopyon, intermediate uveitis, and posterior uveitis or panuveitis may occur between 2 weeks and 7 months following the start of therapy. Symptoms can present with dosage as low as 300 mg/d.3,4Symptoms have been shown to worsen with increasing dose. Most cases resolve within 1 to 2 months of discontinuation of rifabutin and administration of topical corticosteroids. Published reports of rifabutin-associated uveitis have all been associated with concurrent medications like clarithromycin and fluconazole. These medications elevate serum rifabutin levels by inhibition of the hepatic microsomal cytochrome P-450 system that metabolizes rifabutin. This patient was taking concurrent clarithromycin as part of her MAC infection treatment.5,6Patients with rifabutin-associated uveitis have excellent visual prognosis, and most return to 20/30 visual acuity 3 weeks after initiating topical corticosteroid treatment, in some cases without requiring medication cessation.7 The initial clinical presentation of this patient was complicated by the recent history of trabeculectomy with mitomycin C. The constellation of conjunctival hyperemia, anterior chamber cellular reaction, hypopyon, and poor view of fundus in the context of trabeculectomy was highly suspicious for bleb-related infectious endophthalmitis. On clinical examination, the patient did not have a bleb leak or obvious blebitis. However, diagnosis of bleb-related endophthalmitis could not be excluded based on our clinical findings. Studies have shown that blebitis without bleb leak and blebitis with bleb leak present at a similar incidence (0.10% vs 0.11%).8Bleb-related endophthalmitis is one of the most serious sight-threatening late sequelae of trabeculectomy surgery for glaucoma. Treatment is extremely time sensitive. Therefore, in this clinical scenario, it was important for the patient to undergo immediate aqueous sampling to rule out infectious etiology and receive immediate hyperemia of intravitreal antibiotics. The patient was referred back to her infectious disease specialist for discontinuation of rifabutin and consideration for alternative treatment of her MAC infection. Topical corticosteroid treatment was initiated, and the patient will be followed up closely.

caption: Optic nerve photographs of the right eye (A) and left eye (B) revealing elevated, multilayered peripapillary hemorrhages and whitening, with obscured optic nerve margins except for the temporal aspect of the left optic nerve.
scenario: A 57-year-old man with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) refractory to multiple tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ie, imatinib, nilotinib, and bosutinib) presented for subacute-onset blurry vision in both eyes. He had been admitted for an upcoming bone marrow transplant. The patient had floaters without flashes and denied any eye pain. A review of symptoms found chronic fatigue and a new, mild headache beginning a few days prior. On examination, his visual acuity was 20/50 OU; intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 13 mm Hg OS; and pupils were equal, round, and reactive, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Extraocular movements, confrontational visual fields, and Ishihara color plates were full. An anterior segment examination had normal results. A fundus examination revealed clinically significant peripapillary intraretinal and preretinal hemorrhages obscuring the optic disc margins of both eyes (Figure 1). A peripheral retinal examination of both eyes had normal results.

options.A: Bilateral intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor injections
options.B: A rapid referral to radiation oncology for bilateral optic nerve radiation
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits

answer: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
distractors: Bilateral intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor injections
A rapid referral to radiation oncology for bilateral optic nerve radiation
explanation: Terson syndrome in a patient with CML with central nervous system involvement C. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits This patient, who had refractory CML and blurry vision, presented with bilateral peripapillary hemorrhages and whitening suggestive of possible optic nerve edema. His presentation was concerning for leukemic optic nerve infiltration. Also considered were hypertensive papillopathy, an intracranial mass with intracranial hypertension, an intracranial hemorrhage with Terson syndrome, and inflammatory or infectious sources of bilateral atypical optic neuritis. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits was ordered (choice C), and high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone was started. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage without optic nerve enlargement or enhancement, findings that did not suggest leukemic optic nerve infiltration.1A lumbar puncture demonstrated red blood cells, a mildly elevated opening pressure of 31 cm H2O, and cytology findings of malignant cells consistent with CML with central nervous system (CNS) involvement. Given the intracranial hemorrhage with both intraretinal and preretinal hemorrhages, a diagnosis of Terson syndrome was made. Terson syndrome occurs when intraocular hemorrhage presents in patients with intracranial hemorrhage or traumatic brain injury. The intraocular hemorrhage can occur in the vitreous, subhyaloid, intraretinal, or subretinal spaces.2Rupture of small retinal venules secondary to increased intracranial pressure is the leading proposed mechanism. The source of increased venous pressure is debated and thought to be attributable to either direct compression of the central retinal vein from optic nerve–sheath hemorrhage or increased orbital venous pressure from increased intracranial pressure.2,3 Although there was no leukemic optic nerve infiltration, an appropriate workup revealed previously unsuspected subclinical CNS involvement of CML. Extramedullary CNS involvement of CML is rare but can occur because of poor blood-brain barrier penetration of tyrosine kinase inhibitors.3Leukemic optic nerve infiltration is uncommon in CML but should be ruled out when any suspicion occurs, since it warrants emergency treatment. This often includes radiotherapy, since the optic nerves are considered pharmacologic sanctuaries from chemotherapy.4,5 Contacting radiation oncology (choice B) without first initiating a workup to confirm suspected leukemic infiltration is inappropriate. After ruling out leukemic infiltration, methylprednisolone was discontinued and intrathecal chemotherapy was started. The patient was observed and reassured that his visual acuity could improve when the hemorrhages resolved, since most patients with Terson syndrome achieve 20/30 visual acuity or better.6Reassurance prior to confirming the diagnosis (choice D) is inappropriate. Pars plana vitrectomy may be performed in cases of nonresolving hemorrhage.7Intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (choice A) is not indicated in Terson syndrome. Intracranial hemorrhage is the second most common complication, after infection, among adults with hematologic malignant conditions, and it is often the presenting sign of CNS involvement.8Terson syndrome has been described in the context of systemic CML but not with concurrent CNS involvement.9This case represents the rare occurrence of Terson syndrome leading to the diagnosis of extramedullary CML in the CNS. This patient underwent intrathecal chemotherapy with a subsequent bone marrow transplant. At 2-month follow-up, his visual acuity had improved to 20/40 OD and 20/30 OS, with resolving peripapillary hemorrhages (Figure 2).

caption: Slitlamp photographs of the right and left eyes show significant diffuse scleral injection, which did not blanch following administration of phenylephrine, 10%.
scenario: A 68-year-old man presented to the clinic with bilateral eye redness and pain for the past 6 months. He had a history of dry eye disease for which he was treated with preservative-free artificial tears. He also noted a medical history of well-controlled HIV with highly active antiretroviral therapy. His last CD 4 lymphocyte count was 750 cells/mm3with an undetectable viral load. A review of system produced negative results, including absence of weight loss, fevers, headache, joint pain, respiratory symptoms, or skin rash. The patient reported having unprotected sexual contact with multiple male partners in the past few years. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS. Slitlamp examination demonstrated diffuse scleral injection in both eyes without any scleral thinning. The redness did not blanch after administration of phenylephrine, 10% (Figure 1). Both eyes appeared to be moderately tender to touch. The rest of the anterior segment examination was within normal limits without any evidence of intraocular inflammation. Dilated fundus examination was also unremarkable in both eyes.

options.C: Laboratory work-up for infectious and autoimmune disease

answer: Laboratory work-up for infectious and autoimmune disease
explanation: C. Laboratory work-up for infectious and autoimmune disease Topical phenylephrine is used to differentiate episcleritis from scleritis. Episcleritis causes congestion of superficial episcleral vessels, which constrict when exposed to phenylephrine, whereas scleritis causes congestion of deeper vessels, which are not significantly affected by phenylephrine.1 Scleritis is often associated with a systemic disease, so further investigation is recommended prior to starting treatment (choice C).2Differential diagnosis includes autoimmune causes (rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatous polyangiitis, relapsing polychondritis, etc) and infections (syphilis, herpes viruses, etc).1,2Work-up should be tailored to clinical presentation and review of systems and includes serum autoantibody testing (rheumatoid factor, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, etc), sarcoidosis screening, syphilis testing, urinalysis, and others.1-3Nodular and diffuse anterior scleritis often respond to oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (choice A).2Corticosteroids (choice B) and systemic immunosuppression are recommended for patients who do not respond or necrotizing scleritis.1,3Topical corticosteroids (choice D) can reduce inflammation, but systemic treatment is often required.1 Syphilis is caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidumand has 4 stages.4The primary stage presents with a nontender chancre at the site of inoculation.1Secondary syphilis is characterized by a skin rash that resolves with or without treatment.1Untreated patients develop latent syphilis and 30% of these patients progress to tertiary syphilis, characterized by gumma, cardiovascular involvement, and neurosyphilis.5All cases of syphilis must be reported to the public health department for contact tracing.6 Ocular involvement occurs in 10% of patients with secondary or tertiary syphilis, and uveitis is the most common finding.5Scleritis is usually seen in tertiary syphilis.7Other manifestations of ocular syphilis include interstitial keratitis, chorioretinitis, papillitis, and Argyll Robertson pupil (light-near dissociation).1Patients with HIV infection are at an increased risk of neurosyphilis and bilateral ocular involvement.8 Serologic testing for syphilis includes nontreponemal tests (ie, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] and rapid plasma reagin) and treponemal tests (ie, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed andT pallidumparticle agglutination).1In the US, patients are usually tested using a nontreponemal screening test followed by a treponemal test to confirm positive results.9However, some researchers advocate for initial screening with a treponemal test owing to the reduced sensitivity of nontreponemal tests during late stages of the disease.10Because ocular syphilis often occurs in the tertiary phase, all patients with ocular involvement should undergo lumbar puncture with VDRL testing of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to evaluate for neurosyphilis. This test lacks sensitivity and, therefore, a reactive CSF-VDRL result confirms the diagnosis but a negative test result does not exclude it.7 Patients with tertiary syphilis are treated with 10 to 14 days of intravenous penicillin. Systemic corticosteroids may be added to prevent a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (a febrile reaction occurring in response to the release of endotoxins after initiation of treatment).7 All laboratory test results (including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and urinalysis) were negative except for syphilis IgG and rapid plasma reagin. Lumbar puncture showed a positive CSF-VDRL. The patient received a 14-day course of intravenous penicillin, which resulted in resolution of eye pain and redness within a few days (Figure 2).

scenario: An 80-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset bilateral horizontal diplopia accompanied by left-sided upper eyelid ptosis. On further questioning, she reported a 1-week history of drooling when eating. She had no other associated neurological or constitutional symptoms. No anhidrosis was noted. Her medical history was significant for a 2-year history of constant, dull, left-sided facial pain diagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia by her treating neurologist and moderately improved with gabapentin and nortriptyline. Recent computed tomography (CT) of the brain, conducted as part of her headache workup, had been reported as normal. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OU. Extraocular motility testing demonstrated no abduction of the left eye with corresponding large-angle incomitant esotropia increasing when looking to the left (Figure 1). There was 2 mm of left upper eyelid ptosis with preserved levator function. The left pupil was 1 mm smaller than the right in the light, with the difference increasing to 2 mm in the dark. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated reduced sensation in the left V1-V3 distribution and mild flattening of the nasolabial fold. Corneal sensation was slightly decreased on the left. Intraocular examination, including dilated fundus examination, was normal in both eyes.

options.B: Perform lumbar puncture to analyze cellular composition of cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast
options.D: Order tests of inflammatory markers: erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and complete blood cell count

answer: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast
distractors: Obtain CT angiography of head and neck
Perform lumbar puncture to analyze cellular composition of cerebrospinal fluid
Order tests of inflammatory markers: erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and complete blood cell count
explanation: Trigeminal schwannoma involving left cavernous sinus and the Meckel cave C. Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast This patient’s abnormalities comprise left sixth nerve palsy with ipsilateral Horner syndrome and trigeminal nerve palsy. This process localizes to the left cavernous sinus where the sixth nerve, trigeminal nerve, and sympathetic fibers travel in proximity: third-order sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus exit the internal carotid artery adventitia and pass alongside the sixth nerve as it courses through the cavernous sinus. The trigeminal ganglion is located in the Meckel cave, a dura-lined cavity lateral to the cavernous sinus, where the peripheral trigeminal divisions originate. Divisions V1 and V2 are pure sensory nerves, whereas V3 also carries motor nerves involved in mastication, explaining impaired chewing and drooling in this patient. All 3 divisions enter the cavernous sinus after exiting the Meckel cave. While brainstem lesions can cause multiple cranial neuropathies, slow progression of symptoms without accompanying neurological deficits make this unlikely in this case. In this patient, high-resolution neuroimaging is the next best step (option C). CT angiography (option A) can reveal vascular abnormalities of the cavernous sinus but will not identify subtle nonvascular lesions. Here, long-standing trigeminal numbness suggests a compressive etiology best visualized on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Lumbar puncture (option B) can rule out infectious, neoplastic, or inflammatory processes but would not localize the pathology. Elevated inflammatory markers (option D) may suggest giant cell arteritis, which can rarely present with sixth nerve palsy. However, slow-evolving symptomatology in this patient and trigeminal nerve involvement essentially rule out this diagnosis. Brain MRI demonstrated an expansile lesion at the left cavernous sinus and the Meckel cave with extension into the pterygopalatine fossa and foramen ovale (Figure 2). Radiographic characteristics were consistent with trigeminal ganglion schwannoma with compression of adjacent structures. Subsequent cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal composition and cytology. Intracranial schwannomas are the most common benign intracranial tumor in adults following meningiomas and pituitary tumors.1Occurrence may be sporadic or in association with neurofibromatosis type 2, and malignant transformation is very rare.2,3Treatment entails surgical resection4,5or, increasingly, stereotactic radiosurgery.6Despite radiosurgery, approximately one-third of cases may progress and symptomatic improvement is seen in fewer than 50% owing to the challenging tumor location.7As in the present case, trigeminal schwannomas are often misdiagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia is a distinct syndrome characterized by short, recurrent episodes of sharp pain. Atypical cases may feature prolonged facial pain.8In contrast, trigeminal schwannomas frequently present with chronic facial parasthesias.9Diplopia is also common due to cavernous sinus involvement.5,9To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of trigeminal schwannoma presenting with abducens palsy and Horner syndrome. Ophthalmologists must assess for Horner syndrome in patients with new abducens nerve palsy, as this suggests cavernous sinus pathology and necessitates urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain. Recognizing atypical headache syndromes can help ophthalmologists identify cases requiring further investigation. The patient underwent radiotherapy in an attempt to reduce tumor burden. Unfortunately, the tumor size and accompanying symptoms remained unchanged.

scenario: A 14-year-old boy was referred to us because of ocular and periocular pain with photophobia in his right eye for the last 5 days. Aside from atopic dermatitis, his medical history was unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Slitlamp examination of the right eye disclosed conjunctival hyperemia and ciliary congestion, anterior chamber flare 2+, and a few nongranulomatous keratic precipitates; the left anterior segment was quiet. Intraocular pressure was 15 mm Hg OU. Pupillary light responses were normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed 1+ of vitritis (binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy score) in the right eye and swelling of the optic disc in both eyes, to a greater extent in the right eye (Figure, A). Routine blood tests, including full blood cell count, plasma glucose levels, liver function test, and kidney function test, were performed on the same day and showed a serum creatinine level of 1.57 mg/dL (reference range: 0.5-1.0 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4). Antibodies anti–Treponema pallidumwere tested and the results were negative. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography at presentation showed increased thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer in both eyes, to a greater extent in the right eye. Fluorescein angiography revealed dye leakage of the right optic disc (Figure, B); no further abnormalities were found in both eyes. Indocyanine green angiography findings were normal.

options.A: Start treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics without further investigations
options.B: Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test
options.C: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits

answer: Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test
distractors: Start treatment with topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics without further investigations
Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
explanation: Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome B. Order urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin test Starting topical treatment with corticosteroids and cycloplegic eye drops without further investigations (choice A) would not be the preferred answer because abnormal kidney function warrants further investigations. Indeed in this case, urinalysis and urinary β2-microglobulin (β2M) testing (choice B) revealed normoglycemic glycosuria and increased β2M levels (6.6 mg/24 h; reference range, 0.02-0.37), suggestive of tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome (TINU).1Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits (choice C) was not indicated as urgent investigation, because the observed optic disc edema was most likely secondary to the intraocular inflammation rather than a central nervous system dysfunction. However, MRI of the brain and orbits was performed electively and did not show any abnormalities. Finally, observation (choice D) in symptomatic and active uveitis is not recommended. TINU is a rare cause of uveitis accounting for less than 2% of cases of uveitis and mostly affecting young patients with a median age at onset of 15 years.2,3Prevalence of TINU may be underestimated because of lack of recognition mainly in patients without evidence of kidney dysfunction or when proper laboratory testing is not performed at the first presentation.4Diagnosis requires both tubulointerstitial nephritis, suggested by kidney dysfunction and urinalysis, and uveitis. Notably, both kidney and eye disease can be asymptomatic and have independent progression.2Kidney dysfunction, whose clinical presentation is usually nonspecific (rash, arthralgia, and fever), is the result of an acute kidney injury that can eventually lead to chronic kidney disease.2,5Urinalysis may be positive for proteinuria, glycosuria, and cells, while urinary β2M is increased in the vast majority of cases.4Kidney biopsy is the definitive diagnostic procedure to confirm tubulointerstitial nephritis. Hettinga et al,1though, have shown that increased urinary β2M, combined with increased serum creatinine levels, is a reliable marker with high positive and negative predictive values for the diagnosis and monitoring of TINU. Other causes of uveitis with possible kidney involvement, such as sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, should always be excluded.1,2,6 Uveitis onset is variable but usually occurs 3 months after the onset of nephritis, and younger patients are more likely to develop a chronic course of uveitis (more than 3 months), despite proper treatment.2,7Although second-eye involvement can occur after presentation, uveitis is most commonly bilateral anterior.3Posterior ocular involvement or panuveitis are less common, although the optic disc may be involved in almost half of the patients at presentation.3-5,7,8Photophobia, loss of vision, and painful and red eye are the main presenting symptoms. The mainstay of treatment of TINU is topical and systemic corticosteroid therapy, which provides overall favorable outcomes. A close ophthalmic follow-up is recommended over the first year after the diagnosis, since recurrences are common and the use of immunomodulatory therapy is often needed.2,4 This patient presented with unilateral anterior uveitis and bilateral posterior ocular involvement, indicating that TINU may have a broad clinical presentation. Therefore TINU should be always considered as a possible cause of uveitis in pediatric population. A kidney biopsy to confirm the diagnosis was deemed unnecessary because of the morbidity of the procedure. The patient was given a tapering course of oral steroid and topical treatment of anterior uveitis. Both the uveitis and the kidney function dramatically improved after treatment. Optic disc edema improved 1 week after the start of oral steroid treatment and the patient was later switched to mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing agent. Mild disc swelling persisted over several months despite normal findings on repeated automated visual field examinations.

caption: Fundus photography of the right and left eyes showing slightly elevated and blurred optic disc margins (asterisk), mildly tortuous and dilated retinal vessels (black arrowheads), and intraretinal hemorrhages (pink arrowheads) in all quadrants in both eyes. In the left eye, a superficial optic nerve drusen (white arrowhead) was noted.
scenario: A 47-year-old woman, with dyslipidemia, presented to the emergency department with sudden vision loss in the right eye. Visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/20 OS. Anterior segment, tonometry, and pupillary light reflex were unremarkable. Ophthalmoscopy of the right eye showed discretely blurred optic disc margins, tortuous and dilated retinal veins, and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants; the left eye was unremarkable. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan showed a cystoid macular edema (CME) in the right eye; the left was unremarkable. Retinal nerve fiber layer thickness was 133 μm OD and 82 μm OS (reference value, 95.4 ± 10.48 μm).1A fluorescein angiography was scheduled. One week later, the patient returned to our department due to multiple episodes of amaurosis fugax in left eye. By that time, ophthalmoscopy disclosed a mild optic disc swelling, tortuous venous vessels, and retinal hemorrhages bilaterally (Figure 1). The OCT scan showed a CME spontaneous resolution in the right eye while the left eye was unremarkable. Fluorescein angiography revealed a slight delay in venous filling but no capillary nonperfusion areas. These features were compatible with bilateral nonischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), with spontaneous reperfusion in the right eye. A hypercoagulability and autoimmune workup—including peripheral blood smear, complete blood cell count, serum hyperviscosity, total protein level, protein electrophoresis, factor V Leiden, prothrombin, protein C and S, antithrombin, anticardiolipin, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies—gave normal results. A brain angiomagnetic resonance imaging scan was performed, which excluded central thrombosis.

options.B: Perform a thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography scan
options.C: Follow-up without further intervention
options.D: Initiate acetylsalicylic acid and no further intervention

answer: Perform a thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography scan
distractors: Initiate acetylsalicylic acid and no further intervention
explanation: Occult tumor presenting with bilateral CRVO B. Perform a thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography scan The fundus findings were consistent with bilateral CRVO. An extensive hypercoagulability and autoimmune workup producing normal results raised the suspicion of an underlying paraneoplastic syndrome. The patient was sent for an urgent thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography scan that revealed a right paratracheal adenopathy conglomerate with a dimension of 39 × 28 × 62 mm (Figure 2) and a thrombosis of the middle suprahepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome). Meanwhile, the patient promptly initiated anticoagulation treatment with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 hours. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration biopsy and anatomopathological results were inconclusive. A positron emission tomography scan was performed. In addition to the mediastinal mass, a supraclavicular adenopathy with increased fluorine 18–labeled fluorodeoxyglucose uptake was detected. A biopsy of this adenopathy revealed a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. To identify the primary tumor, extensive workups by gastroenterology, otorhinolaryngology, gynecology, and dermatology were performed. Despite the efforts, the primary location of the tumor was not identified. As such, the patient was diagnosed with an occult tumor and chemotherapy was initiated with carboplatin and placlitaxel. The management of this patient’s condition required a multidisciplinary approach. In the presence of bilateral CRVO, a proper systemic evaluation should be done, so option C—“Follow-up without further intervention”—wasn’t accurate. After ruling out the most frequent conditions, such as autoimmune and hematological diseases, paraneoplastic conditions need to be discarded. Additionally, option D—“Initiate acetylsalicylic acid and no further intervention,” would not be wise because there is no proven benefit of oral aspirin in cases of bilateral CRVO. In fact, it could lead to further vision loss because it may exacerbate the retinal hemorrhages.2Finally, because the anterior segment examination and fluorescein angiography did not identify neovascularization, there was no indication for panretinal laser photocoagulation, thereby excluding option A. Bilateral sequential CRVO is an extremely rare presenting feature of a solid tumor, in part because bilateral CRVO is very uncommon. Nonetheless, unilateral forms of CRVO are seldom found in patients with hypercoagulable states (eg, protein C and S, homocysteine) deriving from solid tumors, myeloproliferative disorders (eg, leukemia, multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia), or inflammatory diseases (eg, systemic lupus, sarcoidosis).3-6 In 1865, Trousseau7was the first to observe a positive correlation between tumors and increased likelihood of venous thrombosis. It is estimated that about 15% of these patients have thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications.8 In this case, the CRVO with vision loss was the only manifestation of an undisclosed malignancy. The complete systemic workup and the multidisciplinary approach led to a diagnosis of a potential life-threating disease. After initiating chemotherapy, the frequency of amaurosis fugax episodes significantly decreased. Her visual acuity improved to 20/20 OU and a significant attenuation of venous engorgement, decrease of retinal hemorrhages, and resolution of optic disc edema was observed. In the case of nonsystemic treatment response and persistence of CME, the patient will initiate intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor treatment.

B, Structural optical coherence tomography (inset image) and green fundus autofluorescence (main image) of the right eye show a macular atrophy that also involves the peripapillary region. The area of retinal pigment epithelium loss is featured by well-demarcated reduced autofluorescence (pink arrowhead) surrounded by speckled hyperautofluorescent areas (yellow arrowhead). scenario: A 45-year-old woman was referred to the medical retina service for evaluation of bilateral macular atrophy noted by her general ophthalmologist. Medical history was positive for bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with cochlear origin as determined by an otolaryngologist and headache since age 35 years. She had no history of longer-term use of medications. There was no family history of hearing and vision loss in all immediate family members. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/63 OS. Her pupils were round and reactive. The anterior segment was unremarkable. Fundus examination confirmed the presence of bilateral macular atrophy. Fundus autofluorescence revealed a fairly symmetric loss of autofluorescence in the macula and in the regions surrounding the optic disc (Figure). In proximity of these areas of reduced autofluorescence, a speckled fundus autofluorescence pattern of alternating spots of increased and decreased autofluorescence was also noted. Optical coherence tomography displayed the presence of a bilateral atrophy of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (Figure). The patient’s family underwent a complete ophthalmologic evaluation, which did not display any alteration.

options.A: Prescribe laboratory testing to investigate causes of intraocular inflammation
options.B: Genetic testing to rule out pattern dystrophy
options.C: Genetic testing to rule out a mitochondrial disease
options.D: Genetic testing to rule out Stargardt disease

answer: Genetic testing to rule out a mitochondrial disease
distractors: Prescribe laboratory testing to investigate causes of intraocular inflammation
Genetic testing to rule out pattern dystrophy
Genetic testing to rule out Stargardt disease
explanation: Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and strokelike episodes–related syndrome C. Genetic testing to rule out a mitochondrial disease Macular atrophy may represent the clinical outcome of different disorders sharing some overlap in the biological pathways. While age-related macular degeneration is the most common disorder associated with macular atrophy, macular atrophy may be also the result of medications-associated retinal toxicity, ocular inflammation, and genetically determined retinal dystrophies. A detailed collection of medical and family history is mandatory as initial workup in cases of macular atrophy. Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and strokelike episodes syndrome (MELAS) represents a clinical entity associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.1,2As with  other mitochondrial disorders, MELAS is maternally inherited and is characterized by incomplete penetrance.1-3MELAS is due to mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations. Specifically, theMT-TL1mitochondrial gene (OMIM590050) is the most frequently mutated and, in particular, the most frequent is the point mutation m.3243A>G/MT-TL1.4,5Besides the full-blown MELAS,1,2this disorder may have variable clinical expressivity with a broad spectrum of manifestations.4,5This variability is partially related to the phenomenon of heteroplasmy, defined as the coexistence of wild-type and mutated mtDNA copies in the same cell. As distinct cells and tissues may have different heteroplasmy percentages, the phenotypic expression may vary among patients.6-10 The retinopathy associated with MELAS has heterogeneous presentations, and De Laat et al10differentiated the MELAS-associated retinopathy in 4 stages, as follows: (1) presence of fine pigment changes, (2) evidence of yellowish or mildly pigmented deposits, (3) outer retina and RPE atrophy outside the fovea; and (4) atrophy involving the fovea. For these reasons, when a middle-aged patient presents with a macular atrophy associated with neurologic manifestations, the suspect of a mitochondrial disease (MELAS or maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) is mandatory. First, a detailed family history should be collected. However, family history may be unrevealing because mitochondrial disorders may have incomplete penetrance, and de novo mutations, although uncommon, may also occur. Second, blood tests for lactic acidosis and genetic testing should be performed. Nonetheless, the diagnosis can be complicated as heteroplasmy may be a cause of false-negative blood genetic testing to identify mtDNA mutations in leukocytes. Therefore, genetic testing should be replicated on other epithelial or postmitotic tissues (eg, urinary epithelial cells, buccal mucosa, or skeletal muscle) in cases of high suspicion and negative results on blood cells. In this patient, blood test results were negative for both lactic acidosis and presence of mitochondrial gene mutations. However, the subsequent genetic testing on urinary epithelial cells was positive for m.3243A>G mutation (52% of heteroplasmic load) and a diagnosis of MELAS-related syndrome was made. Prescribing laboratory testing to investigate causes of intraocular inflammation (choice A) would not be the preferred answer because a bilateral macular atrophy is an uncommon presentation for uveitis, especially in a patient without other ocular signs of inflammation. A genetic testing for pattern dystrophy (choice B) was not recommended as the next step as this disease is not usually associated with neurologic disorders (ie, headache and hearing loss). A genetic testing for Stargardt disease (choice D) would not be the next recommended step because of the presence of atrophy around the optic disc, which is unusual in Stargardt disease. The patient was extensively informed about her condition and the prognosis. Genetic counseling was recommended to illustrate the risk of this disease to other family members. Moreover, the patient underwent tests aimed at assessing the degree of mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction and including lactic acid at rest and after standardized exercise, levels of plasmatic amino acids including arginine, alanine, and citrulline, and brain1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Although MELAS is considered an untreatable disorder, novel therapeutic options are available that are mainly aimed at slowing down the disease course by ameliorating the mitochondrial respiratory chain dysfunction. These treatments include antioxidants such as arginine, citrulline, and taurine.
