scenario: A 70-year-old woman with an ocular history of primary open-angle glaucoma on latanoprost, bilateral trabeculectomies, and argon laser trabeculoplasties presented with several months of worsening vision in the left eye. On examination, her best-corrected distance visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/60 OS (baseline 20/40 OU). Pupils were equally round and reactive, without afferent pupillary defect. Findings of Amsler grid testing were notable for a small area of distortion inferiorly in the left eye. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 13 mm Hg in both eyes. Findings of anterior segment examination were unremarkable. Findings of dilated fundus examination were notable for cup-disc ratio of 0.9 in the right eye and 0.85 in the left eye with temporal thinning, stable from prior, and new intraretinal thickening in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging of the left eye revealed schiticlike separation of the outer plexiform and outer nuclear layers extending from the temporal edge of the optic nerve head to the fovea (Figure 1A), continuous with the peripapillary nerve sheath.

options.C: Observation
options.D: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene

answer: Observation
distractors: Genetic testing for the RS1 gene
explanation: Macular retinoschisis in the setting of glaucomatous optic atrophy The patient’s decreased vision was due to macular retinoschisis, an abnormal splitting of the neuroretina associated with glaucomatous optic atrophy. Observation (choice C) is correct because the patient noted only mild distortion, and retinoschisis can remain stable1or resolve spontaneously2,3in up to 40% of cases.3Schisis can resolve after vitrectomy,1so surgery (choice A) could be pursued if symptoms worsened. Barrier laser (choice B), as described by Prinzi et al,4has been used to treat retinoschisis in glaucoma; however, peripapillary laser photocoagulation carries risk of vision loss and the patient had only a 2-line decrease in vision. Testing for theRS1gene (choice D) would be indicated if X-linked retinoschisis was suspected; however, this disease appears almost exclusively in boys. Retinoschisis is rare in patients with glaucoma, with a reported rate of 5.9%3in 1 study. In this study, retinoschisis in glaucoma originated from the optic disc and overlapped with retinal nerve fiber layer defects, suggesting that schisis correlates with glaucomatous damage to the optic nerve head. Similarly, patients with schisis had worse visual field mean deviations compared with patients without.3Approximately one-third of eyes with schisis also had an acquired optic disc pit (aODP).3The relationship between glaucoma, aODPs, and retinoschisis is unclear. aODPs may represent areas of increased susceptibility owing to damage from glaucoma5and could be an entry point for liquified vitreous to enter the retina, initiating retinoschisis.6Therefore, the presence of an aODP in a patient with glaucoma could increase the likelihood of retinoschisis development. The patient had an optic disc pit that was visible on OCT imaging at the time of schisis onset (Figure 1B). The contribution of IOP to retinoschisis in glaucoma is not well understood. In 1 study, patients with glaucoma with retinoschisis at the initiation of the study had higher IOPs than patients without retinoschisis.3However, retinoschisis has also been reported in normal tension glaucoma,7suggesting high IOP is not a requisite for retinoschisis development. Patients who developed retinoschisis over time did not have changes in IOP before and after retinoschisis development, suggesting IOP fluctuations are not causative.3Interestingly, resolution of retinoschisis was associated with either trabeculectomy or the initiation of IOP-lowering medications. Similarly, there are case reports of retinoschisis resolving after glaucoma surgery.1,8In this patient, IOP had been well controlled prior to schisis development and no trigger could be identified, suggesting that it was the result of chronic glaucomatous damage rather than an acute process. In conclusion, the development of macular retinoschisis is associated with glaucoma and can cause decreased visual acuity in a patient with glaucoma, even with well-controlled IOP. Mild vision loss can be managed conservatively with observation. The patient was monitored with serial OCT imaging, which showed gradual improvement of the schisis over an 18-month period (Figure 2), with residual persistence along the nasal edge of the macula and return of visual acuity to baseline of 20/40 OU. The patient’s glaucoma continued to be successfully managed medically.

scenario: A woman in her 20s with a history of daily soft contact lens (CL) wear was referred by her local ophthalmologist for a recalcitrant central corneal ulcer in her left eye. She had no history of eye trauma, did not sleep in her CLs, and stopped using CLs at symptom onset. Of note, she had recently been swimming in a freshwater lake prior to the onset of the ulcer. She was initially treated with topical besifloxacin and followed up daily. She appeared to improve clinically with resolution of her epithelial defect after 3 days, and topical loteprednol was added. Results of initial corneal cultures were negative. One week later, she presented with worsening pain and vision, which prompted referral to our cornea clinic where, 2 weeks after her initial presentation, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/150 OS. Left-eye examination demonstrated diffuse microcystic corneal edema and stromal thickening with no Descemet membrane folds (Figure 1A). A 2 × 2-mm stromal opacity was noted paracentrally with no epithelial defects. The anterior chamber demonstrated 1+ cell. Intraocular pressure was 17 mm Hg OS. Corneal cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acanthamoeba were repeated, and in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) was performed on the stromal infiltrate (Figure 1B). After reviewing the IVCM images, what empirical treatment would you recommend while awaiting the results of the repeated corneal cultures?

options.C: Voriconazole

answer: Voriconazole
explanation: Purpureocillium lilacinum keratitis confirmed by culture growth 21 days later We present a case of a young patient with a contact lens–associated infectious keratitis. IVCM (Heidelberg Retina Tomograph 3 with Rostock Cornea Module; Heidelberg) of the anterior stroma (Figure 1B) revealed a collection of hyperreflective septate branching hyphae, compatible with filamentous fungi such asAspergillus,Fusarium, and rarelyPurpureocillium lilacinum(PL). The diagnosis of filamentous fungal keratitis was made, and therapy was started with topical voriconazole (choice C), in addition to oral voriconazole. Vancomycin (choice A) is commonly used as empirical therapy for moderate to severe corneal infections, since gram-positive bacteria are a frequent etiologic microbe. However, IVCM findings suggested a fungal etiology for this ulcer. Fluconazole (choice B) is an azole antifungal agent with great efficacy against yeast, such asCandidaspecies. Filamentous fungi are better treated with voriconazole or natamycin. Lastly IVCM demonstrated the presence of hyphae, which are elongated branching structures, unlike acanthamoeba, which typically presents as hyperreflective double-walled cystic lesions. Therefore, polyhexamethylene biguanide and propamidine isethionate were not indicated (choice D). PL (formerly known asPaecilomyces lilacinus) is a filamentous fungus found throughout the world in decomposing plants and soil.1In a series of 28 patients with PL keratitis,2CL use represented the biggest risk factor, present in 71% of patients. Thus, even in the absence of trauma with organic material or corneal surgery, CL use should raise the suspicion for filamentous keratitis. Other known risk factors include trauma1and immunosuppression.3However, 1 study found PL keratitis was most common in individuals with an absent ocular history.4Prognosis is variable and better when linked to a timely diagnosis. Presentations may range from rapidly resolving keratitis to endophthalmitis requiring enucleation.3Importantly, patients presenting 2 weeks after onset of disease, or who had received prior steroids, carry a significantly worse visual prognosis.2Thus, for ulcers recalcitrant to initial treatment, we recommend prompt referral to a cornea specialist. Unlike other filamentous fungi, PL does not reliably respond to commonly used topical antifungals such as natamycin and amphotericin B; thus, early diagnosis is critical to direct accurate treatment. Effective treatment regimens may include topical voriconazole, oral terbinafine, and oral voriconazole.3In refractory cases, oral posaconazole has also shown efficacy.5The role of IVCM is crucial to rapidly diagnose fungal etiologies. Prior studies of patients with microbial keratitis demonstrated that confocal microscopy had a diagnostic sensitivity of 71% to 94% and a specificity of 78% to 89.6% for fungal keratitis.6,7 In summary,P lilacinumis a rare, yet potentially devastating corneal pathogen if not diagnosed early. IVCM, if available to the clinician, should be performed on suspected microbial keratitis, especially when cases progress despite empirical treatments or have negative culture results. After 1 week of treatment with topical and oral voriconazole, corneal edema was significantly decreased, the epithelium had healed, and conjunctival hyperemia was improving. At 1 month, visual acuity was 20/30 OS. On examination, the cornea was nearly clear, except for a central superficial anterior scar of 2 × 2.5 mm (Figure 2).

scenario: A patient in their early 20s with no medical history or previous symptoms presented for severe frontal headaches and progressive blurred vision in the left eye more than the right eye for several weeks. No localizing signs were documented on neurologic examination. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without contrast, magnetic resonance angiography of the head, and magnetic resonance venography of the head were obtained and were unremarkable. The result of a lumbar puncture showed 101 white blood cells per high-power field (75% lymphocytes). Results of syphilis serologic tests were negative. The patient was discharged with suspected viral meningitis. At a follow-up visit in an ophthalmology clinic 1 week after discharge, visual acuity was 20/25 OD and counting fingers OS. There was no afferent pupillary defect, and an anterior segment examination was within normal limits. A dilated fundus examination showed numerous bilateral creamy-yellow lesions in the peripheral retina with discrete nummular lesions in the posterior pole (Figure 1A). Fundus autofluorescence showed focal areas of hypoautofluorescence with surrounding hyperautofluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1B). The patient continued to report severe and progressive headaches along with blurred vision. A review of systems was otherwise unremarkable.

options.A: Send for infectious and inflammatory tests and follow up within 1 week
options.B: Send for infectious and inflammatory tests, begin oral prednisone therapy, and follow up in 1 week
options.C: Send to emergency department for admission and initiation of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone sodium succinate therapy

distractors: Send for infectious and inflammatory tests and follow up within 1 week
Send for infectious and inflammatory tests, begin oral prednisone therapy, and follow up in 1 week
explanation: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy C. Send to emergency department for admission and initiation of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone therapy Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy is associated with cerebral vasculitis, which should prompt consideration of immediate treatment with high-dose corticosteroids. Headache is the most common symptom in patients with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) and central nervous system (CNS) involvement. Normal MRI and magnetic resonance angiography do not exclude cerebral vasculitis in APMPPE.1Outpatient follow-up in 1 week could be dangerous because of the high morbidity and mortality of untreated cerebral vasculitis (choices A and D). Corticosteroid therapy should be considered but delaying full neurologic workup for 1 week could also be dangerous (choice B). Recognition of this association by an ophthalmologist can be lifesaving. Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy is an inflammatory chorioretinopathy that typically presents with bilateral multifocal, placoid, creamy-white lesions in the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid.2Patients are usually young healthy adults; 33% report antecedent flulike illness.3Fluorescein angiography typically shows early hypofluorescence and late staining of the lesions, which resolve spontaneously after several weeks.4 Central nervous system involvement in patients with APMPPE appears to be rare but well documented and includes headache, hemiplegia, hemiparesis, incontinence, seizures, paresthesia, and cranial nerve palsies.1,5,6Although at least 60 cases of APMPPE with CNS involvement have been reported in the literature, its precise incidence is unknown.6,7Severe cerebral vasculitis and death may also occur.5Patients presenting with APMPPE and headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms should be sent to an emergency department for urgent neurovascular imaging with neurologic consultation.6The most common finding on imaging is hemorrhagic infarcts; however, 1 review found that findings of MRI scans in 33% of patients were interpreted as normal.1Lumbar puncture may be a more sensitive test because 94% of patients with APMPPE and CNS manifestations have an elevated white blood cell count.1Angiogram is the most sensitive test for cerebral vasculitis and may detect signs of cerebral vasculitis in patients with negative imaging results.1 A narrative review of patients with APMPPE found that 56% of the eyes were treated with medical therapy in the form of topical, oral, or intravenous corticosteroids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or systemic immunosuppressive agents.3No prospective trials exist on the potential benefit of corticosteroids for visual acuity outcomes in patients with APMPPE. Many authors have recommended observation because of the likely spontaneous resolution of the lesions.2Some investigators have advocated for the use of oral corticosteroids in cases involving the fovea and in recurrent cases on the basis of anecdotal evidence and a presumed underlying inflammatory cause (choice B).8,9If CNS involvement is present, intravenous corticosteroids with concomitant immunosuppressive agents should be considered (choice C).1We recommend that any patient with APMPPE who experiences headache, fever, or other neurologic symptoms be evaluated for cerebral vasculitis. The patient was admitted, received 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone, and had resolution of headaches. The patient was discharged and began a prolonged oral prednisone taper. The patient’s visual acuity improved to 20/20 OD and 20/100 OS at a 3-month follow-up visit, with resolution of lesions (Figure 2). The patient had no ocular recurrences during the next year but experienced recurrence of headaches while decreasing the dose of corticosteroids, which resolved with a slower corticosteroid taper. No additional neuroimaging was performed because of the stable neurologic examination and resolution of symptoms.

scenario: A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertensive retinopathy presented with acute-onset, painless vision loss in his right eye accompanied by tinnitus and severe intermittent headaches. His extraocular movements were full, and he had no other neurologic deficits. His visual acuity was 20/400 OD and 20/30 OS, respectively, and his fundi were notable for bilateral optic nerve edema. Results of recent computed tomography and angiography of the head and neck and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits were reportedly normal, and lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 26 cm H2O (normal range, 6 to 25 cm H2O) with elevated protein. The patient was given acetazolamide and referred to neuro-ophthalmology. On examination by neuro-ophthalmology 4 months later, his visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. He had an afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, and Humphrey visual fields (24-2) showed binasal inferior defects with a superior defect in the right eye that was considered an artifact of testing. According to the Ishihara color plates test, color vision was full in both eyes. Fundus examination was remarkable for pallor of both optic nerves, more notably in the right eye, without edema (Figure 1). Findings of screening for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzyme,Bartonella, HIV, tuberculosis (Quantiferon),Treponema pallidum, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a complete blood cell count were normal.

options.C: Start high-dose corticosteroids
options.D: Continue acetazolamide and repeated Humphrey visual fields test and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer in 3 months

answer: Repeated lumbar puncture with serologies
distractors: Continue acetazolamide and repeated Humphrey visual fields test and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer in 3 months
explanation: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system B. Repeated lumbar puncture with serologies Bilateral disc edema, transient vision loss, and elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture are suggestive of intracranial hypertension, which may be idiopathic intracranial hypertension or secondary to a mass-occupying lesion, dural venous sinus thrombosis, or another underlying disease, including anemia, Addison disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus.1While tighter blood pressure control (choice A) would be helpful in hypertensive retinopathy, elevated blood pressure medications do not mitigate elevated intracranial pressure. With negative laboratory findings for autoimmune or inflammatory disease, there is no indication to start high-dose corticosteroids (choice C). The patient had persistent visual field deficits despite acetazolamide use, which requires further investigation beyond monitoring with serial testing (choice D). A repeated lumbar puncture (choice B) revealed an opening pressure of 18 cm H2O, an IgG level of 6.6 mg/dL (normal range, 0.5 to 5.9 mg/dL; to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 0.01), and 4 oligoclonal bands (normal range, 0 to 1). Throughout this workup, the patient began to develop new neurological symptoms, including persistent left cranial nerve V numbness, paresthesia, fatigue, cold intolerance, throbbing headache, and bradyphrenia (ie, slowing of cognition). A repeated brain magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance venogram of the head showed no evidence of venous sinus thrombosis but identified multifocal enhancing and nonenhancing signal abnormalities of the brain at the callososeptal interface, juxtacortical regions, basal ganglia, and brainstem. In light of these findings and given the cerebrospinal fluid serology results, the patient was urgently referred for neuroinflammatory evaluation. A few weeks later, the patient was hospitalized after developing sudden-onset confusion. During his hospitalization, an extensive workup of serum and cerebrospinal fluid studies for infectious, autoimmune, and demyelinating diseases was performed. Within the context of this patient’s clinical course, a brain biopsy that showed histopathologic features suspicious for vasculitis helped determine the diagnosis (Figure 2). Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is a rare idiopathic disorder characterized by vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord. The clinical spectrum of PACNS remains poorly understood given its diverse and nonspecific clinical manifestations.2Headache is the most common symptom, occurring in roughly 60% of patients. Ocular abnormalities occur in 41% of cases, including visual-field defect (18%), diplopia (14%), blurred vision or decreased visual acuity (11%), and papilledema (4.3%).3,4Diagnosing PACNS frequently involves a combination of clinical findings: an unexplained neurological deficit, laboratory workup that rules out secondary causes of central nervous system vasculitis, imaging findings, and/or histopathologic features of vasculitis on brain biopsy.2,5,6Treatment of PACNS includes induction therapy of high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide with periodic reassessment of neurologic symptoms and neuroimaging for treatment response. Maintenance therapy with a corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressive agent, such as azathioprine, is typically started after 4 to 6 months. Favorable response to treatment is reportedly greater than 80%.4,7 The patient’s cognitive function showed remarkable improvement following induction of glucocorticoids in combination with cyclophosphamide at 7-month follow-up.

scenario: A 54-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of right ptosis and double vision. He was otherwise healthy and did not take any regular medications. Initially, he had horizontal diplopia on the first day that was worse at the end of the day, but this resolved when the right eyelid ptosis became complete. He denied any difficulty with his speech, swallowing, weakness, or sensory changes. He presented to the emergency department, and the emergency department physician reported a normal neurological examination result apart from the right-sided ptosis and limited eye movements. He was referred to ophthalmology and had a visual acuity of 20/20 OU. Both pupils were equal sizes and reactive to light. He was found to only have a complete limitation of elevation of his right eye and a limitation of abduction in his left eye (Figure). He was orthophoric in primary position, and there were no eyelid twitches. Orbicularis oculi strength was reduced on both sides. A dilated fundus examination had normal results bilaterally. An initial neurological examination, including assessments of motor strength in the upper and lower extremities and reflexes and a sensory examination, had normal results.

options.A: Complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein tests
options.B: Computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the head
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits with contrast

answer: Ice pack test
distractors: Complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein tests
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the head
Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits with contrast
explanation: This patient had new-onset right ptosis with an inability to elevate his right eye and abduct his left eye, with otherwise normal neurologic examination results. This combination of examination findings cannot be localized in the central nervous system, because there is involvement of the levator muscle and superior rectus on the right (innervated by cranial nerve III) and the lateral rectus on the left (innervated by cranial nerve VI). This should raise concern for ocular myasthenia gravis, and a readily accessible test in the clinic is an ice pack test or rest test, which should result in an improvement in the ptosis, as was seen in this patient. His palpebral fissure measured 1 mm before ice was applied and 6 mm 5 minutes after the application of ice. The ice test has been reported to have a sensitivity of 0.94% and specificity of 0.97% in ocular myasthenia1and is based on the principle that cooler temperatures result in reduced acetylcholinesterase activity.1It involves placing ice on the involved eyelid for at least 2 minutes and comparing the pretest to posttest measurements. The test is considered to have positive results when there is an increase in the size of the palpebral fissure compared with the pretest measurement. This patient had no symptoms of giant cell arteritis, such as headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication, and he was relatively young for this condition, which is why choice A was not the next best option. Neuroimaging would not be the next best step, because his examination findings could not be localized. Computed tomography angiography or magnetic resonance angiography would be indicated in a third nerve palsy, but this patient did not have this, which is why choice B was not correct. He had no orbital signs (eg, proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, eyelid retraction), and an orbital lesion would not explain the ptosis, which is why choice C was not correct. Ocular myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction confined to the ocular muscles. In ocular myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies develop against the acetylcholine receptors (commonly) or other associated proteins at the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle weakness and fatigability.2Patients typically present with ptosis and diplopia that is worse with muscle use, with normal pupil reactions. While more than 85% of patients with the systemic variant have detectable autoantibodies in their serum, patients with the ocular variant have 45% to 60% sensitivity with the same test.3In seronegative ocular myasthenia gravis, single-fiber electromyography may be used to evaluate neuromuscular transmission.4In this patient, serum acetylcholine receptor antibody tests had negative results, but single-fiber electromyography was highly suggestive of a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder. Initial therapy for ocular myasthenia gravis consists of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as 30 to 150 mg of pyridostigmine 3 to 4 times daily.5Many patients need additional immunosuppression for full clinical remission, including prednisone, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil.6Approximately two-thirds of patients with ocular myasthenia gravis will progress to systemic disease,7and patients should be counseled on seeking medical attention if they have clinically significant sequelae, such as difficulty breathing. The patient’s ptosis and diplopia mildly improved with 60 mg of pyridostigmine 3 times daily, and prednisone daily was started at 10 mg and titrated up to 40 mg, resulting in complete remission. At his 6-month follow-up, a slow taper of prednisone was initiated because he continued to have no ptosis and normal ocular motility.

scenario: A 47-year-old man presented with gradual onset of blurry vision in both eyes for several months. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS. Intraocular pressure was 23 mm Hg in both eyes and was more than 21 mm Hg in both eyes on multiple visits. Medical history included hypertension, obesity, left adrenalectomy, and pterygium excision surgery in the left eye. The patient denied previous episodes of blurry vision, history of corticosteroid use, sleep apnea, or type-A personality. Complete review of systems was otherwise negative. Amsler grid testing revealed paracentral metamorphopsia in both eyes. Extraocular motility, pupillary light reactions, and confrontational visual fields were normal. Slitlamp examination and gonioscopy results were normal in both eyes. An external photograph of the patient is shown inFigure 1A. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple areas of late pinpoint leakage and patches of mottled hyperfluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1B).

options.A: Intravitreal injection of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agent
options.C: Draw morning plasma cortisol levels
options.D: Bone marrow biopsy for tumors associated with paraproteinemias

answer: Draw morning plasma cortisol levels
distractors: Intravitreal injection of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agent
Bone marrow biopsy for tumors associated with paraproteinemias
explanation: Bilateral central serous chorioretinopathy secondary to pituitary microadenoma C. Draw morning plasma cortisol levels This patient exhibited signs of hypercortisolism, including central obesity (Figure 1). He had systemic hypertension, which occurs in most patients with endogenous hypercortisolism,1,2and elevated intraocular pressure, which has been reported in endogenous hypercortisolism and can be caused by corticosteroid use.3,4His hemoglobin A1clevel was elevated (6.8%), which is consistent with impaired glucose metabolism in endogenous hypercortisolism.2 Fluorescein angiography showed multiple areas of late pinpoint leakage and guttering, which is patchy, mottled hyperfluorescence caused by gravity-related descending tracts of subretinal fluid (Figure 1). These fluorescein angiography findings are typical of central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), which is characterized by serous detachment of neurosensory retina/retinal pigment epithelium (Figure 2) and choroidal hyperpermeability. The leakage on fluorescein angiography is most consistent with active CSC, whereas the patches of mottled fluorescence are more typical of chronic CSC. The patient denied corticosteroid exposure; given the possibility of hypercortisolism of unknown cause, he was referred to the endocrinology unit for further evaluation. Cortisol testing (choice C) was performed and showed elevated 8amplasma cortisol (15.2 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588). Overnight challenge with 1 mg of dexamethasone resulted in an 8amplasma cortisol of 17.8 µg/dL, confirming hypercortisolism. Adrenocorticotropic hormone levels were not suppressed, raising suspicion for a central cause of hypercortisolism. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling confirmed a central source of adrenocorticotropic hormone, and pituitary magnetic resonance imaging revealed a pituitary microadenoma. The differential diagnosis for this case included CSC associated with exogenous, or rarely, endogenous hypercortisolism, neovascular age-related macular degeneration, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy or pathologic myopia with choroidal neovascularization, and paraproteinemia. However, the patient’s relatively young age and lack of drusen were not consistent with age-related macular degeneration. Moreover, the patient lacked polypoidal lesions on indocyanine green angiography findings, making polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy less likely. The patient did not have myopia, making pathologic myopia unlikely. Intravitreal injection of an anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agent (choice A) would be an appropriate treatment for CSC with choroidal neovascularization but not in this patient without choroidal neovascularization.5,6Bilateral retinal pigment epithelium detachments can also be found in paraproteinemia, although the patient had normal blood cell counts and did not report any B-signs of malignancy. Therefore, bone marrow biopsy (choice D) was not indicated. Neither oral spironolactone (choice B), a mineralocorticoid antagonist, nor eplerenone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, improve visual acuity in patients with CSC.7,8A workup for underlying causes of hypercortisolism (choice C) should be considered prior to retinal management of CSC in a patient with Cushingoid appearance. Risk factors for CSC include corticosteroid use in any form.9CSC is rarely caused by endogenous hypercortisolism.10Ophthalmologists should be cognizant that while Cushing syndrome is most commonly caused by corticosteroid-containing medications, it may also result from an adrenocorticotropic hormone–secreting pituitary tumor (Cushing disease). The patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary microadenoma. His vision remains stable, but serum cortisol levels have not yet normalized.

scenario: A woman in her 50s with hypertension who was otherwise in good health presented for new ophthalmologic evaluation in the setting of mild, long-standing blurred vision with slight metamorphopsia in the right eye. She had a history of high myopia (approximately 9 diopters [D]OD; 8DOS). Examination revealed an otherwise normal left eye with 20/20 best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). The right eye demonstrated a BCVA of 20/25 and normal anterior segment, including lenticular examination. Dilated fundus examination showed wrinkling of the neurosensory retina at the fovea (Figure 1A) without posterior vitreous detachment. options.C: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition

distractors: Vitrectomy with epiretinal and internal limiting membrane peeling
explanation: Foveal retinoschisis with epiretinal membrane in the setting of pathologic myopia D. Observation without considering intervention unless visual acuity deterioration is found A diagnostic explanation for retinal splitting, hyporeflective spaces, or cystoid abnormalities is necessary when evaluating retinal problems with optical coherence tomography, which sometimes can be multifactorial. The differential diagnosis for these findings in the macula includes inherited retinal disorders (eg, X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, Goldmann-Favre syndrome), medications (eg, antimicrotubular agents), vascular insults (eg, retinal vein occlusion), and trauma. In this case, the presence of an epiretinal membrane with pathologic myopia was suggestive of foveoschisis. Visualization can be supplemented by en face images and vitreoretinal interface segmentation. Myopic foveoschisis, typically with associated features, including staphyloma,1can be associated with substantial visual acuity loss that may not always be correctable with surgical intervention. These problems are often compounded by other visual acuity loss from pathologic myopia, such as myopic degeneration in the posterior pole, in addition to epiretinal proliferation or dense remnants of cortical vitreous following posterior vitreous detachment. Foveoschisis does not always have to be accompanied by epiretinal membrane, and the causative mechanism of myopic foveoschisis remains unknown.1 Given mild visual impairment for this patient, observation was elected (choice D) instead of opting for surgical peeling (choice A). Surgery is warranted if there is substantial visual impairment, assessed through BCVA and metamorphopsia by Amsler grid testing. Judgment involves determining the effect on function by considering the patient’s occupation and activities of daily living. It is often reasonable to monitor for clear disease progression before proceeding with vitrectomy and membrane peeling. Many cases are successful with both epiretinal and internal limiting membrane peeling for reducing recurrence.2 Periocular steroids (choice B) may benefit macular edema arising from diabetes or inflammatory conditions, but they are unlikely to be helpful for this causative mechanism of retinoschisis. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition (choice C) with either topical dorzolamide or oral acetazolamide is known to help macular edema associated with retinitis pigmentosa, but it is not typically used for retinoschisis. Spontaneous resolution of foveoschisis without intervention has been reported, independent of the status of the posterior hyaloid.1,3-5Release of epiretinal membrane and posterior hyaloid may follow known age-associated changes at the vitreomacular attachment interface.6Close observation is therefore reasonable in select cases, depending on impairment and overall clinical context. Additional research is needed to further characterize the natural history of this condition, including frequency of progression, spontaneous resolution, and recurrence. Four years after presentation and electing observation, the patient returned with resolution of the foveoschisis and release of posterior hyaloid. She achieved 20/20 OU visual acuity, which was sustained 9 years later (Figure 2).

caption: Wide-field retinal photographs (Optos) of the right (A) and left (B) eyes show tractional retinal detachment (white arrowheads), hemorrhage (red arrowheads), neovascularization (blue arrowheads), and proliferative vitreoretinopathy in front of the optic nerve (black arrowheads).
scenario: A 28-year-old man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) presented with a recent bilateral and painless decrease of best-corrected visual acuity to light perception OD and counting fingers OS. Results of a slitlamp examination showed iris neovascularization and posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye and no anterior segment abnormalities, including no iris neovascularization, in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 60 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. The fundus in the right eye (Figure, A) showed a total retinal detachment with hemorrhagic prepapillary fibrosis reaching up to the posterior capsule; the left eye (Figure, B) showed peripapillary tractional retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy, retinal neovascularization, and vitreous hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography showed extensive retinal capillary and arteriolar nonperfusion and peripapillary neovascularization in both eyes. The patient denied diabetes, sickle cell disease, radiotherapy exposure, and any ophthalmic history. He was not followed up regularly by an ophthalmologist but had consulted an outside clinic 3 weeks before for a loss of visual acuity, which measured at 20/400 OD and 20/63 OS. Visual acuity preceding this consultation was not known.

options.A: Perform a pars plana vitrectomy with chorioretinal biopsy
options.B: Contact the patient’s general practitioner and cardiologist to obtain hemoglobin and cardiac ejection fraction levels
options.C: Administer an intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor injection

answer: Contact the patient’s general practitioner and cardiologist to obtain hemoglobin and cardiac ejection fraction levels
distractors: Perform a pars plana vitrectomy with chorioretinal biopsy
Administer an intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor injection
explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy–associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy B. Contact the patient’s general practitioner and cardiologist to obtain hemoglobin and cardiac ejection fraction levels Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy caused by absent or altered dystrophin production with an incidence of 1 per 3500 male births.1First symptoms appear around 3 to 5 years of age with most patients requiring the use of a wheelchair by age 12 years. The median survival is 24 to 27 years with major reported causes of death attributable to heart failure and respiratory insufficiency. Duchenne muscular dystrophy–associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy is a rare and rapidly progressive retinal disorder described in patients with DMD, usually after age 20 (range, 18-30) years.2-7Extensive areas of retinal capillary and arteriolar nonperfusion can lead to widespread peripapillary neovascularization. Patients may present late with advanced disease and fronds of neovascular tissue emanating from the optic nerve and iris neovascularization. The pathophysiology of the vasculopathy is not fully understood and is most likely multifactorial. First, the dystrophin is known to be expressed in the retina in the internal limiting membrane and around retinal vessels and is important for neurotransmission because its deficiency produces abnormal transmission between photoreceptors and bipolar cells.8Dystrophin is also expressed on endothelial cells. Nico et al9found alterations in dystrophin-deficient mice affecting the endothelial junctions, vessel permeability, and tissue edema as well as increased expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The upregulation of VEGF alone is most likely not sufficient to cause vasculopathy and requires other hypoxic or ischemic components.10 Published cases of DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy usually report respiratory and cardiac insufficiency with a diminished cardiac ejection fraction,2-6which, in conjunction with pathological regulation of endothelial permeability and VEGF in a DMD retina, could potentially induce levels of retinal hypoxia necessary to trigger the massive proliferative retinopathy. One report of DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy described a patient with normal cardiac function (cardiac ejection fraction of 70%), albeit with respiratory insufficiency, mild anemia, and early diabetes,7that could all have contributed to the proliferative disease. The differential diagnosis includes proliferative diabetic retinopathy and familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. The patient did not have diabetes, and the course of the disease was not typical for familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. According to the patient’s cardiologist, he had a severely altered cardiac ejection fraction of 25%, abnormal lung function with a forced vital capacity of 15%, and anemia with serum hemoglobin levels of 91 g/L (normal range is 140 to 180 g/L; to convert to g/dL, divide by 10). Results of carotid ultrasonography were normal. The chorioretinal biopsy (choice A) would not have been an appropriate way to diagnose and treat the patient, and the anti-VEGF injection (choice C) and panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) alone (choice D) would not have contributed to the repair of the complex retinal detachment. The anti-VEGF agents and PRP should have been used early and aggressively at the first signs of the disease to treat retinal ischemia and prevent neovascularization and rapidly progressing retinal detachment.3,4 The DMD-associated proliferative retinal vasculopathy is an entity rarely seen by ophthalmologists, most likely because most patients with DMD die before the retinopathy develops. With improved survivability, notably due to ventilation therapy, ophthalmologists may see more of these cases in the future. Periodic ophthalmic testing should enable clinicians to detect retinopathy and treat it with PRP and anti-VEGF injections early and with vitrectomy in more advanced cases.4-6 The patient elected to undergo surgery in the left eye, consisting of lensectomy, pars plana vitrectomy, endolaser coagulation, and silicon oil tamponade. The retinal anatomy could not be reestablished because of the extensive retinal fibrosis. The final visual acuity was light perception OD and counting fingers OS, and both eyes remained quiescent and painless.

scenario: A 37-year-old man with no history of vision problems presented with subacute loss of vision in his right eye for 1 week. The patient described a paracentral scotoma that progressed to involve central fixation over the course of 3 days. Two weeks earlier, the patient and his children had developed malaise, low-grade fever, and a rash. He worked in the armed services and denied foreign travel, tick bites, or recent immunization. The patient had been evaluated by his primary care clinician and was referred to an ophthalmologist for further evaluation. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70 OD and 20/20 OS. Test results of intraocular pressures, ocular motility, and pupillary reactions were normal. Confrontation visual fields showed inferonasal and central defects in the right eye. External examination revealed a macular rash of the scalp and all 4 extremities, including the soles and palms (Figure 1A). Anterior segment examination was normal. Posterior segment examination revealed irregular, gray-white pigmentation of the temporal macula of the right eye without vitritis, optic nerve edema, or vasculitis (Figure 1B). Ocular coherence tomography (OCT) revealed focal, heterogenous disruption of the inner segment ellipsoid zone without neurosensory detachment. Fluorescein angiography showed late staining at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) superotemporal to the fovea. Findings from a dilated fundus examination were normal in the left eye.

options.B: Send an aqueous sample for herpesvirus polymerase chain reaction
options.C: Inquire about toxic medication exposure

answer: Order coxsackievirus serologic testing
distractors: Send an aqueous sample for herpesvirus polymerase chain reaction
explanation: D. Order coxsackievirus serologic testing The subacute development of unilateral vision loss in an otherwise healthy young patient with recent viral illness initially led to a referral for possible optic neuritis. However, the lack of pain or relative afferent pupillary defect and irregular macular pigmentation raised concern for an inflammatory maculopathy, such as acute macular neuroretinopathy or unilateral acute idiopathic maculopathy (UAIM). Although these 2 entities both present with inflammatory changes of the RPE, the unilateral nature and more substantial acuity decline favored UAIM. Furthermore, characteristic unilateral gray-white retinal pigment changes with heterogeneous disruption of the photoreceptor layer and hyperreflective thickening of the apical RPE in the foveal region (Figure 2) on OCT confirmed the diagnosis of UAIM. Despite similarities in temporal profile of vision loss with optic neuritis, UAIM does not involve the retrobulbar optic nerve or intracranial structures, so neuroimaging (choice A) is not indicated. Herpesvirus infection (choice B) may cause focal retinal whitening secondary to acute retinal necrosis but has not been implicated in UAIM. Although hydroxychloroquine and other potential retinal toxins (choice C) can present with similar patterns of maculopathy with ellipsoid zone disruption, they are typically insidious and bilateral. Unilateral acute idiopathic maculopathy is a rare maculopathy first described by Yannuzzi et al1in 1991. Characteristic findings were inflammatory RPE changes with exudative macular detachment and spontaneous near-complete resolution of vision loss over weeks to months following viral illness. A follow-up case series by Freund et al2in 1996 expanded the clinical spectrum of the disease, describing cases with papillitis, bilateral involvement, and fewer retinal hemorrhages. These first series postulated that UAIM is an inflammatory process and noted potential associations with pregnancy, HIV, and coxsackievirus. Coxsackievirus is a well-known cause of the highly contagious hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) that is characterized by its namesake viral exanthem. In 2004, Beck et al3presented 2 cases of adult-onset HFMD associated with UAIM. The author group posited that coxsackievirus may have been the cause. Subsequently, numerous case reports have been published of patients with UAIM and concomitant adult-onset HFMD,4-8supporting the potential association. Among these reports, there is no consensus regarding treatment, with many clinicians choosing to observe the often self-limited disease. The potential unproven benefit of using systemic corticosteroids that others elected to provide should be balanced with the potential harm for patients at high risk for systemic complications of treatment. Regardless of treatment, the prognosis is generally good, with most patients recovering near-normal vision. The patient was diagnosed with adult-onset HFMD. He elected to receive 60 mg of oral prednisone daily with planned taper over 6 weeks for presumed coxsackievirus-related UAIM. Two weeks later, his uncorrected distance visual acuity improved to 20/20 OD, with subjective reduction in scotoma size. There was substantial reduction of the ellipsoid zone disruption on OCT. After 2 months, the patient’s visual acuity improved to 20/15 OD with near complete resolution of visual field defect and minimal persistent outer retinal changes on OCT.

caption: A, The cosmetic iris implant (yellow arrowhead) is seen overlying the native iris (white arrowhead). B, The cosmetic iris implant (white arrowhead) is seen overlying the native iris with its edge extending into the angle and prompting iridolenticular touch (yellow arrowhead).
scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with photophobia in both eyes. Six months earlier while abroad, the patient had bilateral cosmetic iris implants (BrightOcular) placed. The patient had a mild change in refractive error postoperatively and was offered laser in situ keratomileusis surgery for correction. She did not report any other immediate postoperative complications. For 4 weeks before presentation, she had blurred vision of the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/25 OS. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 31 mm Hg in the right eye and 17 mm Hg in the left. The pupillary reflex could not be visualized secondary to the iris implants. Slitlamp examination revealed trace anterior chamber cell bilaterally with pigmented keratic precipitates. The implants were overlying the iris structures (Figure 1A). Results of an ultrasonographic biomicroscopy are shown inFigure 1B. Posterior examination was limited by the iris implants, but the optic nerve did not reveal edema or hemorrhages. The peripheral retina could not be visualized in either eye. The patient was prescribed topical prednisolone acetate in both eyes and timolol maleate, dorzolamide hydrochloride, and brimonidine tartrate in the right eye only. On follow-up 2 days later, the IOP in the right eye had decreased to 17 mm Hg.

options.B: Maintain IOP-lowering therapy with continued observation
options.C: Begin oral acyclovir
options.D: Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically

answer: Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically
distractors: Maintain IOP-lowering therapy with continued observation
explanation: Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome secondary to cosmetic iris implants D. Remove the cosmetic iris implants surgically Herpetic keratouveitis can present with elevated pressure, anterior chamber cells, and keratic precipitates, as in this patient’s case. However, these findings are most commonly unilateral in herpetic disease.1Thus, initiating oral acyclovir (choice C) would not be the most appropriate option. Instead, on the basis of the initial presentation of anterior chamber cells, elevated IOP, and pigmented keratic precipitates, a diagnosis of uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome secondary to the patient’s cosmetic iris implants was made. Initially conceived for use in patients with congenital or traumatic aniridia, iris implants were first used in 1994.2A decade later, anterior chamber iris implants were marketed for cosmetic purposes. These cosmetic implants have been associated with multiple complications aside from UGH syndrome, including corneal decompensation, synechiae formation, iris and retinal neovascularization, and cataracts.3-5 Uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome was first described in 1978 and traditionally presents when an intraocular chamber lens or haptic rubs against iris tissue, leading to chafing.6However, other sources, such as cosmetic iris implants, have also been reported to be associated with UGH syndrome.5The mechanical irritation of iris tissue may lead to the triad of uveitis, elevated IOP, and hyphema, although the diagnosis is often made without the complete triad. Diagnosis of UGH syndrome is clinical but can be aided by imaging. Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy can be used to visualize the position of intraocular lenses or other iatrogenic sources of iris irritation. Optical coherence tomography can be used to diagnose and monitor cystoid macular edema. The definitive treatment in UGH syndrome is removal of the inciting cause of iris irritation.7Topical IOP-lowering therapy (choice B) could be used as a temporary measure but would not be definitive therapy. Although IOP-lowering therapy could be used as a bridge to implant removal, it would not address the inciting factor, irritation of the iris by the implants. Additionally, IOP-lowering drops would not prevent other complications, including uveitis, ocular ischemia, and corneal decompensation. Surgery to place a glaucoma implant device (choice A) would not be an appropriate first step because though it may lower the IOP, it would not address the underlying cause of mechanical iris irritation. In addition, the patient’s pressure was controlled with topical therapy; incisional glaucoma surgery for IOP control would be premature at this juncture. Instead, the definitive treatment in this case is removal of the inciting factor (choice D), the cosmetic iris implants. In this case, despite counseling, the patient refused to have the implants removed. She was lost to follow-up for 4 months. On her return, the patient’s visual acuity had deteriorated to 20/400 OD and hand motions OS. The IOP was elevated to 33 mm Hg OD and 38 mm Hg OS. Diffuse keratic precipitates and 2+ anterior chamber cells were seen in both eyes. Both optic nerves showed considerable advanced cupping compared with the initial visit, and robust fine radial neovascularization at the optic nerve head was visualized in the left eye (Figure 2). At this time, the patient agreed to surgery, and both implants were removed.

caption: Right eye. A, Optic atrophy and fine mottling pigmentary changes are evident at the fovea. B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) shows disruption of the outer retinal layers and multiple hyperreflective deposits at the fovea.
scenario: A 26-year-old man presented with reduced visual acuity in both eyes since early childhood. He had short stature (1.52 m [−3.6 SD]) and progeroid appearance. His parents and brother had normal stature. His medical history was significant for frequent upper respiratory tract infections since infancy. He had no intellectual disability, neurologic symptoms, or hearing impairment. There was no family history of visual impairment or neurologic disorders. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressure was normal. He could not identify any Ishihara color plate. Slitlamp examination was unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination results showed diffuse optic atrophy (OA) and fine pigmentary mottling changes at the fovea in both eyes (Figure 1A). Electroretinography (ERG) showed normal dark-adapted responses and severely reduced light-adapted responses. Optical coherence tomography showed thinning of retinal nerve fiber layers and disruption of outer nuclear layers and the ellipsoid zone at the center of the fovea (Figure 1B). Leber hereditary optic neuropathy sequencing was negative for 3 hot spot mutations.

options.A: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.B: Check blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels
options.C: Order trinucleotide repeat sequencing for spinocerebellar ataxia

answer: Order whole-exome sequencing
distractors: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Check blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels
Order trinucleotide repeat sequencing for spinocerebellar ataxia
explanation: Short stature, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly syndrome Diagnosis of hereditary OA is challenging for ophthalmologists, especially when combined with retinal dystrophy. Because the optic nerve may have variable degrees of temporal pallor in cone dystrophy, cone disorders should be included in the differential diagnosis. Optic atrophy is usually accompanied byCACNA1Fcongenital stationary night blindness,1or it can be a late manifestation of retinitis pigmentosa. However, patients with congenital stationary night blindness typically have normal fundus and negative ERGs in scotopic response. Spinocerebellar ataxia andSSBP1variant also cause OA and variable retinal degeneration.2,3 Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed and revealed novel compound heterozygousNBASc.3493del:p.(Val1165Serfs*31) c.5740C>T:p.(Arg1914Cys) variants. The 2 variants were in-trans, confirmed by trio WES, and are likely pathogenic.4Results of further workups, including peripheral blood smear examination, showed bilobulated granulocytes (Figure 2) and hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG, 524.4 mg/dL [normal range, 800-1800 mg/dL]; IgA, 19.0 mg/dL [normal range, 105-500 mg/dL]; to convert IgG and IgA to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10); however, liver enzyme levels were normal. TheNBASgene encodes a component protein of the syntaxin 18 complex and is involved in Golgi-to-endoplasmic reticulum transport.5﻿NBASgene mutations cause either infantile liver failure syndrome (OMIM616483) or short stature, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly (SOPH) syndrome (OMIM614800) depending on the location of the variants.6TheNBASgene has 3 functional domains as follows: beta-propeller domain and Sec39 domain, plus an unknown function of the C-terminal. The novel C-terminal variant discovered in the patient is the same amino acid residue p.(Arg1914His) known to be a founder mutation in the Yakut population.7To our knowledge, hepatic dysfunction has never been reported in patients carrying the homozygous p.(Arg1914His) variant,7but variable hepatic involvements have been observed in patients with compound heterozygousNBASvariants.8A SOPH syndrome diagnosis is based on the clinical constellation of short stature, senile facial appearance, OA, Pelger-Huët anomaly, and normal intelligence. The key feature in this case is the extreme short stature, progeroid appearance, and cone dystrophy. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (choice A) was deferred because the patient had no neurologic signs or symptoms. Wolfram syndrome should be considered in the differential diagnosis. Although growth hormone deficiency has been reported in Wolfram syndrome, checking the blood glucose and hemoglobin A1clevels (choice B) are inappropriate given the absence of diabetes and hearing impairment at his age.9Moreover, visual acuity in Wolfram syndrome is typically worse then 20/200. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 also causes variable degrees of cone dystrophy and OA,3but trinucleotide repeat sequencing (choice C) was deferred because the patient had no ataxia. Therefore, WES is the most appropriate next step. The ophthalmologic manifestation of SOPH syndrome is characterized by OA and color vision loss. Other ophthalmologic manifestations, including horizontal nystagmus, retinal dystrophy, foveal hypoplasia, gray sclera, and corneal opacity, were also reported.7,8,10Vision loss and OA can be initial manifestations in SOPH syndrome. Recognition of syndromic features and a high index of suspicion can identify the underlying causes of OA. In addition, theNBASgene should be included in the targeted workup for both OA and cone dystrophy. During the 5 years of follow-up, the patient’s visual acuity was maintained. We advised regular monitoring of liver function.

caption: Right eye. A, Marked purulence (asterisk) is noted under the sterile drape along the upper eyelid and stretches between the arms of the eyelid speculum. Marked corneal inflammation is evident. The central portion of the arrowheads point to a 1.8 × 2.2-mm area of marked corneal thinning within which is a smaller area of perforation. B, This optical coherence tomographic (OCT) image shows marked corneal thinning and areas (asterisk) of corneal stromal necrosis.
scenario: A 65-year-old man presented with worsening right eye pain and purulent discharge. He reported being hit in the face by a tree branch several days prior. His medical history was notable for HIV, with a last known CD4 lymphocyte count of 112 cells/mm3and variable adherence to antiretroviral therapy. At an outside hospital, cultures were obtained, and treatment was initiated with ofloxacin eye drops, 0.3%, ciprofloxacin hydrochloride ointment, 0.3%, and oral moxifloxacin hydrochloride, 400 mg daily. His symptoms worsened, and he was referred 3 days later for further evaluation. On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was hand motions. The left eye examination results were unremarkable. Slitlamp examination was limited by patient discomfort but revealed purulent discharge, a markedly inflamed conjunctiva, diffuse cornea opacification and thinning, and a flat anterior chamber. Given the history of tree branch trauma, the patient was brought to the operating room. Intraoperatively, a 0.5-mm corneal perforation was identified within an area of thinning (Figure, A). Microbial cultures were repeated, and corneal glue was applied. Gram stain of the purulent discharge demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes only. All subsequent microbiology cultures were negative. Despite treatment with topical fortified vancomycin, 25 mg/mL, tobramycin, 13.3 mg/mL, intravenous levofloxacin, 750 mg daily, and doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily, the purulent conjunctivitis and corneal stromal necrosis did not improve (Figure, B).

options.A: Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician
options.B: Pursue serologic workup for autoimmune disease
options.C: Begin empirical treatment for acanthamoeba
options.D: Return to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty

answer: Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician
distractors: Pursue serologic workup for autoimmune disease
Return to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty
explanation: A. Obtain initial culture results from the referring physician Given persistent marked purulence and stromal necrosis, the negative culture results were surprising. However, these microbiology studies were obtained while the patient was receiving broad-spectrum topical antibiotic therapy. Initial culture results were obtained from the referring physician (choice A), which grewNeisseria gonorrhoeae. The patient then disclosed that his partner recently had a penile ulcer. He was immediately treated with saline lavages and single doses of intramuscular ceftriaxone sodium, 1 g, and oral azithromycin, 1 g, for gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis. Although this patient was initially transferred with concern for a traumatic ruptured globe, the history of prior tree trauma was a red herring. The persistent purulence and corneal stromal necrosis raised concern for infection. Yield of ocular surface cultures are decreased when samples are obtained with concurrent topical antimicrobial therapy.1This case also emphasizes the potential importance of follow-up on primary data. When patients are transferred between institutions with different medical record systems, information can be lost. Serologic workup for autoimmune keratitis (choice B) is not the preferred answer because the hyperpurulence and beefy conjunctival injection would be atypical for this sterile inflammatory presentation. Starting empirical treatment for acanthamoeba (choice C) is incorrect because hyperpurulence is unusual in acanthamoeba keratitis, and the patient had no freshwater risk factors or history of contact lens wear. With progressive corneal necrosis, returning to the operating room for therapeutic keratoplasty (choice D) may have been required; however, the initial best step in management is to obtain confirmative diagnosis. Gonorrheal keratoconjunctivitis is due to infection withN gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus. In populations other than neonates, transmission mostly occurs via direct sexual contact with infective secretions or indirectly via fomite transmission.2A study in Ireland found the prevalence of gonococcal conjunctivitis to be 0.19 cases per 1000 patients evaluated for eye emergencies, with the majority in young adult males.3 Treatment of gonorrheal keratoconjunctivitis is both systemic and local. Recommended systemic treatment includes administration of intramuscular ceftriaxone, 1 g, in a single dose.4,5Systemic azithromycin, 1 g, in a single dose or oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice a day for 7 days, is also added owing to frequent coinfection withChlamydia trachomatis.6Topical treatment is ancillary and can include a fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and/or saline lavages.3,7Gonorrhea is a reportable disease. Notification of risk of this disease and treatment of all sexual partners is necessary. Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis may lead to serious ocular complications. Corneal stromal necrosis can occur, as with this case, in a fulminant fashion. Treatment of corneal stromal necrosis depends on the size and extent of stromal involvement and whether perforation of the cornea is present. Medical management of corneal stromal necrosis includes systemic antigonorrheal antibiotic therapy and anticollagenase medications. Surgical management for descemetoceles and perforations may include glue, amniotic membrane transplant, therapeutic lamellar, or full-thickness corneal and conjunctival flaps. In this case, corneal gluing was pursued because the area of perforation was small. The diagnosis of gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis should be considered in individuals who present with markedly purulent conjunctivitis with or without genital symptoms. History may not be forthcoming. Presentation classically includes conjunctival injection, eyelid edema, hyperpurulent discharge, and preauricular lymphadenopathy. With prompt, effective treatment, the infection can be eradicated and complications, such as corneal melt and perforation, can be avoided. After treatment with intramuscular ceftriaxone, 1 g, oral azithromycin, 1 g, gentle saline lavage, and topical moxifloxacin, 0.5% four times a day, this patient’s anterior chamber reformed, the corneal epithelial defect decreased in size, and iris structures were visible owing to improvement in the corneal infiltrate. The patient was subsequently discharged from the hospital and lost to follow-up thereafter.
