scenario: A 64-year-old woman in excellent general health who was not taking any medications was referred for evaluation of an epiretinal membrane of her right eye. She reported no blurry vision, metamorphopsia, photopsias, floaters, or nyctalopia, and she had no history of refractive surgical procedures, ocular surgical procedures, or trauma. Her family history was negative for ocular conditions, and there was no consanguinity in her family. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU with correction (plano +0.25 × 153 OD and −0.50 + 0.25 × 009 OS). External and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable except for mild nuclear sclerotic cataracts. Results of a dilated ophthalmoscopic examination showed radial spokelike striae of the fovea, with a central cyst in the right eye and macular edema of the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging of the right macula showed cystlike changes in the outer retina in the foveal and parafoveal regions and in the inner retina in the temporal macula. Optical coherence tomography imaging of the left macula showed cystlike changes in the outer retina in the inferior macula (Figure). Of note, OCT scans of the optic nerves did not reveal an optic disc pit.

options.C: Prescribe antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy
options.D: Prescribe topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy

answer: Order an electroretinogram
distractors: Prescribe antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy
Prescribe topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy
explanation: Stellate nonhereditary idiopathic foveomacular retinoschisis We present a case of a 64-year-old woman with no ocular history and a negative family history. The OCT imaging showed schisis primarily of the outer retina that was consistent with bilateral stellate foveomacular retinoschisis. The most appropriate next step is to order an electroretinogram (ERG) (choice A) to rule out congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis (CXLR), which is caused by a variation in theRS1gene (OMIM300839). Congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis typically has an electronegative ERG but can be variable and even normal in some patients. Congenital juvenile X-linked retinoschisis is most commonly found in males; however, there are reports of females with this disease due to lyonization or homozygosity.1,2This patient was unlikely to be a carrier because she did not have white flecks in the periphery on fundus examination and had a negative family history. The patient’s ERG was unremarkable in both eyes. Performing pars plana vitrectomy (choice B) and prescribing antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy (choice C) would not be the preferred answer because they are not proven to benefit patients with stellate nonhereditary idiopathic foveomacular retinoschisis (SNIFR). Both are inappropriate as the next step in management of this patient. Prescribing topical prednisolone or ketorolac therapy (choice D) was not indicated because the cystic areas were from retinoschisis and not cystoid macular edema. Foveomacular retinoschisis can be associated with optic pit maculopathy, myopic retinoschisis, retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, vitreomacular traction, or degenerative retinoschisis, which were ruled out by the patient’s clinical examination results, ERG, and imaging. Enhanced S-cone syndrome is inconsistent with the patient’s good vision throughout her life and the unremarkable fundus examination and ERG results. There are no known genetic associations with SNIFR. However, testing to rule out other genetic diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa or X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, which can be associated with a similar appearance, could be performed as indicated based on clinical history and findings. The patient was not taking any medications associated with retinoschisis, including niacin or taxanes. The patient was asymptomatic, had excellent visual acuity, and had no evidence of hereditary or acquired retinoschisis. Given this clinical picture, the patient likely had bilateral SNIFR. A case of bilateral non–X-linked macular schisis was described inGass’ Atlas of Macular Diseases3and possibly represented a case of SNIFR. In the largest reported case series, most patients were asymptomatic or had minimal symptoms with unilateral findings.4In addition, splitting was most common in the outer plexiform layer, with lesser involvement of the outer nuclear layer, as was seen in this patient.4The typical stellate pattern of the macula was visible in 1 eye of this patient, but reports have been published of patients with SNIFR without this fundus finding, perhaps due to concurrent neovascular age-related macular degeneration.5 SNIFR is typically managed with observation, as patients generally have good vision.6Treatment of SNIFR with dorzolamide therapy has been reported to result in complete resolution of SNIFR and improvement in vision.7We could consider this option if the patient’s vision deteriorated. Performing surgical procedures is not indicated for these patients. It is important to consider SNIFR in a patient with foveomacular retinoschisis without a family history, degenerative condition, or acquired etiology. Follow-up was indicated to monitor for possible loss of visual acuity. There are no clear guidelines on frequency of follow-up. One study reports biannual follow-up of a patient with unilateral SNIFR and best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in the involved eye.6 This patient was followed up every 6 months. If the patient becomes symptomatic or shows progression of disease on OCT imaging, the patient should be more closely monitored with shorter intervals for follow-up.

caption: A slitlamp photograph of the right eye shows a translucent grayish-white cystic mass in the inferonasal aspect of the iris stroma.
scenario: A 14-month-old boy presented with a sudden-onset, rapidly enlarging lesion in the right eye detected by his parents 2 weeks earlier. The patient had normal tracking bilaterally. Under anesthesia, findings from an examination of the right eye revealed an inferonasal translucent gray-white iris mass with numerous intralesional lacy cystic structures (Figure 1). There was no microphthalmia, cataract, lens subluxation, anterior or posterior synechiae, glaucoma, or uveitis. Findings from a fundus examination were normal. High-resolution anterior segment echography results revealed an iridociliary mass that extended posteriorly to the pars plicata with overall dimensions of 7.7 × 6.0 × 1.9 mm. There were no associated calcifications, retrolental membranes, or seeding.

options.C: Perform plaque brachytherapy

answer: Perform plaque brachytherapy
explanation: The differential diagnosis of an amelanotic iris mass in a young child includes retinoblastoma, medulloepithelioma, juvenile xanthogranuloma, leukemia, and metastatic cancer. In this patient, the absence of intralesional calcifications or retinal tumors would be atypical for retinoblastoma. The absence of characteristic skin lesions and a yellowish-orange, vascularized iris mass is unusual for juvenile xanthogranuloma. Leukemia and metastatic cancer are unlikely in an otherwise healthy young child. The translucent tumor with intralesional cystic structures is characteristic of medulloepithelioma. Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor that was first described in 1892 and has also been referred to ascarcinoma primitif,terato-neuroma, anddiktyoma.1,2Although retinoblastoma and medulloepithelioma both arise from primitive neuroepithelium derived from the inner layer of the optic cup,3their clinical features are distinct. Retinoblastomas are white vascularized retinal tumors that usually arise before 2 years of age. They frequently contain intratumoral calcifications and are multifocal and bilateral in patients with germlineRB1(OMIM180200) variants.4In contrast, medulloepitheliomas arise from the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium and most commonly present as a grayish-white translucent mass involving the ciliary body and/or iris.1Characteristic features of medulloepithelioma include multiple intralesional cysts and a neoplastic retrolenticular membrane. Because of the ciliary body origin and slow growth of medulloepithelioma, diagnosis is often delayed until an older age (median age of 5 years) than in retinoblastoma.5Presenting symptoms and signs include decreased vision, ocular pain, cataract, and glaucoma. Ultrasound biomicroscopy may help identify a retroiridal ciliary body tumor. Histopathologically, medulloepithelioma demonstrates pseudostratified loops of embryonic neuroglial structures with a surrounding matrix of hyaluronase-rich mesenchymal tissue.1Medulloepithelioma can be classified as nonteratoid or teratoid, the former resembling ciliary epithelium and the latter displaying differentiation of multiple cell lineages.1 Although most cases of intraocular medulloepithelioma are sporadic, 5% of cases are associated with a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome attributed to germline variants in theDICER1gene (OMIM606241) and associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma.5In addition, 20% of cases are associated with persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.6 The diagnosis of an iridociliary medulloepithelioma was made on the basis of the clinical characteristics of the iris mass. Because of its malignant potential, observation is not recommended (choice A). Biopsy is generally not performed because of concern for dissemination of malignant cells (choice B). Enucleation is the preferred treatment in large invasive tumors, owing to the high recurrence rate after local surgical resection. Plaque radiotherapy is a reasonable globe-sparing therapy in localized tumors that can be adequately covered by the plaque (choice C).2Although intra-arterial chemotherapy is an established treatment option for retinoblastoma, there are no data to support its use for medulloepithelioma (choice D). In this patient, findings from a baseline systemic evaluation were negative for pleuropulmonary blastoma or metastatic disease. The patient underwent treatment with iodine 125 plaque brachytherapy, with a total dose of 40 Gy directed to the tumor apex. There was complete regression within 4 weeks following brachytherapy (Figure 2) and no local recurrence or metastasis after 6 years of follow-up. Final best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD.

caption: Fluorescein angiographic photograph at presentation showing mild leakage of retinal vasculature and retinal pigmented epithelium changes at the posterior pole in both eyes (A and B) along with vitreous opacities in the left eye (B).
scenario: A 65-year-old woman was referred for symptoms of painless and progressive bilateral loss of central and peripheral vision over the last 6 months, associated with floaters in the left eye. The patient reported difficulty in performing essential daily tasks, such as driving and walking without assistance. She denied photopsias. Her previous ocular and medical history were unremarkable. She denied any systemic symptoms as well as any family history of inherited ocular diseases. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/32 OU. Fundus examination results showed attenuated arterial and venous retinal vessels and slight retinal pigmented epithelium changes at the posterior pole, consisting of atrophy and pigment migration in both eyes, associated with vitreous opacities in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography examination results showed a mild leakage of arterial and venous retinal vasculature (Figure). Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography exhibited disruption at the photoreceptor level and multifocal hyperreflective material depositions at the retinal pigmented epithelium level. Computerized perimetry demonstrated severe visual field bilateral constriction. Full-field electroretinography showed decreased scotopic and photopic responses. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable, and an extensive workup for underlying infectious or inflammatory causes was unrevealing.

options.A: Obtain a temporal artery biopsy specimen owing to suspicion of Horton disease
options.B: Perform molecular analysis for heritable retinal degeneration
options.C: Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm
options.D: Obtain a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis

answer: Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm
distractors: Obtain a temporal artery biopsy specimen owing to suspicion of Horton disease
Perform molecular analysis for heritable retinal degeneration
Obtain a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis
explanation: C. Investigate serum positivity for antiretinal antibodies and obtain an extensive workup to rule out a malignant neoplasm Autoimmune retinopathy (AIR) is a rare form of immune-mediated retinal degeneration. It is characterized by progressive vision loss along with electroretinographic, visual field abnormalities, and the presence of circulating ARAs. Autoimmune retinopathy can be categorized as paraneoplastic (pAIR), which includes cancer-associated retinopathy and melanoma-associated retinopathy, or nonparaneoplastic in the absence of a malignant neoplasm.1,2 Diagnosis remains a challenge because of its variable presentation and fundus appearance, which may be initially normal or with minimal unrevealing alterations despite central vision loss and a severely decreased visual field.1,2Moreover, in contrast with previous reported cases,3,4the patient did not show any systemic symptoms that would have been helpful toward the diagnosis. A differential diagnosis might include heritable retinal degenerations, because clinical findings in AIR, including peripheral visual field loss, reduced electroretinogram waveforms, retinal pigmented epithelium atrophic changes, pigment migration, and photoreceptor loss on optical coherence tomography, can be suggestive of heritable diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa.5In this case, molecular analysis for heritable retinal degenerations (choice B) would not have been the preferred next step because the patient had no family history of inherited ocular diseases and did not experience typical symptoms, such as nyctalopia, photophobia, or dyschromatopsia. Furthermore, the relatively rapid progression of photoreceptor loss was not typical for retinitis pigmentosa and no bone spicule-like pigmentary changes were present during the fundus examination. The presence of circulating ARAs is important in the pathophysiology and diagnosis of AIR, although it is not pathognomonic, as they have been identified in other retinal diseases, such as uveitis,6in patients with systemic autoimmune disorders,7and in healthy controls.8Given the absence of standardized diagnostic criteria, it has been proposed that an AIR diagnosis should require serum positivity for ARAs associated with progressive loss of visual acuity, visual field defects, and abnormal responses on electroretinography, in the absence of fundus lesions or degenerative retinal disease that might explain these pathologic findings.1,2 Therefore, given the clinical features found in the patient, investigating the presence of ARAs (choice C) was considered to be the most suitable next step to confirm the diagnostic suspicion of AIR. Furthermore, because serum positivity for ARAs and visual symptoms may be present many years before detecting malignant neoplasms in patients with pAIR,9,10an oncologic workup was deemed appropriate for clarifying the paraneoplastic nature of the AIR. Obtaining a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous and aqueous sampling for cytologic analysis (choice D) would not have provided useful information for definitively clarifying the diagnosis and would not have guided us toward the detection of malignant neoplasms. Obtaining a temporal artery biopsy specimen because of suspicion of Horton disease (choice A) would not have been the proper management option. In fact, the patient did not experience typical symptoms, such as headache, jaw claudication, sensitivity on the scalp, or prominent temporal arteries. The patient underwent antiretinal antibody testing that demonstrated reactivity to multiple ARAs. She was referred to the oncology department to undergo a systemic workup for malignant neoplasms and was found to be affected by stage IV, poorly differentiated, gastric adenocarcinoma with multiple metastasis to the abdominal and supraclavicular lymph nodes. She started palliative chemotherapy with FLOT regimen (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel). After 4 months, the treatment helped to slow the progression of visual field loss, with preservation of central vision and best-corrected visual acuity improvement to 20/25 OU. In addition, a regression of the vitreous opacities in the left eye was detected.

caption: Fundus image shows inferior retinal whitening with a round, discrete white infiltrate overlying the optic nerve. The arrowheads point to sparing in the distribution of the cilioretinal artery. Inset, Intravenous fluorescein angiography shows an inferior filling defect consistent with a hemicentral retinal artery occlusion.
scenario: A 55-year-old man was referred to the eye clinic for unilateral uveitis and 2 days of sudden vision loss in his right eye. He reported experiencing light sensitivity and mild eye pain. He was in otherwise good health without any chronic medical problems. He reported receiving anticoagulation therapy in the past for a mitral valve problem. His visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS. The examination of the left eye was unremarkable. Slitlamp examination of his right eye revealed 3+ anterior chamber inflammation with vitreous cells. An examination of the dilated fundus showed optic nerve edema with an overlying white infiltrate. In addition, there was inferior retinal whitening consistent with an artery occlusion (Figure 1A). The whitening was attributable to inner retina ischemia, with sparing in the distribution of the cilioretinal artery. An inferior hemicentral retinal artery occlusion was confirmed on intravenous fluorescein angiography (Figure 1B). No embolus was noted at any retinal artery branch points. Notably, a dog bit the patient’s hand 2 months before presentation. Since that time, the patient developed a persistent cough, night sweats, and low-grade fevers that were treated unsuccessfully with 2 courses of oral antibiotics.

options.A: Prescribe a course of oral prednisone
options.B: Perform audiometry evaluation for hearing loss with Susac syndrome
options.C: Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram
options.D: Evaluate carotid arteries as a potential embolic source

answer: Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram
distractors: Prescribe a course of oral prednisone
Perform audiometry evaluation for hearing loss with Susac syndrome
Evaluate carotid arteries as a potential embolic source
explanation: Hemicentral retinal artery occlusion secondary to septic embolus C. Obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram This patient experienced a hemicentral retinal artery occlusion with early endogenous endophthalmitis secondary to a septic embolus in the setting of bacterial endocarditis with bacteremia fromStreptococcus viridans. This retinal artery occlusion was presumptively related to the recent dog bite and an underlying diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse. Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis is an uncommon subset of endophthalmitis, accounting for approximately 2% to 8% of all endophthalmitis cases.1A systematic review of endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis showed that most patients (77%) had an identifiable preexisting condition, 64% had an identifiable extraocular focus of infection, and 8% had endocarditis.2As in this patient, 73% of patients in the review had systemic symptoms preceding ocular symptoms.2Despite adequate treatment, visual prognosis remains poor for most patients with endogenous endophthalmitis.3 In addition to the unifying diagnosis discussed above, the differential diagnosis at initial presentation included both noninfectious uveitis and classic causes of retinal artery occlusions. Although rare, there have been reports of artery occlusion in the setting of uveitic conditions, such as Behçet disease.4However, an initial course of oral prednisone (choice A) is inappropriate when infectious causes have not been ruled out, especially given the persistent fevers. Susac syndrome presents with multiple recurrent branch retinal artery occlusions that are not at branch points, along with leakage at occlusion sites. This patient’s clinical picture was not consistent with Susac syndrome; thus, audiometry (choice B) would not have been warranted. The correct answer is obtaining blood cultures and an echocardiogram given the history of previous valve disease (choice C). Obtaining a carotid ultrasound to identify embolic sources (choice D) is always prudent in patients presenting with retinal artery occlusions given the high risk of critical neurologic disease.5Concomitant uveitis and a white vitreous infiltrate pointed to an infectious source, making a carotid workup secondary. This case highlights the importance of noting medical history and systemic symptoms when encountering an atypical presentation of a classic ocular condition. Ignoring the systemic symptoms could have led to missing a life-threatening diagnosis. With the patient’s underlying heart condition, weeks of systemic symptoms following a dog bite, and the ophthalmic findings, the clinical suspicion for systemic infection was high. This patient had a life-threatening illness requiring immediate treatment with other specialists. Ophthalmologists must maintain a high index of suspicion for serious extraocular conditions and continue to think beyond the eye when evaluating a patient’s clinical picture. This patient was sent immediately to the emergency department for a full infectious workup and echocardiogram. Blood cultures grewS viridans, and the infectious disease service recommended intravenous ceftriaxone. Transesophageal echocardiogram showed mitral valve prolapse with a 9-mm mitral valve vegetation as the likely source of the septic embolus (Figure 2). An adjuvant injection of intravitreal vancomycin was administered because of worsening vitritis. On follow-up, inflammation had resolved; however, vision loss persisted secondary to the artery occlusion.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of the left eye after subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide injection shows 2 temporal nodules (asterisks), conjunctival hyperemia, and surrounding scleral thinning (yellow arrowheads). Superiorly, remnant subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide can be seen (white arrowhead).
scenario: A 50-year-old woman presented with left eye redness and headaches for 2 months. Results from a previous computed tomographic scan of the head were unremarkable. She denied ocular disease, trauma, or surgery. She had no medical problems aside from chronic back pain due to a herniated disc. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS. Intraocular pressure, extraocular motility, and pupillary examination results were normal. The right eye was unremarkable. Examination of the left eye showed 2 temporal scleral nodules with surrounding hyperemia and no scleromalacia. She experienced substantial pain with palpation. Posterior examination results were unremarkable. The results of the following laboratory tests were all unremarkable: tuberculosis interferon-γ release assay, rapid plasma reagin, fluorescent treponemal antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme. The rheumatoid factor level (18 IU/mL [normal range, <14 IU/mL]) and C-reactive protein level (26 mg/L [normal range, 0-5 mg/L]) were elevated. In addition, Lyme IgG, IgM, and reflex Western blot assays were positive for antibodies. The patient denied travel to Lyme-endemic regions, tick bites, or rashes. The patient started oral prednisone therapy for possible rheumatoid arthritis (RA)–associated nodular scleritis, doxycycline therapy for positive Lyme studies, and was referred to a rheumatologist for further RA evaluation. Two weeks after presentation and initiation of oral prednisone therapy, the patient noted improvement in pain, but the scleral nodules and hyperemia persisted. Therefore, subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide (0.5 mL of 40 mg/mL) was administered to the left eye. Further confirmatory RA workup by rheumatology did not reveal other systemic findings thought to be associated with RA on review of symptoms or clinical examination. The patient's back pain was associated with her herniated disc. Subsequently, the patient’s examination results showed new scleral thinning of the left eye with persistence of the scleral nodules (Figure 1).

options.C: Transition to noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy

answer: Perform a scleral biopsy
distractors: Transition to noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy
explanation: B. Perform a scleral biopsy Anterior scleritis, the most common form of scleritis, presents with eye redness, substantial pain, and globe tenderness.1Many systemic diseases are associated with scleritis, and diagnosing underlying systemic conditions is important in managing ocular disease. Etiologies include autoimmune, infectious, and traumatic causes. Of autoimmune causes, RA is the most common.2 Treatment options for autoimmune scleritis include oral prednisone and noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapies. However, increasing the oral prednisone dosage (choice A) or starting noncorticosteroid systemic immunosuppressive therapy (choice C) would not be the best course of action in this clinical context. The cause of scleritis was still unknown. Immunosuppression in the setting of an infectious origin could worsen the disease. Although she had a mildly elevated rheumatoid factor level, results of further testing by a rheumatologist did not support a diagnosis of RA-associated scleritis. Lyme disease can present with ocular inflammation, including scleritis, but not with rapid scleral thinning or suppuration.3,4There was also no travel to endemic areas, rash, or tick bites, or improvement with doxycycline therapy. Repeating doxycycline treatment (choice D) would therefore not be the most appropriate selection. Of note, although the scleritis initially improved symptomatically with oral prednisone therapy, it worsened with new necrosis after subconjunctival triamcinolone injection, raising concern for a nonspirochetal infection. Performing a scleral biopsy and culture (choice B) was the most direct way to evaluate the patient at this point. Local triamcinolone injection can be a useful adjunctive therapy in nonnecrotizing anterior scleritis but should be avoided in cases with necrosis owing to the risk of scleral melt and perforation.5In scleritis of unknown etiology without initial necrosis, as in this case, local corticosteroid injection should be cautiously administered with close observation, and a biopsy should be performed if indicated. A scleral biopsy was performed in the operating room under local anesthesia. Dissection of the scleral nodules released purulent material, which was cultured. Necrotic sclera was debrided, and an amniotic membrane was sutured over the scleral thinning. Cultures from surgery grewMycobacterium abscessus1 week later. The patient then started treatment with topical amikacin sulfate eyedrops (8 mg/mL every hour) and oral clarithromycin (500 mg twice daily), and was given a 1-mL subconjunctival injection of amikacin sulfate (40 mg/mL). Infection, most commonly bacteria, causes 5% to 10% of scleritis cases.6,7Ocular surgery or trauma are predisposing factors especially in rare, nontuberculous mycobacterial infections, which overwhelmingly occur after surgery or trauma.8Obtaining a good clinical history is therefore essential. The patient had no prior ocular trauma or surgical procedures performed. An infectious cause was suspected owing to worsening of her condition subsequent to local injection of depot corticosteroids, prompting performance of a biopsy. Paradoxical worsening or failure of scleritis to improve with corticosteroid therapy should suggest an infection. Debridement during the biopsy was an important adjunct to medical treatment. During 6 weeks of treatment with topical amikacin and oral clarithromycin, the patient reported resolution of pain. The hyperemia improved, and the scleral thinning stabilized (Figure 2). Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 + 2 OS 3 months after surgery. Salvage of this eye was possible because a biopsy was performed early, facilitating control of the infection with topical, injectable, and oral antibiotic therapies.

caption: Preoperative photograph shows orthotropic eye position during a period of inattention. Note the right esotropia and right dissociated vertical divergence during left eye fixation at near (left inset) and larger left esotropia during right eye fixation at near (right inset).
scenario: A 33-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of intermittent esotropia. When playing video games at a distance or when reading, she developed oscillopsia with eyestrain and noted that her right eye turned up and in. She had undergone strabismus surgery for crossed eyes as a young child and more recently had laser in situ keratomileusis performed. She was medically healthy and neurodevelopmentally normal but had been born 4½ weeks premature. There was no family history of strabismus, and she denied diplopia. On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/30 − 2 OD and 20/15 OS. Both pupils reacted briskly to light with no afferent pupillary defect. She had 1+ apparent overaction of the right inferior oblique and superior rectus muscles. When she was inattentive, her eyes appeared to be straight (Figure 1). Prism and alternate cover testing during near fixation showed a right esotropia and dissociated vertical divergence when fixing with her preferred left eye (Figure 1, left inset) and a larger left esotropia during forced fixation with her right eye (Figure 1, right inset). She had no cycloplegic refractive error, and retinal examination showed no objective torsion. Placement of +3.00 lenses eliminated her esotropia at near but could not be used to alleviate her symptoms at distance, showing a high accommodation-to-convergence ratio.

options.C: Reversed fixation test

answer: Reversed fixation test
explanation: The termdissociated horizontal deviation(DHD) was originally used to describe a unique form of intermittent exotropia in which the measured exodeviation was larger with 1 eye fixating than the other.1-4In some cases, the exodeviation resolves or converts to a large esodeviation when the patient fixates with the nonpreferred eye. Associated clinical findings include latent nystagmus, dissociated vertical divergence, and sensorial suppression of the nonfixating eye, indicating that DHD develops only when binocular visual input is preempted early in life.3-6Some cases arise spontaneously, but most patients have undergone previous bimedial recessions.5 Originally attributed to unequal convergence damping of latent nystagmus,1,2it is now clear that this variable exodeviation is driven by a change in the sensory balance of visual inputs from both eyes.7In patients with DHD, monocular fixation induces a dissociated esodeviation (greater during fixation with the nonpreferred eye) that is usually superimposed on an exotropic resting position of the eyes (as found under nondepolarizing general anesthesia). Thus, when the baseline vergence position of the eyes is orthotropic, DHD can generate an esodeviation of variable amplitude in both eyes. Gräf et al8described this phenomenon in a patient who presented with unilateral accommodative esotropia. This patient’s eyes were aligned when examined under nondepolarizing anesthesia (Figure 2), confirming that DHD must arise from excessive esotonus during conditions of monocular fixation. The oscillopsia resulted from her latent nystagmus, which manifested during periods of intense fixation and esodeviation. The initial confirmatory test for DHD is the reversed fixation test (choice C).9After measuring the horizontal deviation in the nonfixating eye using alternate cover testing, the occluder is shifted back to the nonfixating eye, which normally shows no movement because the horizontal deviation has already been neutralized by the prism. In DHD, however, a horizontal movement of the fixating eye is seen, showing the presence of fixation-dependent innervation.9,10 The differential diagnosis of intermittent esotropia in adulthood includes decompensating esotropia (often caused by early presbyopia, necessitating excessive accommodative effort), anisometropia, and DHD. Retinoscopy ruled out anisometropia. An esodeviation produced by excessive accommodative effort owing to early presbyopia would be symmetrical in both eyes. Forced duction testing (choice A) was not indicated as ocular rotations were full. The absence of diplopia and the presence of latent nystagmus showed that this esotropia arose from a long-standing strabismus rather than a new-onset neurologic condition. Magnetic resonance imaging (choice B) was therefore not warranted. An increase in the exodeviation during periods of inattention (ie, nonfixation) is a useful clinical clue to the diagnosis of DHD.10In this patient, resolution of the esodeviation (due to suspension of dissociated esotonus) was seen during periods of nonfixation. Genetic testing (choice D) was not indicated as infantile strabismus is rarely hereditary, and she had no family history of strabismus. The patient was treated with small bilateral lateral rectus resections, which produced a consecutive exotropia. After small bilateral lateral rectus recessions, her eyes were straight at distance and near, and her symptoms abated.

caption: Clinical photographs of the left eye showing a diffuse yellow-pink lesion on the inferior palpebral conjunctiva (arrowheads) (A), and the yellow velvety appearance of the upper palpebral conjunctiva (arrowheads) (B).
scenario: A 73-year-old man was referred to our service for assessment of a slow-growing conjunctival lesion in the left eye. He had first noticed left eye discomfort and a fullness of the left lower eyelid 3 months previously. He denied any vision or systemic symptoms. His ophthalmic history was noncontributory. The patient’s medical history was notable only for prostate carcinoma, which was treated with radiotherapy 12 years ago. On examination, his visual acuities were 20/25 OU. Slitlamp examination of the anterior segment revealed diffuse yellow-pink polypoidal papules affecting the inferior fornix and inferior palpebral conjunctiva of the left eye (Figure 1A). The upper palpebral conjunctiva in the left eye had a velvety yellow appearance (Figure 1B). The remainder of the examination of both eyes was unremarkable. Initial investigations, including a complete blood cell count, urinalysis, and measurement of inflammatory markers, kidney function, and prostate-specific antigen level, were within normal limits. Serum electrophoresis showed raised monoclonal IgM bands (7.25 g/L; reference range, 0.50-2.00 g/L) with a κ/λ light-chain ratio of 2.92 (reference range, 0.260-1.65).

options.A: Commence lubricating eye drops and topical corticosteroids
options.B: Perform a complete excisional biopsy of the lesion
options.C: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
options.D: Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion

answer: Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion
distractors: Commence lubricating eye drops and topical corticosteroids
Perform a complete excisional biopsy of the lesion
Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits
explanation: D. Perform an incisional biopsy of the lesion The appearance of this conjunctival lesion is suggestive of amyloidosis. Amyloid is an insoluble, fibrillar protein that can form tissue deposits, leading to functional impairment. The kidneys and heart are the most commonly affected organs in systemic amyloidosis. Primary localized conjunctival amyloidosis is a rare but well-described entity, most frequently affecting the palpebral conjunctiva and superior fornix.1The diagnosis of amyloidosis is based on its characteristic histologic features that help differentiate it from other conditions, such as malignant neoplasms (lymphoma, squamous, or sebaceous cell carcinomas) and inflammatory disorders (pyogenic granuloma, sarcoidosis). Clinically, it is most easily distinguished from a more defined, pedunculated, and highly vascular pyogenic granuloma. Amyloid characteristically stains with Congo red and exhibits apple-green birefringence on polarization microscopy examination (Figure 2). Therefore, an incisional biopsy should be performed (choice D) for diagnostic purposes. This can also provide symptomatic relief by debulking the conjunctival mass with an estimated recurrence rate of less than 30%.1A complete excisional biopsy (choice B) may be performed for solitary or more confined lesions, but it is less suitable for diffuse involvement of the conjunctiva as in this case.1,2Unlike inflammatory conditions, localized conjunctival amyloidosis does not respond to corticosteroid therapy (choice A). Lubricants can provide temporary symptomatic relief; however, surgical debulking remains the mainstay of therapy. If orbital amyloidosis causes substantial ptosis, proptosis, or eye movement restrictions, further surgical intervention and targeted external beam radiotherapy may be considered.3,4 Histologic examination confirmed conjunctival amyloidosis of no specific subtype in this patient. More than 20 different types of amyloid protein have been described. Secondary amyloidosis occurs in the context of systemic conditions, leading to the accumulation of AA amyloid derived from the acute-phase protein serum amyloid A. In primary amyloidosis, immunoglobulin light-chain–derived protein (AL) deposits in tissues. The condition may be localized or associated with an underlying plasma cell disorder. In a small proportion of patients, systemic AL amyloidosis may eventually progress to multiple myeloma,5whereas systemic AL amyloidosis may subsequently develop in approximately 1% of patients with multiple myeloma; this development confers a poor prognosis.6 Conjunctival amyloidosis is usually primary and localized, with no systemic associations.1,4However, a basic examination to rule out systemic disease is recommended.1Investigations typically include a complete blood cell count, bone profile, kidney and liver function tests, urinalysis, and serum and urine electrophoresis.1Presence of monoclonal gammopathy warrants further hematologic assessment by performing a bone marrow biopsy to exclude underlying multiple myeloma and other blood dyscrasias. Finally, ordering imaging of the orbits is useful to determine the extent of the condition, including any orbital involvement.2,4 Performing the incisional biopsy sufficiently debulked the lesion to alleviate the patient’s ocular symptoms. At the 6-month follow-up, the conjunctival appearance remained stable. Systemic examination findings, including magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits, bone marrow aspirate, and transthoracic echocardiogram, were unremarkable. Despite an elevated IgM level, no underlying plasma cell dyscrasia was identified. The patient continues to receive regular examinations from the oculoplastics service and has been referred to the National Amyloidosis Center.

caption: A, Fundus photograph shows scattered, punctate hypopigmentation and subtle irregular hyperpigmentation in the macula. B, Fundus autofluorescence shows irregularly distributed, speckled hypoautofluorescence, most prominent in the inferior macula. Findings were similar, although not symmetric in distribution, in the left eye.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman with interstitial cystitis presented for pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron) maculopathy screening. She reported no visual symptoms or ocular history, and routine eye examination results 6 months prior were reportedly normal. She was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis in 2004 and had been taking pentosan polysulfate, 100 mg twice daily, for 4½ years for a cumulative dose of 324 g. Her medical history was otherwise significant for moderate bilateral hearing loss detected in early childhood and type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism treated with a therapeutic regimen of metformin, pravastatin, and levothyroxine supplementation, respectively. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20−2 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures by rebound tonometry were normal, and anterior segment examination results were unremarkable. She had trace cortical cataracts and nuclear sclerosis in each eye. Dilated fundus examination in each eye revealed cup-disc ratios of 0.2, mild retinal pigment epithelium mottling, and scattered, deep punctate, hypopigmented lesions. Macular optical coherence tomography imaging demonstrated trace irregularity to the outer retinal bands. Fundus autofluorescence imaging showed irregularly distributed speckled hypoautofluorescence in the posterior pole of each eye (Figure).

options.A: Inform patient that she has changes from drug toxicity
options.B: Initiate nutritional supplement therapy for treatment of age-related macular degeneration per Age-Related Eye Disease Study recommendations
options.C: Advise patient that family members are at risk for pattern dystrophy
options.D: Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid

answer: Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid
distractors: Inform patient that she has changes from drug toxicity
Initiate nutritional supplement therapy for treatment of age-related macular degeneration per Age-Related Eye Disease Study recommendations
Advise patient that family members are at risk for pattern dystrophy
explanation: D. Obtain a more detailed medical history and provide an Amsler grid Additional questioning revealed the patient’s mother was diagnosed with “German measles” early in pregnancy and expected her child might be blind and/or deaf. The patient was born in Canada and was small for gestational age, but had no apparent visual, auditory, or cardiac issues at birth. In early adulthood, when joining the military, the patient was tested and informed of her serologic rubella immunity. This patient’s presentation with early-onset hearing loss, granular retinal pigmentary mottling with punctate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (“salt and pepper”), and irregularly distributed speckled fundus autofluorescence changes is consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Although the patient used pentosan polysulfate, her cumulative exposure was relatively low; in a series of 35 cases of pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, the median (range) cumulative exposure was 1.61 kg (0.44-4.32 kg).1In addition, her pattern of fundus autofluorescence abnormality, with loosely spaced speckled hypoautofluorescence, did not resemble pentosan polysulfate maculopathy, which typically manifests a symmetric dense pattern of hypoautofluorescent and hyperautofluorescent spots centered on and involving the fovea (choice A).1,2This case is not consistent with age-related macular degeneration (choice B) given the absence of drusen and the unique fundus autofluorescence abnormalities. She had no family history of macular disease, and her imaging results were not consistent with the classic phenotypes of pattern dystrophy (choice C), which encompass a variety of presentations typically featuring more prominent, discrete, and symmetric pigmentary changes centered on the fovea. Congenital rubella syndrome occurs by transplacental transmission of the rubella virus, initially described as a triad of neonatal deafness, cardiac anomalies, and cataracts.3,4Most affected infants have no detected abnormality at birth, but nearly all eventually display variable multiorgan involvement (commonly auditory, ophthalmic, and endocrine) in early childhood owing to persistent viral replication.5In a 20-year follow-up of 125 patients with CRS, ocular disease was most prevalent, affecting 78% of the patients, and, of these, 53% also had hearing loss.5Retinopathy was the most common ophthalmic manifestation, although other reported findings included microphthalmia, glaucoma, corneal clouding, and strabismus.5,6A potential complication of rubella retinopathy is choroidal neovascularization, which has been reported in numerous cases but without known incidence.6Amsler grid testing may aid in early detection of choroidal neovascularization. However, Amsler grid testing has relatively poor sensitivity and specificity when used in patients with age-related macular degeneration, and it is unknown how effective it is in patients with rubella retinopathy. While the incidence of rubella has decreased since the introduction of vaccination programs in 1969, mothers pregnant prior to that introduction were potentially still exposed, and there are occasionally imported cases.7Industrialized countries are experiencing more outbreaks given growing antivaccination movements.7,8The incidence of rubella is approximately 1.3 of 100 000 population worldwide and 0 of 100 000 population in the US.9From 2004 to 2012, there were 79 cases of primary rubella in the US and 6 cases of CRS, all from mothers who traveled in Africa during pregnancy.4,10Congenital rubella syndrome will remain an important clinical challenge given its endemic nature in developing nations, globalization, and antivaccination trends. Notably, rubella retinopathy is a clinical diagnosis. Serologic immunity can occur with vaccination or after infection; therefore, proving a remote previous infection is challenging. However, proper diagnosis is important given the potential serious and multiorgan involvement. Results of the patient’s cardiac workup were normal. She was advised to discuss with her prescribing physician whether she should discontinue pentosan polysulfate given her potential heightened risk for pentosan polysulfate maculopathy in the setting of CRS retinopathy. She is using the Amsler grid test to monitor her vision and will undergo annual retinal evaluation.

caption: A, Wide-angle fundus photography of the left eye showing an intraocular mass inferotemporally (arrowhead), overlying an encircling band. B, B-scan ultrasonography documenting an echodense lesion (arrowhead) indenting the globe and with posterior shadowing.
scenario: An 89-year-old asymptomatic woman presented to a new eye care professional for a routine examination. Examination findings showed a large choroidal mass in the left eye suspicious for a malignant neoplasm. The patient’s ocular history showed a cataract surgical procedure, YAG capsulotomy, and subsequent repair of retinal detachment with scleral buckle and pneumatic retinopexy in the left eye approximately 30 years earlier. Ophthalmoscopic examination results of the left eye revealed a peripheral retinal atrophy from previous cryotherapy treatment. A large choroidal mass was observed in the inferotemporal region. The patient was referred for further evaluation of the mass, which was suspected to represent choroidal melanoma. Our examination findings showed a visual acuity of 20/20 OD and 20/60 OS, with intraocular pressures of 20 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS measured using a tonometer (Tono-pen; Reichert Inc). Ophthalmoscopy results of the right eye were normal. In the left eye, a 360° encircling band with overlying retinal atrophy was documented. There was a variably pigmented, abruptly elevated mass deep in the inferotemporal retina, measuring 12.0 mm in diameter (Figure, A) and without overlying drusen, orange pigment, or subretinal fluid. Ultrasonography results showed that the mass was dome shaped and echodense, with posterior shadowing (Figure, B); it measured 4.6 mm thick. Optical coherence tomographic imaging revealed an intact macula.

options.B: Apply radioactive iodine I 125 plaque radiotherapy
options.C: Order magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Suspect an association with prior ocular surgery

answer: Suspect an association with prior ocular surgery
distractors: Apply radioactive iodine I 125 plaque radiotherapy
explanation: Choroidal pseudomelanoma secondary to scleral buckle D. Suspect an association with prior ocular surgery Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignant neoplasm in the United States, affecting 5.2 per million population.1Pseudomelanoma is a condition that simulates choroidal melanoma. In an analysis of approximately 12 000 patients referred to a tertiary care center with uveal melanoma over a 25-year period, 1739 (14%) proved to be pseudomelanoma.2Of these, the most common pseudomelanomas included choroidal nevus (851 [49%]), peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (139 [8%]), and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigmented epithelium (108 [6%]).2Much less commonly, compression by an orbital mass (3 [0.2%]) was noted, as in this case with compression by a radial scleral sponge. Several features in this case suggest that the intraocular mass represents compression by an external device, likely a radial sponge from the previous scleral buckle surgery. The chorioretinal atrophic scar over its apex suggests previous cryotherapy, and the abrupt echodense appearance with shadowing on ultrasonography suggests a foreign body, such as an indentation sponge. Thus, choice D is correct, as a suspected correlation to previous retinal surgery would be revealing. These features suggest a radial sponge presenting as pseudomelanoma; therefore, performing a fine-needle aspiration biopsy (choice A) or applying radioactive iodine I 125 plaque radiotherapy (choice B) would not be necessary. Ordering magnetic resonance imaging (choice C) could be helpful if the medical records denied a scleral buckle, as this would document a nonenhancing mass external to the globe, unlike melanoma, which generally shows gadolinium enhancement within the globe. Scleral buckle can closely simulate choroidal melanoma clinically, but it can be differentiated by buckle features showing lack of flow on fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography, echodensity with shadowing on ultrasonography, and lack of gadolinium enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging. The hydrogel variant of scleral buckle can even more closely resemble choroidal melanoma because it slowly swells over time, demonstrating pseudoenlargement.3Some intraocular tumors exhibit echodensity on ultrasonography, including choroidal nevus, metastasis, osteoma, scleritis, sclerochoroidal calcification, retinoblastoma, and retinal astrocytic hamartoma. Despite the benign nature of the scleral buckle in this case, the clinician should recognize that choroidal melanoma can occur overlying scleral buckle, and the differentiation can be challenging.4In this patient, observation was advised, and the radial sponge remained. The patient was reassured as to the benign nature of this lesion and observation was provided.

A, Examination showed nonspecific lymphocytic infiltrate in the adventitia (arrowheads) and pale, amorphous, eosinophilic amyloid deposits (asterisk) in the muscularis of the vessel wall (original magnification ×25). scenario: A patient in their late 70s with a history of Crohn disease, coronary artery disease, hypercholesterolemia, and transient ischemic attack presented with sudden, painless, left-sided vision loss. They denied headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 103 mm/h and a magnetic resonance angiographic examination of the brain was negative for mass, infarction, and hemorrhage. Examination results of a right, superficial, temporal artery biopsy specimen showed chronic, nongranulomatous inflammation surrounding adventitial vessels and extensive subintimal fibrosis, without giant cells or segmental loss of the internal elastic lamina, which was interpreted as compatible with temporal arteritis. High-dose corticosteroid therapy was initiated (1 g methylprednisolone intravenously for 3 days followed by 60 mg/d of oral prednisone). A neuro-ophthalmologic examination performed 1 week later showed an unreactive left pupil with an obvious relative afferent pupillary defect. Optic nerve pallor concomitant with edema and a single flame-shaped hemorrhage at the 4-o’clock position on the disc margin was also observed. Two weeks later, persistent elevation of the ESR and C-reactive protein levels, despite continued oral prednisone therapy, prompted a review of the temporal artery biopsy findings. This disclosed abundant transmural deposits of amorphous eosinophilic acellular material that was congophilic and exhibited apple-green birefringence under polarized light, consistent with amyloid deposits (Figure). Immunohistochemical staining showed IgM and λ light chain restriction.

options.C: Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis
options.D: Order a biopsy of the liver

answer: Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis
distractors: Order a biopsy of the liver
explanation: Systemic amyloidosis in the setting of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) C. Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis An older patient presenting with visual loss and pallid disc edema arouses suspicion for an anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. As the most common vasculitis of older adults in North America, giant cell arteritis (GCA) has become the poster child of the arteritic form of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Well established as visually morbid—with an approximate 8% rate of permanent vision loss and a 50% rate of fellow eye involvement—and responsive to corticosteroid therapy, GCA has a low threshold for diagnosis and treatment.1However, the prevailing criteria for diagnosing GCA (the 1990 American College of Rheumatology classification) is relatively nonspecific, having a specificity of 91.3%.2Other vasculitides, including eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, hypersensitivity vasculitis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, polyarteritis nodosa, and Takayasu arteritis, are all cited as misclassifications for GCA in the original article by Hunder et al.2 Classic histopathologic findings of GCA include marked narrowing of the arterial lumen by concentric intimal fibroplasia and transmural infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages (with or without giant cells), leading to fragmentation, multilamination, and segmental loss of the internal elastic lamina. In chronic cases, a fibrous or fibrovascular scar is present at the level of the internal elastic lamina and frequently involves the tunica media. Examination results of the patient’s temporal artery biopsy specimen were notable for chronic lymphocytic inflammation confined to the adventitia without an appreciable granulomatous component in the vessel wall or breaks in the internal elastic lamina. Although these findings are nondiagnostic for temporal arteritis, they should prompt additional tissue sampling to definitively exclude GCA and call to mind alternative etiologies of adventitial inflammation.3,4Intravitreal corticosteroid therapies have not been shown to significantly improve visual acuity in patients with ischemic optic neuropathy (choice A).5 Patients with clinically diagnosed GCA and partial or absent symptomatic response to corticosteroid therapies should be considered for alternative diagnoses. This includes amyloid deposition in the vessel wall, which may contribute to vision loss via vascular occlusion induced by the amyloid deposit itself or in combination with an inflammatory infiltrate. In the patient, temporal artery amyloidosis was discovered after 1 month of stable vision with persistently elevated inflammatory markers, emblematic of the diagnostic delay frequently seen in these cases. Factors contributing to delay include histopathologic examination misdiagnosis of amyloid as “intimal thickening” or “fibromyxoid change,” and partial clinical improvement with corticosteroid therapy.6Failure to recognize systemic disease has potentially grave implications, as amyloid light chain amyloidosis has an estimated 30% mortality rate within 18 months.7 Patients with temporal artery amyloidosis have a plasma cell dyscrasia in approximately 80% of cases, often in the setting of plasma cell myeloma, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and, less frequently, mature B-cell lymphomas.6Thus, systemic workup for underlying hematolymphoid dyscrasia is warranted and GCA-indicated medications, such as tocilizumab (choice B), are inappropriate. The standard laboratory evaluation includes complete blood cell count with differential and serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (choice C) for monoclonal immunoglobulin. In addition, a positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan, bone survey, and bone marrow biopsy are performed for comprehensive oncologic examination. According to consensus guidelines, performing a liver biopsy is not indicated (choice D) unless end-organ dysfunction is suspected.8 Approximately 1 week after the diagnosis of temporal artery amyloidosis, the patient developed a left footdrop and was hospitalized for uncontrolled atrial fibrillation. Results of a stroke workup were negative for evidence of cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory studies were notable for an elevated ESR of 130 mm/h and mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10.2 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10). Serum protein electrophoresis testing with immunofixation showed marked elevation of IgM (5214 mg/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 0.01]) and free κ light chains (1200 mg/L; reference, 3.3-19.4 mg/L). Examination of the bone marrow biopsy specimen showed a 60% involvement by lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, confirming the diagnosis of IgM-associated monoclonal gammopathy, or Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Treatment with rituximab and bortezomib therapy was initiated.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of left eye indicates lesions throughout the midperiphery of the cornea (A). The top arrowhead shows the posterior stromal location of the deposit. The bottom arrowhead reveals one that is located in the anterior stroma. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the left eye indicates the variable depths of the lesions in the anterior and posterior stroma (arrowheads) (B).
scenario: A 70-year-old White woman with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia was referred to our institution for evaluation of bilateral asymmetric corneal lesions by her primary eye care professional. The patient required spectacles for best-corrected visual acuity but otherwise had no other significant ocular complaints. She was not taking medications known to cause corneal depositions, nor was there a known family history of corneal dystrophy. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Slitlamp examination of the cornea of the right eye revealed multiple, discrete nodular opacities in the superior and inferior quadrants without neovascularization or surface elevation. Similar findings were seen in the left eye, but the superior lesions were notable for possessing well-circumscribed, plaquelike features located in the posterior stroma without involvement of the anterior surface (Figure, A). No crystalline changes were noted with these deposits. For further characterization of the corneal findings, anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) was obtained, revealing multiple anterior stromal and subepithelial opacities without involvement of the deeper stromal layers in the right eye. AS-OCT of the left eye showed multiple anterior and posterior stromal opacities with sparing of the central stromal layers (Figure, B). While the posterior lesions caused a bulging of Descemet membrane, the endothelial layer was intact in both eyes.

answer: Additional laboratory workup
distractors: Treatment with frequent lubrication and topical steroids
explanation: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance When encountering asymmetrical, bilateral anterior and posterior stromal corneal lesions, clinicians should consider systemic causes (infectious, autoimmune, and hematologic) and pursue laboratory workup. Salzmann nodular degeneration was deemed less likely, given the variable lesion depth and lack of surface elevation. The following diagnostic workup was pursued: complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum and urine protein electrophoresis, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus/herpes zoster virus, Lyme antibody titers (IgG/IgM), rapid plasma reagin, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption, QuantiFERON Gold, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti-SSA (Ro)/anti-SSB (La) antibodies. Results revealed an elevated γ globulin M spike (0.8 g/dL), cytomegalovirus IgG, and herpes simplex virus IgG. Notably, herpes simplex virus IgM, Epstein-Barr virus, and other autoimmune laboratory values were negative. The abnormal serum proteins prompted referral to a hematologist. Monoclonal gammopathies encompass a spectrum of diseases, including multiple myeloma and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). While multiple myeloma is one of the most common hematologic malignancies, a forme fruste, premalignant stage-termed MGUS may precede it.1,2Estimated to have a prevalence of 3% to 4% in individuals older than 50 years, MGUS progresses to multiple myeloma at a rate of 0.5% to 1% per year.2Traditionally, it has been considered an asymptomatic disease stage and requires the absence of hypercalcemia, kidney failure, anemia, and bone lesions.2,3Although visual symptoms are minimal in MGUS, ocular findings may be the first sign of systemic disease, providing ophthalmologists with an important role in diagnosing underlying disease. Clinical descriptions of paraproteinemic keratopathy were first reported in the early 1900s, and approximately 1% of patients with gammopathies have corneal involvement.1,4-6Given the protean nature of corneal deposition patterns, recognition of these findings may be challenging. Clinical appearance can range from crystallinetype deposits to nodular lesions in multiple levels of the corneal stroma, as in this patient.1,3,7To our knowledge, this nodular pattern is uncommon.1,8For patients with crystalline deposits, in vivo confocal microscopy is a diagnostic modality worth considering. Given the wide array of corneal deposition patterns, ophthalmologists should consider bilateral ocular findings as possible manifestations of systemic disease, necessitating multidisciplinary investigation for diagnostic confirmation.9,10This patient had no known history of blood dyscrasia, yet the corneal findings led to the discovery of underlying MGUS. Ocular involvement could represent a sign of progression from MGUS to frank multiple myeloma, prompting a recent call for a new categorization of disease: monoclonal gammopathy of ocular significance.1,3Therefore, ophthalmologists encountering these corneal findings should consider a multidisciplinary approach, which might help to ensure that at-risk patients are monitored closely for the development of potentially life-threatening disease. Multiple approaches have been proposed for diagnosis, depending on the depth and location of corneal pathology. Serial imaging, corneal biopsy, and aqueous sampling for detection of monoclonal proteins have been reported.3In this patient, AS-OCT accurately highlighted the location, depth, and extent of the lesions and avoided more invasive options (choices A and C). The posterior lesions, preserved endothelial layer, and the absence of corneal neovascularization increased our suspicion for a depositional disorder, rather than an infectious or inflammatory process (choice D). Clinicians may consider AS-OCT or in vivo confocal microscopy as part of their diagnostic armamentarium in these patients, especially for long-term serial monitoring. This case provides a tangible reminder that ophthalmologists are critical in diagnosis of systemic (and sometimes life-threatening) diseases, which often necessitates multidisciplinary management. The hematologist confirmed the diagnosis of MGUS. We instructed the patient to return in 6 months for follow-up, photo documentation, and further monitoring.
