scenario: A 40-year-old man with refractory glaucoma was referred for decreased vision in the right eye after an aqueous shunting surgical procedure 3 weeks prior. The surgical procedure was a 2-staged Baerveldt implantation after which he developed fluctuating but progressive visual decline. The patient’s ocular history was significant for Sturge-Weber syndrome with bilateral cutaneous port-wine stains, secondary glaucoma in the right eye, and an irregular globe with a white cataract and chronic retinal detachment (RD) in the left eye. At presentation, visual acuity was hand motion OD and a long-standing history of no light perception OS. Intraocular pressures by Goldmann applanation tonometry were 16 mm Hg OD and 28 mm Hg OS. Anterior segment examination of the right eye revealed a properly positioned plate and tube, and dilated fundus examination revealed a red glow of the fundus with shifting subretinal fluid and RD extending from the 2- to 11-o’clock position (Figure 1A). B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye confirmed the RD and demonstrated homogeneous diffuse choroidal thickening (Figure 1B).

options.A: Perform subretinal fluid drainage and silicone oil tamponade
options.C: Treat with radiotherapy

answer: Treat with radiotherapy
distractors: Perform subretinal fluid drainage and silicone oil tamponade
explanation: Diffuse choroidal hemangioma with exudative retinal detachments The patient had classic ophthalmologic features of Sturge-Weber syndrome, including eyelid angiomas, glaucoma, and diffuse choroidal hemangioma (DCH). Early-onset glaucoma can develop from anterior chamber abnormalities and late onset from increased episcleral venous pressure.1Glaucoma in the patient’s right eye, likely owing to the latter, was refractive to medical therapy. He underwent 2-stage Baerveldt insertion—in the first stage, the plate was attached to the globe and 1 month later, allowing for scarring and capsule formation, the tube was placed into the anterior chamber.2This approach has been reported effective at avoiding rapid intraocular pressure lowering that could result in fluid transudation due to increased hydrostatic pressure between the choroidal and abnormally high-pressure Sturge-Weber syndrome venous system.3Despite these measures, an exudative RD associated with DCH developed. Choroidal hemangiomas are diffuse in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome, and contrast with nonsyndromic circumscribed hemangiomas.1Characteristically, in DCH, an A-scan exhibits high internal reflectivity and a B-scan demonstrates highly echogenic, diffuse choroidal thickening.4Fluorescein angiography reveals hyperfluorescence in all phases with late staining and variable leakage.4Indocyanine green demonstrates early hyperfluorescence and late “washout” with a hyperfluorescent rim.4Treatment is indicated for visual changes that could benefit from tumor atrophy; namely, hemangioma-induced foveal distortion and subretinal fluid. Although circumscribed tumor treatment with photodynamic therapy is supported by the literature,5there is no DCH management consensus. Modalities used include photodynamic therapy and radiotherapy with external beam radiotherapy, brachytherapy, or proton beam radiotherapy.6Subretinal fluid drainage and silicone oil tamponade (choice A) are not used to treat serous RDs. Oral corticosteroids (choice B) are not beneficial in noninflammatory conditions. Observation (choice D) could result in permanent vision loss. The success of photodynamic therapy is attributable to verteporfin tumor endothelial cell localization causing photochemical vaso-occlusion while avoiding irradiation. However, lack of cooperation and poor visibility limit use.7Also, larger treatment areas require multiple sessions and overtreatment can result in retinal pigment epithelium and choroidal damage.6Successful tumor treatment has been reported with radiotherapy, but complications to consider include cataracts, retinopathy, optic neuropathy, and secondary malignant neoplasms, particularly in young patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome. External beam radiotherapy has the advantage of delivering a homogeneous dose to the choroid but exposes surrounding ocular tissue.8Benefits of brachytherapy are precise focal irradiation with minimal damage to adjacent structures. Nonetheless, brachytherapy requires a pretreatment surgical procedure, masses are often larger than plaque design (although treatment to the thickest portion has been successful),9and delivery is inhomogeneous.6Proton beam radiotherapy delivers a homogeneous dose while sparing surrounding tissue. If a light-field technique without tumor localization is implemented, patients are spared from tantalum ring placement.10However, access to proton beam radiotherapy is limited to specialized centers. In summary, treatment should be guided by tumor size, location, and visibility, as well as the patient’s age and ability to cooperate. The patient was treated with whole-choroid proton beam radiotherapy using a light-field technique, achieved by having the patient look up and avoiding the anterior segment, with exudative RD resolution (Figure 2) and recovery of 20/20 OD visual acuity with an intraocular pressure obtained via Goldmann applanation tonometry of 21 mm Hg OD. At a low dose of 1500 cGy in 4 fractions, he is unlikely to develop adverse effects from radiation.

caption: Slitlamp photograph of the patient’s right eye with posterior synechiae, hypopyon, and rubeosis iridis (arrowheads) after mydriasis.
scenario: A 78-year-old man presented with decreased visual acuity and hypopyon in his right eye. He had a history of Philadelphia chromosome–positive acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (attributable to treatment with the tyrosine-kinase inhibitor [TKI] imatinib), and diabetes. He had senile dementia but did not complain of constitutional symptoms. His visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/32 OS, and his intraocular pressures were 31 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS. A slitlamp examination of the right eye showed redness, with small, white, nongranulomatous keratic precipitate as well as a cataract. His iris was diffusely thickened and the anterior chamber was slightly shallow, with 4+ cells and white hypopyon, which did not change position with head movements (Figure 1). There was also an extensive rubeosis iridis (Figure 1) with posterior synechiae in the right eye. The left anterior chamber was normal. A fundus examination had unremarkable results in both eyes. A complete blood cell count had normal results, and his hemoglobin A1clevel was 16.5%. A syphilis test result was negative.

options.A: Anterior chamber tap for a multiplex polymerase chain reaction test for infectious uveitis
options.B: Anterior chamber tap for hypopyon cytology tests
options.C: Human leukocyte antigen typing

answer: Anterior chamber tap for hypopyon cytology tests
distractors: Anterior chamber tap for a multiplex polymerase chain reaction test for infectious uveitis
explanation: B. Anterior chamber tap for hypopyon cytology tests Hypopyon cytology testing revealed numerous small, atypical lymphocytes (Figure 2). The patient was later diagnosed with Alzheimer disease. It was discovered that the patient had self-discontinued all the medications that he should have been taking (including TKI and antidiabetic drugs) 8 months prior, owing to decreased cognitive function. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and a lumbar puncture revealed no further central nervous system involvement. Messenger RNA from the breakpoint cluster region–tyrosine-protein kinase ABL1 (BCR-ABL) gene was not detected in the peripheral blood. The patient was diagnosed with an intraocular relapse of Philadelphia chromosome–positive ALL. Philadelphia chromosome–positive ALL is the most frequent chromosomal abnormality in adult ALL (20%-30% of adults with ALL).1Ocular manifestations of leukemia (cotton-wool spots, Roth spots, optic nerve involvement, and serous retinal detachments) can be caused by direct intraocular infiltration or associated comorbidities.2Anterior chamber infiltration constitutes approximately 12% in masquerade syndrome and is seen in up to 18% of relapsed cases of ALL but rarely in adults.3,4Few cases of rubeosis iridis in ocular leukemia have been reported.5Pseudohypopyon, which is typically viscous and may be blood stained, occurs as a consequence of sequestration of leukemic cells along the long posterior ciliary vessels and the vessels of the iris into the anterior chamber.2,6An acute rise of intraocular pressure can occur as a result of infiltration of the iris and trabecular meshwork.7 Owing to the absence of ocular trauma or surgery and systemic or ocular findings, an anterior chamber tap for multiplex polymerase chain reaction for infectious uveitis (choice A) was not the optimal answer. Subconjunctival injection of dexamethasone (choice D) before ruling out an infection, such as tuberculosis, would be a premature decision. With the lack of associated systemic symptoms and mobile hypopyon, human leukocyte antigen typing (choice C), suspecting Behçet disease or syndromes associated with human leukocyte antigen–B27, was not recommended as the next step. Ocular involvement in leukemia can be asymptomatic, leading to delayed treatment and poor prognosis systemically. In cases of apparent manifestations, such as pseudohypopyon, anterior chamber taps for cytology should be considered. Although development of TKIs has improved the prognosis of patients with Philadelphia chromosome–positive ALL, the 5-year overall survival rate remains less than 20% for older patients.8Conventional chemotherapy or external beam radiotherapy is usually the treatment of choice in an ocular relapse of ALL; however, their adverse effects can affect the quality of life and the prognosis remains poor.2,4,8Intravitreal methotrexate (400 mg/0.1 mg) injections for the treatment of ocular leukemia, using the treatment strategy for primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (twice weekly in the first month, once weekly in the following 2 months, and once monthly thereafter), have been reported.9,10 Considering the risk of adverse effects of systemic therapy, the patient was treated solely with dasatinib (a TKI), 70 mg, twice daily, and intravitreal methotrexate injections, which were administered less frequently, according to patient’s preference (twice weekly for 2 weeks, monthly for 3 months, and then once every 2 months). The pseudohypopyon and rubeosis iridis resolved completely after 2 injections. His visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD (with a cataract), and his intraocular pressure normalized. He achieved ocular remission, and his regular hematological work-up results have remained negative for systemic relapse.

caption: Cutaneous and retinal vasculitis. A, Purpuric rash involving the left foot. B, Montage fundus photograph of the left eye shows frosted branch angiitis with preretinal hemorrhages over the disc (arrowhead) and macula (arrowhead), intraretinal hemorrhages, perivenular exudates, and sheathing.
scenario: A 49-year-old African American man who was hospitalized with hypervolemia due to supraventricular tachycardia presented with acute unilateral painless vision loss. His active medical problems included atrial flutter on anticoagulation, antisynthetase syndrome (which was diagnosed based on the presence of autoantibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase), fever with negative infectious workup results, and interstitial lung disease that was managed with azathioprine. Two weeks before the onset of sudden vision loss, the patient developed a rapidly evolving purpuric rash on his hands and feet that progressed to digital ischemia (Figure 1A). He was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, which was completed 3 days before the onset of loss of vision and transitioned to treatment with azathioprine, 150 mg, and prednisone, 80 mg, that he was taking at the time of his vision loss. On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OD and hand motions OS (baseline from 2 weeks prior was 20/20 OU), with a briskly reactive right pupil and a left afferent pupillary defect. Left eye examination revealed 2 or more anterior chamber cells, preretinal hemorrhage, frosted branch angiitis with diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, and perivascular exudates (Figure 1B). Fluorescein angiography results revealed extensive vascular nonperfusion and late perivenular leakage. The right eye was normal. Laboratory workup results revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm per hour, C-reactive protein levels of 2.53 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10), negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies test result, antinuclear antibodies, cryoglobulins, syphilis serology, tuberculosis testing, and transthoracic echocardiogram. Skin biopsy results showed medium vessel vasculitis.

options.B: Diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis and intravitreal foscarnet
options.C: Peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry

answer: Diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis and intravitreal foscarnet
distractors: Peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry
explanation: Frosted branch angiitis due to retinal vasculitis that was associated with antisynthetase syndrome B. Diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis and intravitreal foscarnet Despite the patient’s clinical presentation being suggestive of autoimmune retinal vasculitis, the most appropriate initial step is to rule out viral retinitis with an anterior chamber paracentesis and empirical treatment with intravitreal foscarnet (choice B) given the patient’s immunocompromised status. Escalating immunosuppression (choice A) is inappropriate before excluding infectious etiologies. Peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry (choice C) for clonality assessment or positron emission tomography–computed tomography (choice D) for occult malignancy screening are inappropriate in the short-term setting. Frosted branch angiitis is a form of retinal vasculitis that is characterized by diffuse vascular sheathing and various degrees of intraocular inflammation.1Idiopathic frosted branch angiitis occurs in otherwise healthy patients in their first or third decade of life following a viral illness and has a favorable prognosis with systemic steroid therapy.1-3Secondary frosted branch angiitis occurs in patients with an underlying infection, such as cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis, and syphilis, or inflammatory disease, such as Crohn disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, Behçet disease, multiple sclerosis, familial Mediterranean fever, or drug-induced antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody vasculitis,1,3-5and is thought to result from immune complex deposition. The frosted branchlike appearance may be associated with leukemia or lymphoma due to vessel wall infiltration with malignant cells. This patient had a normal whole-blood flow cytometry. Frosted branch angiitis may also present as a paraneoplastic manifestation of Hodgkin lymphoma6; however, this patient had an unremarkable whole-body positron emission tomography–computed tomography. Antisynthetase syndrome is a subset of inflammatory myositis that is characterized by the presence of antibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and clinical features, such as interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, arthritis, fever, and mechanic hands, which refers to thickened and cracked skin involving the hands.7Another article8described a patient with antisynthetase syndrome with a purpuric rash who presented with acute unilateral vision loss and frosted branch angiitis. That patient was treated with intravitreal foscarnet and clindamycin, which was followed by methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide once infectious etiologies were excluded. To our knowledge, the patient in our article is the third reported,8,9but showed a severe case of a rapidly progressive vision loss from retinal vasculitis while receiving systemic immunosuppression for antisynthetase syndrome that occurred 2 weeks following the onset of cutaneous vasculitis. Antisynthetase syndrome is a rare cause of frosted branch angiitis and requires urgent escalation of immunosuppression after infectious etiologies are excluded.8 Twenty-four hours after the diagnostic paracentesis and treatment with intravitreal foscarnet, aqueous polymerase chain reaction results returned negative for cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster virus, and herpes simplex virus. Valganciclovir was discontinued, and immunosuppression was escalated to cyclophosphamide and high-dose prednisone. While the retinal vasculitis responded to this therapy, the patient required bilateral transmetatarsal amputation. There have been no reports of vasculitis recurrence or recommendations regarding follow-up. At 4 months, the patient’s visual acuity remained at hand motions, and examination showed macula-involving tractional retinal detachment, disc pallor, vascular attenuation, and neovascularization elsewhere without active vasculitis (Figure 2). He underwent panretinal photocoagulation and continued to receive cyclophosphamide and prednisone taper. The fellow eye continues to be unaffected.

scenario: An 82-year-old man with an ocular history significant for bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts presented to the Cornea Service at Bascom Palmer Eye Institute, Miami, Florida, with a history of blurred vision in the right eye after phacoemulsification cataract extraction 8 weeks earlier. Current ophthalmic medications included topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, in the right eye 6 times per day. The patient reported no improvement with the treatment. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. Pupils were reactive without relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressures were 18 mm Hg in the right eye and 11 mm Hg in the left eye. A slitlamp biomicroscopic examination of the right eye revealed grade 2 to 3 diffuse central corneal edema and folds (Figure 1). The anterior chamber was deep and the posterior chamber intraocular lens was in good position within the capsular bag. Although the view to the posterior pole of the right eye was hazy owing to corneal edema, dilated fundus examination findings were unremarkable. Examination of the left eye revealed a few guttate. The central corneal thickness by ultrasound pachymetry was 957 μm in the right eye and 547 μm in the left eye.

options.B: Provide medical management with topical corticosteroids and hypertonic saline solution for an additional 3 months
options.C: Obtain an anterior-segment optical coherence tomogram
options.D: Perform an endothelial keratoplasty (Descemet stripping and endothelial keratoplasty or Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty)

answer: Obtain an anterior-segment optical coherence tomogram
distractors: Provide medical management with topical corticosteroids and hypertonic saline solution for an additional 3 months
Perform an endothelial keratoplasty (Descemet stripping and endothelial keratoplasty or Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty)
explanation: Corneal edema after cataract surgery secondary to intraoperative Descemet membrane detachment (Figure 2) C. Obtain an anterior-segment optical coherence tomogram In cases of diffuse corneal edema, where visualization is limited, anterior-segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) can help diagnose pathologies, such as Descemet membrane (DM) detachment (DMD) and/or retained lens fragments. Immediate penetrating keratoplasty (choice A) is not recommended for localized endothelial pathology. Endothelial keratoplasty (choice D), would not be the first step without determining underlying pathology or trying less invasive procedures. Additional treatment with topical agents (choice B) would not be preferred as the patient experienced decreased vision despite 8 weeks of topical therapy. Corneal edema after cataract surgery occurs because of failure of the corneal endothelial pump. Any condition that compromises endothelial cell density, such as endothelial dystrophies, anterior-segment dysgenesis, chronic anterior uveitis, glaucoma, and prior anterior-segment surgical procedures, may potentiate endothelial decompensation after surgery.1 Corneal edema in the early postoperative phase is generally secondary to an intraoperative injury to the endothelium and/or DM.1Inadvertent stripping of DM intraoperatively results in DMD.2The preoperative risk factors include age older than 65 years, dense nuclear sclerosis, preexisting endothelial dysfunction, and history of DMD in the contralateral eye. The intraoperative risk factors are a shallow anterior chamber and misdirected stream of viscoelastic or fluid creating a plane between posterior stroma and the DM.3The most common site of DMD (87.5% of cases) is at the main corneal incision and is associated with insertion and removal of instruments. Incidence of vision-impairing DMD varies between 0.044% and 0.5% of cases.4 Thorough slitlamp examination is the first step in identifying DMD. A bright, thin slit beam shows a clear optical space between the stroma and DM indicating a DMD. When visualization is limited, AS-OCT can help identify the location and anatomic configuration of the DMD.5 Classification of DMD is based on the extent of separation from posterior stroma into planar (≤1 mm) or nonplanar (>1 mm)6; based on location into central or peripheral; based on origin into rhegmatogenous owing to a tear of DM or tractional with fibrotic component; and based on anatomic configuration into bullous, which presents as a smooth bulge, or complex, which has rolls or scrolled edges.7 There are several options for management of DMD; the optimal procedure depends on the extent of corneal edema and location of DMD. Observation with administration of topical corticosteroids and hyperosmotic agents may be adequate in localized DMD because spontaneous reattachment can occur. Surgical intervention is often required in cases with central DMD with scrolled edges. Descemetopexy using intracameral injection of sterile air or gas (14% perfluoropropane or 20% sulfur hexafluoride) for tamponade followed by appropriate positioning for at least 24 hours to allow the air or gas to cover the area of the DM break has been shown to result in successful reattachment.8-10In case of persistent edema, corneal transplant may be required. The patient underwent air descemetopexy. At the 5-day follow-up, AS-OCT showed a completely attached DM. His DM has remained attached with a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 OD at the 18-month follow-up.

scenario: A 71-year-old woman with non-Hodgkin lymphoma receiving maintenance obinutuzumab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) infusions underwent uneventful pars plana vitrectomy of the right eye for vitreomacular traction. Diluted triamcinolone acetonide (TA) was used to stain the posterior hyaloid. After removal of 25-gauge trocar cannulas, subconjunctival TA and ceftazidime was injected. Owing to cystoid changes in the central macula, a short-acting gas tamponade with sulfur hexafluoride was used to tamponade any cystoid abnormalities that may have been unroofed. Despite unremarkable postoperative day 1 (POD1) examination findings, the patient presented on postoperative week 3 with a painless central scotoma and worsening floaters. Her visual acuity was 20/400 OD and intraocular pressure was normal. There was no external hyperemia or chemosis, and the anterior chamber was deep and quiet with no cells or flare. On dilated fundus examination, there were 15 to 20 cells per high-power field (using a 1 × 1-mm2high-intensity incidental slit beam) and a white macular lesion with disc edema and scattered intraretinal and peripapillary hemorrhages and mixed venous and arterial sheathing. Optical coherence tomography of the macula showed atrophy, full-thickness hyperreflectivity, and a residual epiretinal membrane (Figure).

options.A: Perform vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics
options.B: Review medical records to see if gentamicin was given intraoperatively
options.C: Urgently refer patient to emergency department for embolic stroke workup
options.D: Begin valganciclovir hydrochloride therapy and sample intraocular fluid for polymerase chain reaction testing

answer: Begin valganciclovir therapy and sample intraocular fluid for polymerase chain reaction testing
distractors: Perform vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics
Review medical records to see if gentamicin was given intraoperatively
Urgently refer patient to emergency department for embolic stroke workup
explanation: D. Begin valganciclovir therapy and sample intraocular fluid for polymerase chain reaction testing The differential diagnosis of a white macular lesion after vitrectomy is broad. A primary concern in postoperative patients presenting with excessive intraocular inflammation is endophthalmitis, which is treated with vitreous tap and injection of antibiotics (choice A). However, postvitrectomy endophthalmitis usually presents sooner after vitrectomy (median of 1.5 days [range, 1-30 days] in 1 retrospective series) with a more prominent cellular and fibrinous reaction.1Intravitreal and subconjunctival gentamicin have both been known to cause macular infarction.2However, toxic effects would manifest on POD1, and although the gas tamponade on POD1 can make the examination more challenging, the view was clear enough to rule out the dramatic macular pallor and hemorrhages seen with gentamicin toxicity. Therefore, reviewing the medical records to see if gentamicin was given intraoperatively (choice B) is not the best course of action. Macular pallor secondary to central retinal artery occlusion, which would necessitate an urgent patient referral to the emergency department for an embolic stroke workup (choice C), would be expected to have an associated cherry-red spot and would not have intraretinal hemorrhages and disc edema. The characteristic yellow-white granular retinitis with hemorrhages, sheathing, and vitritis in an immunocompromised patient is consistent with cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Therefore, the appropriate next step is to initiate valganciclovir therapy and sample the intraocular fluid (choice D). Cytomegalovirus is a ubiquitous herpesvirus with worldwide seroprevalence of 60% to 100%.3The most frequent ocular manifestation is CMV retinitis, while less frequent manifestations include papillitis, acute retinal necrosis, and endotheliitis.3The classic fundus finding of multifocal granular hemorrhagic necrotizing retinitis with focal sheathing (phlebitis more often than arteritis) is usually seen in HIV-infected patients.4,5In HIV-negative patients, CMV retinitis has been associated with a variety of systemic (eg, hematologic malignancies, chemotherapy, immunosuppressive medications) and local (intravitreal or periocular corticosteroid injections) risk factors, usually has more substantial intraocular inflammation, and can feature occlusive arteritis more typical of acute retinal necrosis.3-9Cytomegalovirus retinitis is diagnosed clinically and supported by ancillary tests (eg, PCR). Treatment is individualized based on immune status, size and location of retinitis, and risk of medication toxicity. Rapid viral suppression is achieved with high-dose systemic antiviral therapy followed by a maintenance phase of less intensive suppressive therapy. While induction therapy traditionally involved administering 1 of 3 intravenous drugs (ganciclovir, foscarnet, or cidofovir), there has been a shift toward using oral valganciclovir owing to its comparable efficacy, lower cost, and convenience. Local intravitreal therapy can be used as adjuvant treatment in patients with sight-threatening disease. The ganciclovir implant is no longer commercially available.10 In this patient, CMV retinitis appeared soon after uncomplicated vitrectomy. During the surgery, we injected approximately 0.1 mL of dilute TA to stain the posterior hyaloid, and at the conclusion of the case we injected routine subconjunctival ceftazidime and approximately 0.3 mL of subconjunctival TA (40 mg/mL). Although the patient had predisposing systemic conditions (non-Hodgkin lymphoma and B-cell immunosuppression from anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody), given that the infection coincided with surgery, we hypothesize that the surgical microtrauma to the retina and/or the TA used intraoperatively triggered the reactivation of latent CMV-infected cells in the retina in an already immunocompromised patient.7,8Despite no similar published reports, the fact that the retinitis occurred in the area of the retina that was directly stained with TA and that underwent the most surgical manipulation is consistent with this hypothesis. Treatment was initiated with oral valganciclovir hydrochloride, 900 mg twice a day, with subsequent gradual resolution of retinitis and vasculitis and the development of macular atrophy and temporal optic pallor. Polymerase chain reaction testing of vitreous aspirate was positive for CMV nucleic acid, and serologic samples were positive for CMV IgG and negative for CMV IgM. Results of further systemic workup, including for HIV, were negative. Her final visual acuity was 20/320 OD.

scenario: A 47-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes for more than 15 years was referred for proliferative diabetic retinopathy management. Her chief complaint was acute onset of blurry vision in the right eye. She described intermittent foggy vision and the appearance of “a hair moving across the vision of her right eye” for the past few weeks. Her most recent hemoglobin A1clevel was 8.3%, and 2 months prior to her visit, she had restarted diabetes medications. Her medications included metformin and glimepiride. Her corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Her pupil, color vision, and anterior segment examinations had normal results bilaterally. A posterior segment examination of the right eye showed mild temporal elevation of the optic disc with blurred margins, mild peripapillary hemorrhages, a small amount of preretinal hemorrhage, and small-caliber branching vessels at the temporal disc with no fibrosis (Figure 1A). The left eye showed a normal optic disc, a cup-disc ratio of 0.1, and some microaneurysms at the macula. There were a few scattered dot-blot hemorrhages bilaterally. Fluorescein angiography of the right eye showed mild leakage from the abnormal vessels at the temporal optic disc (Figure 1B).

options.B: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.C: Treat with an intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor

answer: Maintain observation
distractors: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Treat with an intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor
explanation: Diabetic papillopathy is an uncommon condition found among patients with type 1 or 2 diabetes that can be mistaken for neovascularization of the disc (NVD). Diabetic papillopathy can classically be differentiated from NVD by its radially oriented telangiectasias, which do not extend into the vitreous, while NVD has a random branching pattern and can extend into the vitreous.1,2Diabetic papillopathy has a favorable prognosis, and most cases resolve spontaneously within 4 to 8 months.1,2Small observational studies have reported improvement of optic disc edema with intravitreal or periocular steroids,3vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors (choice C),4or panretinal photocoagulation (choice D).5However, there appear to be no strong data for such treatments, and diabetic papillopathy can typically be observed. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (choice B) can be considered if compressive optic neuropathy or papilledema is suspected; unilateral papilledema cases have been reported but are uncommon.6While it is not unreasonable to rule out these conditions with imaging, the absence of an afferent pupillary defect or other neurological deficits make these diagnoses less likely. Diabetic papillopathy was first described in 1971 in young patients with type 1 diabetes and has since been described in older patients with type 2 diabetes.1,2,7It is characterized by unilateral or bilateral optic disc edema with normal or mildly abnormal visual acuity and spontaneous resolution in most cases. Risk factors include a small cup-disc ratio, long-standing diabetes, and rapid improvement with metabolic control.1,2,8Patients may be asymptomatic or report nonspecific vision complaints, such as mild blurring or distortion of vision. Ophthalmoscopic examinations reveal focal or diffuse optic disc edema, peripapillary hemorrhages, and characteristic dilated telangiectatic vessels overlying the optic nerve head. The preretinal hemorrhages seen in this patient are possible but rare with diabetic papillopathy and are more characteristic of NVD. Fluorescein angiography classically reveals early hyperfluorescence and late leakage around the optic nerve head.1,2 Recent studies suggest that optical coherence tomography angiography may be helpful in differentiating diabetic papillopathy from NVD.9Optical coherence tomography angiography in this case showed abnormal vessels limited to the optic disc without extension into the vitreous, supporting a diagnosis of diabetic papillopathy (Figure 2). Although some suggest that diabetic papillopathy is a mild or early form of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy,10this can be distinguished from diabetic papillopathy by its relatively severe symptoms, including decreased visual acuity, relative afferent pupillary defect, dyschromatopsia, visual field defects, persistent optic nerve pallor, and worse visual prognosis. Other than NVD and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, the differential diagnosis of diabetic papillopathy could include papilledema, papillitis, compressive optic neuropathy, toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy, malignant hypertension, and optic disc drusen. Diabetic papillopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion. A workup for diabetic papillopathy should include fluorescein angiography and potentially optical coherence tomography angiography. Patients with bilateral disc edema or neurologic deficits should undergo neuroimaging. Six months later, the patient reported a complete resolution of her symptoms. An examination revealed complete resolution of optic disc edema and telangiectasias, with stable findings of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy.

scenario: A 9-month-old girl presented to the emergency department with significant left periocular edema and erythema 3 days after receiving intra-arterial chemotherapy (IAC) with 0.4 mg/kg of melphalan, 50 mg of carboplatin, and 2 mg of topotecan (with routine intravenous dexamethasone therapy, 0.5 mg/kg) for treatment of unilateral International Classification of Retinoblastoma group C retinoblastoma in the left eye (Figure, A). At the time of IAC, she had an upper respiratory tract infection (coughing, congestion, rhinorrhea, fever [temperature of 38.9 °C]). On postoperative day 1, her temperature reached 39.4 °C, and she was diagnosed as having bilateral acute otitis media and discharged with amoxicillin therapy. On postoperative day 3, she returned to the emergency department with left eye swelling, continued fever, and poor oral intake. On physical examination, her temperature was 40.2 °C, and periorbital swelling and erythema were present without drainage. Dilated fundus examination at the bedside showed the known large retinoblastoma tumor. A large exudative retinal detachment was noted, which was not present prior to treatment. Blood bacterial culture testing showed no growth, respiratory viral testing revealed rhinovirus, and results of comprehensive metabolic testing were unremarkable. Complete blood cell count showed mild leukopenia (2700/μL [to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001]) and anemia (hemoglobin, 9.2 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but were otherwise within reference ranges. Computed tomography scan of the orbits, recommended by the on-call general ophthalmologist, demonstrated preseptal and periorbital soft tissue swelling and edema with subtle retrobulbar stranding, without substantial proptosis, along with retinal detachment (Figure, B). She was admitted for intravenous fluids for her noted dehydration.

options.C: Start systemic corticosteroids

answer: Start systemic corticosteroids
explanation: Periorbital edema related to administration of IAC The differential diagnosis of eye swelling in a patient with cancer receiving chemotherapy includes infectious (preseptal/orbital cellulitis), neoplastic (extraocular/orbital tumor), and inflammatory causes. IAC involves delivering chemotherapy into the ophthalmic artery via endovascular microcatheter, navigated under fluoroscopic guidance, either directly, balloon assisted, or via an external carotid artery anastomosis.1IAC is increasingly used for retinoblastoma, both as first-line and salvage therapy after failed intravenous chemotherapy, due to increased efficacy of IAC for advanced intraocular disease.2Globe salvage rates for International Classification of Retinoblastoma group D eyes with IAC (85.1%) exceed published rates for intravenous chemoreduction (36.7%).3 IAC may cause several ocular complications, most commonly transient periorbital swelling and erythema, reported in 22% of patients.4This may be more common with an external carotid anastomotic approach5and is most often seen in patients receiving multiagent infusions. Animal models suggest that this is possibly due to carboplatin-induced vascular damage leading to increased exudation/transudation.6,7While generally self-limited, recovery can be hastened by administering systemic steroids, and these can be given prophylactically in patients receiving triple therapy.8Parents should be prewarned that periorbital swelling is a known consequence of IAC that resolves. Other permanent and vision-threatening ocular complications of IAC, though rare, have been reported.3,4 IAC avoids many of the systemic adverse events of intravenous chemotherapy. Neutropenia does occur in approximately 30% to 40% of patients receiving IAC, although at rates much less than those seen with intravenous chemotherapy.3,6IAC is not associated with the degree of profound neutropenia seen with intravenous chemotherapy, and neutropenic fever is extremely rare.9Thus, typical chemotherapy-associated infectious causes of fever are not seen with IAC, as they are with intravenous chemotherapy. In thinking about this patient, the differential should not reflect the common causes of swelling and fever seen in a postchemotherapy (ie, immunosuppressed) patient with cancer. This is especially true here, where there is a more likely explanation for both the swelling (expected post-IAC orbital edema) and the fever (known preexisting bilateral otitis media). Noninfectious, post-IAC periocular inflammation is the most likely etiology for the patient’s findings. While this could be expected to gradually resolve without intervention (D), intravenous steroids hasten recovery, and thus, C is the best option for management8once the otitis media was controlled with antibiotics. Intravenous vancomycin and cefepime (A) is the treatment for infectious orbital cellulitis, which is not the correct diagnosis. Performing an examination under anesthesia (B) is unnecessary since the diagnosis of post-IAC swelling is clear and because results of bedside fundus examination were adequate. Anesthesia should be avoided when unnecessary in children, especially with active otitis media, and the child had received general anesthesia for the IAC procedure just 3 days prior. Lastly, this patient already had computed tomography performed on presentation to the emergency department due to concerns about infectious orbital cellulitis. Although unnecessary, this did not expose this child to significant harm because she had unilateral (nongermline) retinoblastoma. In contrast, in children with bilateral/germline retinoblastoma, all forms of radiation should be assiduously avoided. Children with bilateral/germline retinoblastoma are at risk of developing second (nonocular) malignancies and are highly sensitive to radiation-induced mutations. Studies report that external radiotherapy iatrogenically increases their risk of second malignancies.10 The patient started receiving dexamethasone, 1 mg, once every 6 hours for the periocular edema, which improved within 1 day, and intravenous ceftriaxone, 50 mg/kg, once for the otitis media, which resolved. She was discharged home on postoperative day 5 with an oral steroid taper. She subsequently underwent an additional IAC treatment without complication (same doses, same intravenous dexamethasone, but with oral steroid taper), leading to complete regression of her tumor.

scenario: A 64-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral proptosis and conjunctival erythema. Her medical history was significant for hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine, as well as 2 forms of hematologic malignancy: retroperitoneal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma and indolent-phase T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. She had received no treatment for her hematologic malignancies, as she had been asymptomatic since her diagnoses 6 years prior. Ophthalmological examination revealed 27 mm of bilateral proptosis, conjunctival injection, chemosis, and bilateral lower eyelid retraction (Figure 1A).1Visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary responses were normal. Extraocular motility was full in all positions of gaze, and there was no associated pain. Upper eyelid retraction was minimal. Von Graefe sign (delayed descent of the upper eyelid with initiation of downgaze) and lagophthalmos were absent. Results of slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were normal, including the appearance of both optic nerves. An orbital computed tomography scan revealed marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles (Figure 1B). Thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and thyroid peroxidase antibody levels were normal. Test results for autoimmune diseases, including sarcoidosis, Sjogren syndrome, granulomatous polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, and vasculitis, were negative.

options.C: Perform extraocular muscle biopsy
options.D: Refer for bilateral orbital external beam radiation

answer: Perform extraocular muscle biopsy
distractors: Refer for bilateral orbital external beam radiation
explanation: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia infiltration of the extraocular muscles C. Perform extraocular muscle biopsy Thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) is the most prevalent orbital disease.2Patients typically present in their fourth or sixth decade of life and women are affected 5 times more than men.2TAO is associated with autoimmune thyroid dysfunction: 90% of individuals with TAO have Graves hyperthyroidism, 1% have primary hypothyroidism, 3% have Hashimoto thyroiditis, and 5% are euthyroid.2The most common signs are upper eyelid retraction (38% to 90%) and proptosis (65%), followed by von Graefe sign, lower eyelid retraction, and lagophthalmos.3,4Active TAO may manifest with orbital pain and eyelid, conjunctival, or caruncular inflammation.4 In this study, the patient’s age, sex, hypothyroidism, proptosis, lower eyelid retraction, and inflammatory signs made TAO a likely clinical diagnosis. However, radiographic findings raised suspicion of an alternate pathology: In TAO, the inferior rectus consistently has the greatest diameter, whereas the lateral rectus has the smallest.1,5In this patient, there was marked enlargement of both lateral rectus muscles beyond that of either inferior rectus (Figure 1B).Extraocular muscle (EOM) enlargement in TAO typically appears as fusiform expansion of the entire muscle belly, sparing anterior tendinous insertions to the globe. In this patient, enlargement was predominantly confined to the posterior two-thirds of the muscle belly with rapid tapering into an unaffected anterior third. This finding has been dubbed theamphora signand may be a feature of EOM lymphoma (Figure 1B) (Dr G. Rose, MD, written correspondence, November 12, 2018).A study of 108 TAO orbits demonstrated that, although EOM diameter does not correlate well with clinically restricted ductions, when a rectus muscle diameter exceeds 8 mm, that muscle invariably yields clinical restriction.1This patient demonstrated free ductions, despite each rectus diameter exceeding 8 mm (Figure 1B).1 In TAO, the inferior rectus consistently has the greatest diameter, whereas the lateral rectus has the smallest.1,5In this patient, there was marked enlargement of both lateral rectus muscles beyond that of either inferior rectus (Figure 1B). Extraocular muscle (EOM) enlargement in TAO typically appears as fusiform expansion of the entire muscle belly, sparing anterior tendinous insertions to the globe. In this patient, enlargement was predominantly confined to the posterior two-thirds of the muscle belly with rapid tapering into an unaffected anterior third. This finding has been dubbed theamphora signand may be a feature of EOM lymphoma (Figure 1B) (Dr G. Rose, MD, written correspondence, November 12, 2018). A study of 108 TAO orbits demonstrated that, although EOM diameter does not correlate well with clinically restricted ductions, when a rectus muscle diameter exceeds 8 mm, that muscle invariably yields clinical restriction.1This patient demonstrated free ductions, despite each rectus diameter exceeding 8 mm (Figure 1B).1 Imaging inconsistent with TAO and a history of hematologic malignancy made neoplastic EOM infiltration a plausible diagnosis. Therefore, despite the associated risks, including strabismus, EOM biopsy (C) was the appropriate next step. Biopsy of the left lateral rectus revealed a pale and friable muscle densely infiltrated by small CD4+and CD8−T cells, which mirrored flow cytometry findings from the patient’s prior indolent-phase T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia diagnosis. Orbital myositis, the second most common EOM pathology, was also considered. Orbital myositis is typically a unilateral, acute, painful, diplopia-inducing disease in young women.6Although stereotypical orbital myositis can be empirically treated without biopsy,6this patient’s age and chronic, bilateral, painless presentation rendered this diagnosis unlikely. Intravenous steroids (A) are the first-line therapy for active TAO.7However, when EOMs are enlarged because of hematologic malignancy, corticosteroids may cause misleading improvement and diagnostic delay. Furthermore, prior corticosteroid use may yield false-negative histopathological results from eventual biopsy.8 Orbital decompression (B) is most commonly performed in patients with TAO who have optic neuropathy refractory to steroids, disfiguring proptosis, or corneal breakdown.7Orbital radiation (D) is currently considered a second-line therapy and may be synergistic with corticosteroids in active TAO.8Although radiotherapy may be used in the treatment of orbital hematologic malignancy, this is typically only after confirmatory histopathology. This patient was treated with oral cyclosporine. Within 3 days, EOM volume dramatically decreased and proptosis reduced bilaterally by 9 mm (Figure 2). Improvement was confirmed radiographically and sustained over 9 months of therapy, which will be continued for at least 1 year.

scenario: A 68-year-old white woman was referred for worsening floaters in both eyes starting 2 years before presentation. Her medical history included hypertension and right-sided trigeminal neuralgia. On examination, her visual acuity with habitual correction had decreased to 20/60 OD and 20/40 OS from 20/30 OU 2 years prior. A slitlamp examination revealed normal conjunctivae, nuclear sclerosis cataracts in both eyes, and deep and quiet anterior chambers. On a dilated fundus examination, there was 2+ vitreous cell and floaters in both eyes and a blonde fundus in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography imaging confirmed cystoid macular edema (CME) in both eyes; the right eye had cystoid spaces in the inner nuclear, outer plexiform, and outer nuclear layers, and the left eye had small cystoid spaces in the inner nuclear layer (Figure, A and B). Fluorescein angiography showed leakage of the optic nerve in the right eye, with petaloid leakage in the macular right eye worse than in the left eye. A uveitis workup had unremarkable or negative results for a basic metabolic panel, a complete blood cell count with a differential, Quantiferon gold test, Lyme antibody tests, an angiotensin-converting enzyme level, a serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and chest radiography. Additionally, 4 months prior, the patient developed trigeminal neuralgia, with a magnetic resonance image with contrast of the brain revealing an enhancing mass in the right middle cranial fossa, extending into the Meckel cave and abutting the right trigeminal nerve (Figure, C).

options.C: Perform a vitrectomy with cytology and immunohistochemistry
options.D: Recommend a temporal craniotomy with a brain biopsy

answer: Perform a vitrectomy with cytology and immunohistochemistry
distractors: Recommend a temporal craniotomy with a brain biopsy
explanation: C. Perform a vitrectomy with cytology and immunohistochemistry The differential diagnosis in this older woman with intermediate uveitis and negative bloodwork results includes intraocular lymphoma, sarcoid uveitis, and pars planitis. The patient’s age is inconsistent with pars planitis, which is a diagnosis of exclusion. Because the differential diagnosis includes malignant and vision-threatening conditions, further workup is required, eliminating a conservative approach (choice A). Anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injection is also not an appropriate treatment without a VEGF-mediated process, such as diabetic retinopathy or retinal vein occlusion (choice B). Given the patient’s age and concurrent intracranial lesion, primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL) must be ruled out through a diagnostic vitrectomy with cytology and immunohistochemistry (choice C). In this patient, cytology and immunohistochemistry had negative results for intraocular lymphoma. Six months later, a temporal craniotomy with a biopsy (choice D) was performed because of worsening trigeminal neuralgia, with pathology demonstrating noncaseating granulomatous lesions consistent with neurosarcoidosis. Although the biopsy was eventually performed because of worsening trigeminal neuralgia, the procedure’s inherent risks preclude it as a first-line diagnostic procedure for uveitis. Therefore, a diagnostic vitrectomy was the appropriate next step at the time of intermediate uveitis presentation. Primary intraocular lymphoma has been characterized as a masquerade syndrome because of its challenging diagnosis. This patient’s presentation was concerning for PIOL because of long-term vitreous cells in both eyes and an existing brain lesion. Primary central nervous system lymphoma presents with PIOL in up to 25% of cases, and patients diagnosed with PIOL develop central nervous system disease in up to 80% of cases.1The gold standard for diagnosis of PIOL is vitreous cytopathology, with 1 study2of 217 patients finding detection rates of 44.5% for malignant cytology and 90% for an interleukin 10:interleukin 6 ratio greater than 1.0. Additionally, optical coherence tomography may demonstrate granular subretinal lesions, while fluorescein angiography may demonstrate granular hyperfluorescence or a leopard-spot pattern of hypofluorescence.3The patient in our study presented with CME in both eyes; a study4of 17 patients found CME was associated with treated PIOL and attributable to radiation or prior intraocular surgery but found no cases of PIOL-associated CME without prior treatment or intraocular surgery. Thus, in this case, the lack of intraocular surgery and negative cytology and immunohistochemistry findings likely excludes PIOL. Of note, PIOL may respond to steroids prescribed for uveitis of other causative mechanisms; thus, this response may lead to delayed diagnosis and should not be used to rule out PIOL.5 In this patient with brain biopsy–confirmed neurosarcoidosis, chest radiography (60% sensitivity), the serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level (35% sensitivity), and the serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate (32% sensitivity) were all normal.6The patient did not have lymphopenia or endorse other commonly associated systemic symptoms, such as fatigue, weight loss, or lymphadenopathy. The patient also did not have anterior uveitis, which occurs in more than 70% of cases of ocular sarcoidosis.7In the US, sarcoidosis is classically associated with African American individuals, who are at roughly 3 times greater risk of developing the disease than white individuals.8However, worldwide, Northern European individuals, such as this patient, have the highest incidence of sarcoidosis.9Although clinical manifestations of neurosarcoidosis are heterogeneous and can affect cranial nerves, spinal cord, meninges, brain, and peripheral nerves, facial nerves are most commonly affected, as in this patient.10Initial treatment is typically oral prednisone, but cases often require escalation to second-line (methotrexate) and third-line (infliximab) treatments. Notably, facial nerve paralysis often responds to steroid monotherapy, whereas other manifestations require more aggressive treatment.10 During the initial vitrectomy, intravitreal triamcinolone was given, with resolution of CME at 1 month postsurgery. Surgical debulking of the lesion in the Meckel cave was performed in conjunction with temporal craniotomy, improving the symptoms of trigeminal neuralgia. On diagnosis of neurosarcoidosis, fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography computed tomography was performed and did not reveal further organ involvement. Six months postvitrectomy, the patient’s visual acuity had returned to her baseline of 20/30 OU, with complete resolution of CME.
